Mr Z. B. Oakes
Dr Sir
On my Return
from Charleston last week I stopd
and attended the sale of B. J. Godfrerys
at Black Creek and bought the Family
of Cash whom I purchased of you two
years ago. The woman is now in a
Family way and we think she will not
suit us for a Cook Woman, she is
a small young woman about 30 strong and
Healthy and prefers Field Work Cash
has proved himself an Excellent servant
a great Ax Man and not to be exceld
with the Hoe I can recommend him to be
a most Excellent general servant, and
now what do you think you can
get for the Family Consisting of himself
Wife and three Children say a girl of
10 or 11 year named Bella, Ceasar a boy about
4 or 5, and Rose 2 or three and Mother
in a fair way for another. Please write
and let me know what you think
you could get for them yours Truly
[underline]T. H. Marshall[/underline]

Thanksgiving! How many ideas that word brings
to mind, It's like dropping a stone in a pond,
the ripples spread out in circles, each followed
by another and another and another, Memories.
People, Places, And things to be thankful for,

In these days of constant chafing sometimes
it may seem as though there aren't many things
left for which to be thankful. At the risk of
seeming Pollyanna-ish, let's think upon some of
the things we have to be thankful for.

Be thankful for personal health; some people
have more than others, but it is seldom diffi-
cult to find someone worse off than yourself,
so be thankful for the abilities you have,

Be thankful for the opportunity to live and
work, The place where you are may not be ideal;
indeed, it is probably not. But it's the best
we have, our world,

Be thankful for family and loved ones. Good
personal relationships are the basis of civili-
zation. Without them there is no incentive to
strive to improve the world. Those with a "So
what?" attitude are barren of love and can
neither give nor receive it.

*Be thankful for an opportunity to mend a rift
between yourself and someone with whom you
should be sharing joy; put anger or pride behind
you, reach out and make amends,

Be thankful for the happiness you can give to
someone else, There is no surer way to feeling
the glow of satisfaction than seeing another
person fulfilled, i

Be thankful for the ability to forgive, to
understand, to accept the imperfections of
others. They, too, have difficulty making ad-
justments to this less-than-perfect world.

Be thankful there are qualities of kindness,
honesty, decency and trust to be found in every-
one you know, even if they don't agree with you,
don't live their lives as you wish to live
‘yours, don't give as much weight to your views
and opinions as you would wish.

 

 
 
Be thankful for the beauties ana poufities. of
mature, This is our world; most of the thing
wrong with it result from changes man has made
in it. What man has done wrong, man can make
right.

Be thankful for freedoms we enjoy. In order
to protect them we must protect those of people
with whom we do not always agree. Denying
another's rights ultimately results in the ero-
sion of our own,

Be thankful for feelings of guilt which serve
to bring understanding between peoples of dif-
fering views and make possible improvement in
human relationships.

Be thankful for work; it is the fabric of
purpose. Lack of purpose is uselessness, The
world's unhappiest people are those who feel no
purpose to their lives,

Be thankful for grief, the heart's ease in
time of loss and sorrow which come to us all,

Be thankful for hope. Tomorrow will not
solve all ills, but may bring sur-cease from
the one troubling you most, j

Be thankful for charity; your opportunity to
lighten the burden of your fellowman, :

Be thankful for friendships for they support
us in our bleakest hours and give hope and pur-
pose to otherwise empty futures,

Be thankful for memories. Cherish them,

They give pattern and color and direction to
your life,

It's a different kind of list from the oné
we usually think of at Thanksgiving, isn't it?
Happy Thanksgiving! : :

commonwealth:dv1441451.text:
The Refuge of Oppression
There never has been any part of the Liberator more instructive
to the abolitionist than the portion bearing the title at the
head of this article. The readers of the paper seek it with avidity
second only to that with which they turn to the editorial department.
It is the dark corner of the sheet rendered more dark
by the contiguity of light which the columns containing the
anti-slavery matter cast upon it. Darkness made visible,
standing out in bold relief before the eyes even of those
whose vision is unannointed with eye salve.
The Slaveocrat who loves to see the same matter conspicuous
in the [deletion]proslavery[/deletion] columns of the proslavery press, writhes
in the anguish of impotent rage when he sees these malevolent
productions quietly consigned to this open prison, with the full
glare of the light of impartial liberty shining upon them. - He
then sees his own thoughts in their true colors; the character of
his own soul drawn by a faithful hand. He turns from his
own picture in an agony, but it is an agony of rage and hate
towards that light which faithfully reveals the darkness [deletion]which[/deletion]
which seeks concealment in the mists of prejudice and malevolence.
He feels tormented before his time; stung by his own
weapon; wounded by his own dagger and the torments of the
lost spirits take hold of him.
The unmistakeable truth which intuitively consigns to their
proper place all who rightfully belong to that peculiar department
is most clearly [deletion]is most clearly[/deletion] perceived by two classes
of persons - The slaveholder who would conceal from all the
world the iniquity of manstealing and the uncompromising
abolitionist who would hurl the bloody Moloch from his throne
of sculls over the Tarpean rock of immediate and unconditional
emancipation - regardless of consequences - to cotton and sugar,
to political parties and theological sects, to the Union of
churches and the Union of States - regardless of all consequences
but human liberty and the triumph of truth.

Between these two extremes the proslavery shades tho' intimately
blended yet so gradually deepen or fade as we approach the
one or the other that many persons are at a loss to know their
own position or to determine to which class they properly belong,
and are desirous to show that they do not belong to either; but
the extremes instinctively perceive them to be upon the side of
oppression.
Calhoun Hammond Clay and Preston wince not
at being charged with supporting the bloody system of oppression,
for in it they behold their chief glory and in their eyes a Garrison
abolitionist is the very incarnation of all that they most hate
and dread. In any thing short of that they perceive a gleam
of hope for the continued existence of the sum of all villanies.
Let the people once become Garrisonized and they plainly
see that their idol must fall; that no blustering, no threatenings,
no wheedling, no wailing, can soften their obdurate hearts in
favor of the peculiar institution. Hence at the perception of
the progress of this kind of anti-slavery they cry out in despair
"there is no hope; there is no hope" To put far off the day of its
triumph is their chief desire for they know that this is a
spirit that cannot be laid, an apparition that "will not down
at any man's bidding" It cares not for the errors of antiquity nor
holds any of them sacred. It regards not the opinions nor the
acts of fathers, either dead or living. It bows not [deletion]before the[/deletion] before
judges however honored in life, however distinguished in name.
It reverences no constitutions, no unions, no sects, no orders, no
institutions, that compromise away a single little of man's
inalienable rights
Against this kind of anti-slavery every shade of
proslavery unites. Tho differing in all things else never
so widely, here they find a platform sufficiently broad for
union of all parties, all sects, all that have any sympathy
with and for oppression, from the "shadow of a shade" to
the "blackness of darkness"
Does the slaveholder hear the system spoken

against as an evil? he likes not that. Does he hear the same
lips curse the folly or the fanaticism of abolitionists? Here
they agree and he feels safe. Does he hear a wish expressed
that God in his own good time will bring this "curse of curses" to
an end? He feels a fluttering at his heart. Does he hear the
same lips declare that tho' the sins of slaveholders be many,
the sins of the abolitionists are not a few? He breathes easier
and says there is yet time. Does he hear another say I am
an abolitionist? He trembles. Does he hear the same person
say "I am for gradual emancipation"? He feels there is no danger.
Does he hear any one say I am for immediate emancipation?
He turns pale with rage. Does he hear the same person say
I am against attacking the Church and am for preserving
the Union? He responds "amen for these are our bulwarks".
Does he hear some one say I am for emancipation, but, I
think the slaveholders ought to be paid? He feels perfectly
secure untill he is ready to sell out. Does he hear a
cry to let the oppressed go free regardless of consequences?
and without compensation? He starts up in terror and
his eyes stand out with fear. Does hear the same voice
denounce all organized action and call[deletion]ing[/deletion] upon each
man and woman to act individually and without concert?
He takes hold of his neighbors & bloody hand and says "no
fear from them, for in our union there is strength and even there
oppression finds a refuge. Does he hear a voice crying
"I am a Garrisonian. No Union with slaveholders"? He
sends forth the yell of a lost spirit shrieking, "a
price upon his head; there is no hope; there is no hope".
Does he hear any speak against the Garrisonians?
His hands and his feet applaud, whoever the
speaker may be for he knows that there oppression has
a refuge. Does he hear any sentiment uttered by
a Garrisonian in answer to opposition from any

source of any character and of any profession whatever?
He answers with a hiss and a curse drawn from the depths
of hell. None know better than he the true anti-slavery
compass, always pointing to the pole. None have a deeper conviction
than he that here is the only hope of the slave. None
exercise more faith than he tho' like the devils he believes
and trembles - and with this evidence of the true anti-slavery
standard before me, I hope always to sing
I am a Garrisonian
I glory in the name.
But when I see Wm Lloyd Garrison receiving any
defence from the minions of slavery, when I hear him
lauded by the haters of the anti-slavery enterprise for
sentiments uttered against abolitionists then I
shall think him deserving of a place in the
Refuge of Oppression.
Mrs Chapman
I have written these few lines for
the Liberty Bell if you think proper to
receive them
Yours for liberty
D S Grandin

Mrs M W Chapman

Charleston Nov 30, 1853
Dear Sir
I regret exceedingly not being able
to see [insertion]you[/insertion] in relation [insertion]to[/insertion] the sale of Mr Odum plantation,
There can be no doubt that the place
will in the course of Twelve months bring $ 4,000
Dollars that is if divided in [underline]four equal Farms[/underline]
of 120 acres each, the Rail Road passes directly
through it, the Land is of the first Quality and
abounds in the finest Oak & Hickory wood
which can be delivered in Charleston by Ra. Ro.
at a cost to the owner of [underline]only $ 2 per cord[/underline], These
and other good reasons render it desireable
that the sale should be postponed and the property
not forced into Market, Mr Odum wishes
you to take up the Judgement debt to Yeadon, McBeth
Beth & Ford, and to advance her some two or
three hundred dollars besides, securing yourself
by the Judgement and if necessary a mortgage
of the property, redeemable at the expiration
of Twelve months if the the property should
not be disposed of to advantage [underline]by you[/underline] before -
in the hope Dear Sir that & she will have
to seek no further [deletion]fr[/deletion]than to yourself for this favor
which I shall ever acknowledge with gratitude
I Remain Most Truly Yours

Wednesday morn July 12 1854
Dear Sir
I drop you a line in a great
hurry by Mr McCulley to say my affairs
are going very well, and I have been
offered $ 500 or $ 1.00 per acre for the tract of
land you purchased at sherriff sale.
I think you can do better, the offer is made by
Mr Williams, who owns the adjoining tract
which he purchased of Mc Culley he
gets Serpentine and work about 30 Hands
yours truly in haste
Theod C Tharin
Z. B. Oakes Esq.

commonwealth:w3764957b.text:
Grumesville Sept 11 [insertion]th[/insertion] 1856
Dear Sir
The Deputy has been here since
day before yesterday, and it is impossible
to get hold of the negroes, I have advised
that the parties should go down & see you
they seem willing to consent that the fellow
Tom should go at $ 1000, and a smaller boy
at $ 300 - but a new party entered the
field and recommended a seperance
to Major Rhame - who wants the boys
himself, he is to be requested to go
down and confer with the judgement
creditors and buy them, or propose to
sell out the entire Estate and pay pro-ratio,
the creditors, I presume that
all this could be done better by yourself
and make no doubt a ballance
of some 2,000 dollars retained, I advise
that you should when applied
to take the whole Estate in hand by &
with the Consent of Judgement Creditors
and save the Commission, I could
then speculate on the sale if forced
under the [deletion]e[/deletion]sheriff -
in Lords - yours truly
Theo. C Tharin

commonwealth:w3764352q.text:
Grumesville July 20. 1854
Dear Sir
Yours of the 10th & 12th inst came safely to
hand last night, we do not send oftener than once
a week to the post office, and my deputy is the
nly one of the family that can read, and he is
very seldom at home, and very often our messenger
returns without our papers and letters, this must
by my appology for not replying immediately,
although I sent twice myself I did not get
them, untill a friend called for his, and took
mine out and sent them to me, I think when
I see you I will give a good account of myself
together with the matter you entrusted me with
I am aware of all you have done for Sterling
Doing ?field and how all matters stand, and
you may rely all will be so arranged [deletion]so[/deletion] as
to meet you Views, fully, (and perhaps much earlier
than you suppose), I will bring him down with
me on the first of July next when I come for a
settlement of my contract, at the present [deletion]time[/deletion]
I have every moment of time so occupied in
stacking and getting my timber ready for inspection
that I dine in the woods every day
and seldom get home before midnight
The wages of the hands becoming due on the 5th inst
I made free to use a part of your money and the

 and the Ballance with all other obligatory and Kind
favors I will have to make straight when I see you
you will no doubt feel hurt at this step of
mine but when you consider all things, and that
upon this very step our mutual safety & welfare
depended, why like General Jackson at orleans
I take the Responsibility, and time I hope
will alike prove I was Right
with much Esteem & Regard
I Remain faithfully yours
Theo. C Tharin

Mount Holly } {Three Mount Holly PCV
June 22 { Theo C Tharin PCV
Z.B. Oakes Esq
Charleston

has promised me to sign the other if you think
is necessary, this he assures me he done on the
[underline]27[/underline] [insertion]th[/insertion] [underline]inst[/underline] while in the Sheriffs office, I hope it is
all right, If not write me by return mail and
I will be down upon him for the execution of
the one you sent me and which I have retained
untill I hear from you, I am very busy getting
all things ready, I do not expect to be down before the
5th August unless our Engineer is more at leasure
till which time believe me yours
Most truly
Theo. C Tharin
Z. B. Oakes Esq

commonwealth:vm40xs173.text:
Grumesville Oct 16, 1854
Dear Sir
I have had the good fortune to
 arrange matters satisfactory for my negroe
hire, [deletion]and wo[/ deletion] without again trespassing
on your generosity. Mr Brownfield
(our inspector) has left some three weeks
since for the upCountry & will not be
here again for one month at least. I
can therefore present no claim for work
done, I will push matters all I can and
confer with the direction, in relation
to Mr B. absence and they will I trust
adopt some method to have the inspection
made by that time
Yours Most Truly
Theo. C Tharin

commonwealth:9k41zk125.text:
Charleston 1-6 Dec 1853
Mr Z. B. Oakes,
Dear Sir
I would be glad
to know what you have
determined on in the case
of M Alpine, I bot the
negro from you, it appears
and of course you are
liable to me, I am called
on for the amount of the
verdict, It appears that the
negro was a stolen one. I
of course lay no charge to
you on this score, being accessory
to the affair, but I
do call on on you to
hold me Harmless. - Please
send me your written answer
[underline]this day.[/underline]
Respectfully
[underline]Tho: N. Gadsden[/underline]

Summerville So Ca
April 26th 1854
Mr Z B Oakes
Dear Sir
Your letter
in reply to mine was duly received.
I am willing to value the woman at
$ 800. & be refunded $ 150. or return her
at once to you. Do inform me as soon
as possible as to the decision of
her owner. Yours respectfully
Thos. L Gelzia

 Dear Sir I am Sorry to inform you that

Charleston November 10th 1856
Respected Sir,
I herewith return you the Map of the
State of South Carolina, which you had the kindness to
loan me, accompanied with my sincere thanks for the same.
I have completed my feeble and perhaps presumptuous attempt
in taking a copy with pen and brush. I must apologize for
having kept it so long, as I could only it work on it in leisure
hours at home. I shall feel complimented my dear Sir, if
you will take the trouble to glance at it, as I intend to send
in to the Institute as a humble specimen, from your
young acquaintance.
[underline]Thomas. W. Mordecai. Jr[/underline]
To,
Z.B. Oakes Esq.

The motion was advocated by the
Hon. Messrs Brooks, Welles, Dwight
and Pick-mam; and was opposed by the

ker. We have not time to give the

wealth ; while, at the same time, if the
act of reparation is to Be fulfilled, as

Commission established by that act y for

in common, would not fall short of
SIO,OOO a year. That by the ratifica
tion of the agreement, this annual ex
pense would be saved; and, at the same
time, as the amount to Be paid and'al
lowed by Maine, for the lands, will ex
ceed $200,000, there would be, instead
of this expense, an annual income of
more than that sum. On the other
hand, it was contended that the bar
gain was a hard one for Massachusetts;

emigration, which had set solongfrom

scarce in other States; that there was
every prospect, that lands in Maine
would be in greater demand ; and that,
if the Legislature refused to ratify this

bargain, a -much (better one would at
any time be consented to by Maine.

that the Court was ready

The President rose, and pronounced
the following
JUDGMENT.
Tins Court, for the trial of Impeach
ments, having found James Prescott
guilty of misconduct and mal-adminis
tration in the office of Judge of Probate
of Wills and for granting Letters of Ad
ministration within and for the County
of Middlesex, charged'upon him in the
Third Article and Twelfth Article of
Impeachment, as charged ; against him
by the House of Representatives : It
is considered by this Court; that the
said James Prescott be removed from
the office of J udge as aforesaid, and he
is removed accordingly.
The Court was then adjourned with
out day.
The following are the Articles of
which Judge Prescott has been convict
ed and removed from office.
ARTICLE HI.
“ That said James Prescott, Esq. Judge as
aforesaid, on the second day of Augnst, A. D.
eighteen hundred and nineteen, at his said
office, in Groton, aforesaid, and : not at any
Probate Court, held according* to law, did de
cree and grant Letters of Administration upon
the estate of one Eri Rogers, to one Benjamin
Dix, Esq. and thereupon did' issue a warrant
to appraise said estate ; and the said Prescott
did, then there, and- corruptly, de
mand a'U receive of said Administrator, as
and for the fees of his said'office, in the busi
ness aforesaid, other and greater fees than are
by law allowed therefor, to wit: the sum of
Five Dollars and Seventy Cents. And that
the said Prescott, on the nineteenth day of
said 'August, at his said office in Groton, a
foresaid, and not at any Probate Court held
according to law, did receive the said Admin
istrator’s return of the Inventory of said es
tate ; and, then and there, did decree and grant
a Commission of Insolvency, upon the Estate
aforesaid ; and the said Prescott did, then and
there, wilfully and corruptly receive from said
Dix, other and greater, fees than are bylaw
allowed for the business aforesaid, to wit: the
sum of Thirty-nine Dollars and two Cents.”
ARTICLE XIL
“That' at a Probate Court, holden by the
said Prescott, on’, the twenty-ninth day of
June, in the year of our Lord one thousand
eight hundred’ and fifteen, at Framingham,
in said County of Middlesex, one Alpheus
Ware, who before had been, and then was,
guardian of one’Jotham Breck, a person non
compos mentis, was about presenting his ac
-count of his guardianship of his said wardjfor
allowance, and thereupon a 1 controversy arose
between the said Ware and one Nathan Grout,
,who, as one of the Overseers of the Poor of
the town in which the said Breck had his
settlement, attended the said Court to exam
ine said accounts, respecting some property
belonging to the ward of said Ware, and
thereupon the raid Prescott,. overhearing the
conversation between the said Ware and tlje
said Gtout, respecting the said ward’s estate,
proposed to advise and ipstruct’thnm therein ;
and thereupon the said Prescott, being then
and there Judge as aforesaid, did advise with
and direct the raid Ware and the said Grout,
concerning the settlement of the account afore

Austrian"manifesto.
[From the Baltimore Morning
We publish to-day the Austrian Manifesto ;
and it may be generally remarked, that the
State papers, from this quarter, are drawn up
with a vigour, force and eloquence, unrivalled
by all the European monarchs. But there is
evident anxiety and alarm displayed amongst
the Allied powers. They talk of the Carbo
nari and of a few partizans and mal-contents,
as having accomplished the Neapolitan rev
olution. Yet, against this force,’ so ioconsid- '
erable, they state that the Emperotir of Rus- '
sia is ready to take the field with all his forces,
whenever his interference becomes necessary.
This is a tremendous power to array against a
few daring vagabonds, as these allies would
fain represent those who have prostrated the ;
Government of Naple. The Allies go on to .
complain that plans subversive of the old aud .
settled order of things in Europe are daily i
gaining strength and notoriety, with which it ,
is contended that no government can exist, j
“ Hine illae lychrymae. n What are these !
plans, these projects, these deep and danger- ;
ous designs, so alarming to crowned heads ? ■
They are nothing more nor less than the pro- .
gress of republican sentiments throughout !
—sentiments, it must candidly be confessed, !
utterly hostile to the doctrine that “ Kings >
inherit a divine right to govern wrong ” — ’
These things are no novelties to the ears of
Americans. We are .al most one century in ad
vance of such courtly nonsense. During our
revolutionary war, every man who fought for
the security of his friends and altar was denom
inated a rebel—every exertion made in our
defence was rebellious. Our wives, our hus
bands, and our smiling infants, were all reb
els in the estimation of the subjects of our
legitimate sovereign, King George the third.
Indeed the term rebel was in our revolution
ary day so ludicrously applied, that ft was
thus happily hit off, at the time, by an Amer
ican poet— *
“ The rebel vales, the rebel dales
With rebel hills surrounded,
The rebel woods, the rebel flood
With rebel echoes sounded.”
No, it is not Spain—no, it is not Sicily and
Naples—that now excite these commotions a
mongst the allied monarchs, or accelerate
their appeal to arms. It is something more
deep, more tenacious and more formidable.—
It is, that these monarchs observe, in the dif
fusion of such principles, the shaking of their
own thrones—the dissolution of their own
dynasties—and they now exclaim against the
Carbonari, against the treason, exactly on
the same principles as the invading subjects
of King George exclaimed against American
rebels during our revolutionary war. It is
American rebellion, or, in other words, the
resumption of natural right; the right of the
people to reform, to re-cast, re-fashion and re
mould their own government. This is the
American rebellion in which the Sovereigns of'
Europe discover, and at no distant day, the
downfall of their own dynasties. But what
dactrne dp these gentle monarchical swains
Urge in opposition to all this ? They maintain
the right of one independent Sovereign, at
his own will and pleasure, to over-run the
dominions of another independent Sovereign ;
to dictate laws and to form constitutions for
this independent people. Such are, without
any periphrasis, the opinions advanced in the
Austrian Manifesto, which is now to be pro
mulgated at the point of the bayonet. We
can but believe that this Manifesto, at this
time avowed and promulgated, is more dan
gerous to the Allied Sovereigns, than either
the Spanish, Portuguese, or the Neapolitan
revolutions. It is in the face of enlightened
Europe, boldly and broadly to assert a claim
a claim in defiance of reason and of common
sense, which never can be admitted for a mo
ment, unless we are prepared to plunge
amidst the darkness of the middle ages a
gain. There is no deception on this point,
and there can be none. The allied powers
have, undoubtedly, the same right to declare
that America is governed by a faction, who
have imposed upon them a Constitution differ
ent from the English, and to require, as an
ultimatum, immediate return to the govern
ment of our lawful Sovereign and in case of
non-compliance, to enforce this obedience at
the point of the bayonet. Yet these American
rebelshave their ministers abroad openly ac
knowledged as such in tire Courts of these very
monarchs themselves. Our alliance has been
courted by these very Kings who now threaten
the extinguishment of the Neapolitan revolu
tion, and we now have with most of them,
entered into treaties of amity and commerce.
Here is at least one example acknowledged
by the allied powers themselves, that a gov
ernment may be reformed by the inten ention
of the people, capable of maintaining with
other independent powers the customary re
lations of amity and peace. We are, there
fore, perfectly serious in this declaration, that
we look upon the Austrian manifesto, and the
principles contained in that paper, as by far
more alarming to the repose of Europe, aud
endangering the (quietude of the reigning dy •
nasties, than either the Spanish, the Pcrtu
tuguese, or the Neapolitan involutions.

This, was case ; and the Declaration alleg
ed that the Plaintiff, at the time of commenc
ing his suit, and long before, was a Minister of
the Gospel, settled over the First Congrega
tional Society in Worcester; and that the
Defendant, with an intent to injure him in his
ministerial office, had charged him with em
bezzling, or keeping back, the funds of a cer
tain Society of Ladies in Worcester, called the
Female Western Mission Society, and also the
funds of the Asylum for Deaf and Dumb Per
sons—which were placed in his hands, to be
appropriated in the manner designed by those
who contributed them; and the material alle
gations were as follows“ On the first day of
January, 1820, at said Worcester, in a dis
course which he, the said Moses, then and
there had with divers good citizens of this
Commonwt alth—of and concerning the Plain
tiff, so being a Minister of the Gospel—of and
concerning the said Female Western Mission
Society, and the funds thereunto belonging—
of and concerning the said Asylum for the Ed
ucation of Deaf and Dumb Persons, and the
monies voluntarily contributed in aid thereof,
by the inhabitants of said First Parish—in the
presence and hearing of said citizens, did o
penly utter and publish, in a significant man
ner—and concerning the Plaintiff, in the dis
course aforesaid, the following false, scanda
lous, and defamatory words, to wit:— ‘ Good- :
rich (meaning the Plaintiff) has kept back ‘
(meaning concealed and fraudulently detain- I
ed) fifteen dollars, (meaning fifteen dollars be- i
longing to said Female Western Mission Socie
ty) and three one-dollar bills contributed for
the Hartford Asylum, (meaning three one-dol
lar bills raised by voluntary contribution, in j
said First Parish, in aid of said Institution, I
commonly called the Hartford Asylum for the
Education of Deaf and Dumb Persons, as a
foresaid) which (meaning said bills) were said
to be counterfeit ; but they (meaning said •
bills) were good money. It (meaning said
bank bills and money) has never been heard
of since, (meaning that they have never beeri
accounted for;) and, further, meaning and in
sinuating by said words, and the manner of
uttering the same, that the Plaintiff had wrong
fully and fraudulently detained and kept in
his possession the said money belonging to said
Society, and the said bills so contributed, and
acted otherwise unjustly, deceitfully, and dis
honourably.”
The Detendant plead the general issue—
not guilty— The trial was had before Chief
Justice Parker ; and the Defendant object
ed that the words set forth in the Declaration
were not, when taken in their natural sense,
defamatory; and as they could not be aided
by the inuendoes in giving to them a meaning
different from their common import, they
were not therefore actionable; as, to
charge another with keeping back mon
ey, does not necessarily imply crime, or
imprite to the one so keeping it back any
moral wrong. But the Court overruled the
abjection, observing that as it was alleged in
the Declaration that the Plaintiff was a Minis
ter of the Gospel, and the monies which were
said to be kept back were contributed in aid
of charitable institutions, the words them
selves, without inuendoes, were actionable.
1 he Plaintiff then proved, by a number of
witnesses, the speaking of the words, substan
tially, as set forth in the Declaration, and
many circumstances indicating malice.
The Defendant Called no witnesses.
The Judge summed up the evidence in
an able and lucid manner, and instructed the
jury that if they were satisfied that the words
were spoken by the Defendant with a malic
ious intent to injure the Plaintiff, if was their
duty to return such damages as they, in the
exercise of their discretion, should think prop
er-taking care not to ruin the Defendant,
nor to send the Plaintiff out of Court wi'hout
an indemnity for the expense he had been at,
and in some measure for the injury he had
received.
The jury retired about 7 o’clock in the even
ing (when the Court adjourned) and came in,
at the opening in the morning, with a verdict
of Guilty, and damages 775 dollars.

Hardwick, April 23. 1821.A short time since we informed our readers
that the family of the late President Dwight,
'of Yale College, intended in the ensuing sum*
mer, to publish his travels in the State of New-
York, and the New-England States ; and stat
ed that we should publish, occasionally, some
extracts from the manuscripts, as specimens of
the manner in which the work is executed.—
The author took great pains, in the course of
his various excursions, to collect as much in
formation of the early history of our country,
and as many facts and anecdotes of the in
habitants, particularly during the period of In
dian warfare, as was in Lis power. In this he
was more suc'-essfnl than could have been ex
pected ; and it will probably be owing to his
exertions that many very interesting events,
■which occurred in the first centttry after the
settlement of the country by white inhabit
ants, are not in a great measure lost even to
the present generation. The following ac
count of the sufferings and heroism of one
family in Massachusetts will, we have no doubt,
be read with interest. The events here narrated
took place a little more than one hundred and
twenty years ago. The mind can scarcely real
ise the fact, that the oldest paris of our country
were, even at that period, liable to these sav
age invasions ; and yet such was the case
many years subsequently to the time here
mentioned-. One great object of the author of
these travels was to show the progress of our
conntty, in all the interests and circumstances
of civilization and improvement, from its first
settlement to the date of his observations.

Story of Mr. and Mrs. Dustan.
[From President Dwightls Travels.]
Fol. I.—Letter XL.
“Haverhill was Settled in the year 1637,
and incorporated in 1645. During the first
seventy-five years from its settlement it suffer
ed often, and greatly, by savage depredations.
The story of these depredations is, however,
i nperfectly known at the present tune. Even
the facts w hich are still known, are so dispers
ed in the possession of different persons, as to
render it very difficult to obtain them correct
ly. This kind of knowledge is daily becom
ing less, and will soon be lost. It is much to
be wished that inquisitive men, throughout
this country, would glean and preserve the
little which is left. It is a serious and unfor
tunate errour of men in general to suppose
that events, familiarized to themselves by fire
side repetition, will be uninteresting to others ;
and that efforts to preserve them will be con
sidered as either trifling or arrogant. In no
country, probably, are the inhabitants more
inquisitive than in New-England. But their
inquiries terminate, or have until lately ter
minated, chiefly in things remote in time or
place ; and have been very little occupied by
subjects pertaining to their own country. It
is, perhaps, natural to man to feel that his
own ewem!, or any concerns which are fa
miliar to him, will be little regarded by those
who come after him. Few parents are solici
tous to have their own portraits taken ; yet,
after their decease, scarcely any legacy is
Qiougbt more valuable by their children.
In the year 1697, on the sth day of March,
a body of Indians attacked this town—burned
a small number of houses—and killed aid
captivated about forty of the inhabitants. A
party of them, arrayed in all the terrours of the
Indian war dress, and carrying with them the
multiplied honours of a savage invasion, ap
proached near to the house of a Mr. Dustan.
'i his man was abroad, at his usual labour.—
Upon the first alarm, he flew to the house, with
a hope of hurrying to a place of safety his
family, consisting of his wife, who had been
confined a week only in child-bed, her nurse,
a Mrs. Mary Tass, a widow from the neigh
bourhood, and children. Seven of his
children he ordered to flee with the utmost ex
pedition, in the course opposite to that in which
the danger wa's approaching, and went himself
to assist his wife. Before she could leave her
bed the savages were upon them. Her hus
band. despairing of rendering her any service,
flew to the door, mounted his horse, and de
termined to snatch up the child, with which
be was unable to part, when he should over
take the little flock. When he came up to I
them, about two hundred yards from his house,
he was unable to make a choice, or to leave
airy one of the number. He, therefore, de
temined to take his lot with them, and to de
t°nd them from their mrgderers, or die by their
side. A body of Indians pursued and came
up with him ; and from near distances Cred at
him and bis liftle company. He returned the
fire, and retreated, alternately. For more than
a mile he kept so resolute a face to his ene
my, retiring in the rear of his charge—return
ed the fire of the savages so often, and with so
good success—and sheltered so effectually his
terrified companions—that he finally lodged
all, safe from, the pursuing butchers, in a
distant house. When it is remembered how
numerous Ins assailants were ; how bold,
when an overmatch for their enemies ; how
active ; and what excellent marksmen ; a de
vout mind will consider the hand of Providence
as unusually visible in the preservation of this
family.
Another party of the Indians entered the
house immediately after Mr. Dustan had quit
ted it, and found Mrs. Dustan, md her nurse,
who was attempting to fly with the child in her
arms. Mrs'. Dmtan they ordered to rise in
stantly ; and before she could completely
dress herself, obliged her and her companion to
quit the house, after they had plundered it
and set it o > fire. In company with several
other captives, they began their march into
the wilderness; she, feeble, tick, terrified be
yond measure, partially clad, one of her feet
bare, and the season unfit for comfortable trav
elling. The air was chilly and keen, and the
earth covered, alternately, with snow and deep
mud. Her conductors were unfeeling, inso
lent and revengeful. Murder was their glory,
and torture their sport. Her infant was in her
nurse’s arms ; and infants were the customary
victims of savage barbarity.
The company had proceeded but a short
distance, when an Indian, thinking it an in
cumbranoe, took the child out of the nurse’s
arms and das’jed its head against a tree.—
What were then the feelings of the inotiier 1
Such of the other captives as began to be
weary and to lag, the Indians tomahawked.—
The slaughter was not an act of rev'enge nor
of cruelty. It was a mere convenience ; an
effort so familiar as not even to excite an emo
tion.
Feeble as Mrs. Dustan was, both she and
her nur-e sustained, without yielding, the fa
tigue of her journey. Their intense distress
for the death of the child, and of their com
venions ; anxiety for those whom they had
left behind ; and unceasing terrour for them-

(selves, raised these tmhappy women to such
a degree of vigour, that, notwithstanding their
fatigue, their exposure to cold, their sufferance
of hunger, ai.d their sleeping on damp ground
under an inclement sky, they finished an expe
dition of about one hundred and fifty miles,
without losing their spirits or injuring their
health.
The wigwam to which they were conducted,
and which belonged to the savage who had
claimed them as his property, was inhabited
by twelve person'. In the month of April
this family set out with their captives for a
settlement still more remote; and informed
them that, when they r»rived at the settle
ment, they must be stripped, scourged, and
run the gauntlet, naked, between two files of
Indians, containing the whole number found
in the settlement; for such they declared was
tlie standing custom of their nation. This in
formation, you will believe, made a deep im
pression on the minds of the captive women,
and led them, irresistibly, to devise all the
possible means of escape. On the 31st of the
same month, very early in the morning, Mrs.
Dustan, while the Indians were asleep, hav
ing awaked her nurse, and a fellow prisoner,
(a youth, taken sonic time before, from Wor
cester,) dispatched, with the assistance of her
companions, ten of the twelve Indians. The
other two escaped. With the scalps of these
savages they returned through the wilderness ;
and having arrived safely at and,
afterwards, a( Boston, received a handsome re.
ward for their intrepid couduct from the Leg
islature.
Whether all their sufferings, and all the dan
ger of suffering anew, justified the slaughter,
may probably be questioned by you, or some
other exact moralist. Precedents innumera
ble, and of high authority, may indeed be
urged in behalf of these captives ; but the
moralist will equally question the rectitude of
these. Few persons, however, agonizing as
Mrs. Dustan did, under the evils she had al
ready suffered, and in the full apprehension of
those which she was destined to suffer, would
have been able to act the part of nice casu
ists ; and fewer still, perhaps, would have
exercised her intrepidity. That she herself
approved of the conduct, which was applaud
ed by the magistrates and divines of the day,
in the cool hours of deliberation, cannot be
doubted. The truth is, the season of Indian
invasion, burning, butchering, captivity, threat
ening and torture, is an unfortunate time for
nice investigation, and critical mondizing. A
wife, who has just seen her bouse burned, her
infant dashed against a tree, and her compan
ions coldly murdered, one by one—who sup
posed her husband and her remaining children
to have shared the same fate—who was threat
ened with torture, and indecency more painful
than torture—and who did not entertain a
doubt that the threatening would be ful
filled—would probably feel no necessity, when
she found it in her power, to dispatch the au
thors of her sufferings, of asking questions
concerning any thing but the success of the
enterprize.

But, whatever may be thought of the rec
titude of her conduct, that of her husband is
in every view honourable. A finer succession
of scenes for the pencil was hardly ever pre
sented to the eye, than was furnished by the
efforts of this gallant man, with their interest
ing appendages. The artist must be destitute
indeed of talents, who could not engross eve
ry heart, as well as every eye, by exhibitions
of this husband and father, flying to rescue his
wife, her infant, and her nurse, from the ap
proaching horde of savages ; attempting, on
his horse, to select from his flying family the
child which he whs the least able to spare,
and unable to make the selection ; facing, in
their rear, the horde of hell-hounds ; al
ternately and sternly retreating behind his in
estimable charge, and fronting the enemy a
gain ; receiving and returning their fire, and
presenting himself, equally as a barrier against
murderers, and a shelter to the flight of inno
cence and anguish. In the back ground of
some or other of these pictures, might be ex
hibited, with powerful impression, the kindled
dwelling ; the sickly mother ; the terrified
nurse, with the new-born infant in her arms ;
and the furious natives, surrounding them,
driving them forward, and displaying the troph
ies of savage victory, aud the insolence of
savage triumph.”

LIBEL ON HER MAJESTY.
Mr. Brougham applied to the Court
for a rule to shew cause why a criminal
inform ation should not be filed against
the Rev. R. Blacow, M. A. He made
this motion upon the affidavit of A. Mil
ler, of Liverpool, who savore that, on
the 27th of January last, he bought, at
the shop of a bookseller in that town,
the pamphlet, the title of which was as
follows: “ The substance of the dis
course preached at the Church of St.
Mark, Liverpool, by the Rev. R. Blacow,
M. A. on Sunday evening, the 2Gth of
November last, upon the present aspect
of the times, with additional notes and
an appendix, bearing upon the radical
question.” The affidavit further states,
that the deponent on the same day pro
duced it to the said R. Blacow, M. A.
who admitted that he was the author of
it, an’.that he preached it.
Mr. Justice Bayley. —“ That he preach
ed it; but did he admit that he publish
ed it ?”
Mr. Brougham— “ My Lord, he ad
mitted this—that he was the author of
the sermon, as stated and contained in
the said pamphlet.”
Chief Justice Abbot. —“ Well, go on.”
Mr. Brougham said the Court would
collect the import of the publication
from the extract which he should read.
“ The Radicals have one feature a
bout them, even more hideous ’and dis
gusting than the Jacobins themselves.
They fell down, and worshipped the
goddess of reason—a most respectable
and decent sort of being, compared with
that which the Radicals have set up as
the idol of their worship. They have ele
ele vated the goddess of Lust on the pedes
tal of shame—an object, of all others, the
most congenial to their taste—-the most
deserving of their homage—the most wor
thy of their adoration. After exhibiting
her claims to their favour in two distant

quarters of the globe—after compass
ing sea and land with her gmlty para
mour, to gratify to the fill her impure
desires, and even polluting the Holy
Sepulchre itself with her presence, to
which she was carried in mock majesty
astride upon an ass, she returned to this
hallowed soil, so hardened in sin, so
bronzed with infamy, so callons to eve
ry feeling of decency or of shame, as to
go on Sunday last, clothed in the mantle
of adultery, to kneel down at the altar
of that God who is ‘ of purer eyes than
to behold iniquity’—when she ought to
have stood bare-footed in the aisle, cov
ered with a sheet as white as ‘ unsunned
snow,’ doing penance for her sins. Till
this had been done, I would never have
defiled my hands by placing the sacred
symbols in Ker’s; and this she would
have been compelled to do in those good
old days, when church discipline was in
its pristine vigour and activity. But, m-.
stead of this, we behold her ‘glorying
in her shamed tcumphing in her guilt,
placing herself in the attitude of defi
ance, and at the head of her radical
troops, demanding those rights she has
so deservedly forfeited, and which, in
the name of ever’ thing good and vir
tuous and sacred unong us, she never
-can, she never must have.”
Chief Justice Abbot. —l think, Mr.
Brougham, that you kave shewn causes
enough for your rule.
Mr. Brougham. —The deponent, of
course, my Lord, swears that her Maj
esty the Queen is the person alluded to
in the sermon. And this part of her
conduct alluded to, namely, her going
to church on the Sunday at Hammer
smith, is now for the first time called in
question. It was never in issue before.
Mr. Justice Bayley. —You have your
rule ; there is no necessity to read over
any further passages.
The rule was accordingly granted.

■ NEW-YORK, AVRIL 13.
The County Court of Hartford coun
ty has been in session since the 12th
day of March. The causes originating
in that county, which a late law required
should be first disposed of, occupied the
Court until the 22d, on which day the
trial ot remov ed from Baltimore
county, commenced. Among the caus
es so removed for trial, were the indict
ments against the Officers of several
of the Banks in this city, including the
Branch of the Bank of the United
States. These cases excited great at
tention and expectation, from the char
acter and high standing in society of
the persons indicted—the nature of the
charges, the talents and respectability
ol the counsel employed for and against
the prosecution, and the great number
of witnesses summoned to support and
repel the charges.
The indictments were numerous ; but,
except in two instances, were either a
gainst a single officer, charging him
with secretly and fraudulently using, for
his own benefit, the funds of the Bank
entrusted to his care, contrary to his
duty and to the loss and injury of the
Stockholders—or against two or more
officers for conspiring together secretly
and fraudulently to use the funds, &c. '
Much the greater number of indict
ments were for a conspiracy; the gen
eral ground of defence on behalf of the
persons indicted, was, that a conspiracy
for the purposes alleged in those in
dictments was not a criminal offence
—an additional ground, in the cases
against the officers of the Bank of the
U. S. was, that the Court had no juris
diction. The question of law, as to
both grounds, was brought before the
Court on an indictment against three
of the officers of the Bank of the U. S.
charging them with a conspiracy, se
cretly and fraudulently to use, for their
own benefit, the funds of that Bank en
trusted to them, to a large amount. The
argument was ably supported on the
side of the prosecution, by Mr. Murray,
the Attorney for the District, Mr. Mitch
ell, Mr. Harper, and Mr. Wirt; and as
ably maintained on the part of the trav
ersers, by Mr. Winder and Mr. Pinkney.
The argument, •which lasted twelve
Jays, was concluded at two o’clock, P.
M. on Saturday last. The Judges, who
were all attending during the whole of
the interesting discussion, deemed it im
portant to intimate their opinions, ver
bally, before the Court adjourned; as
it would depend on their decision wheth
er the further attendance of a great
number of witnesses would be required.
The two Associate Judges, Hanson and
Ward, united in opinion, and decided that
a conspiracy for the purpose charged
in the indictments is not a Criminal of
fence, inasmuch as the fraud contem
plated to be effected by such conspiracy
was of a private nature, and such as, ifef
fccted by any one of the persons indicted,
without the aid or concurrence of anoth
er person, would not be an indictable
or criminal offence under the law's of
this state. The chief Judge, Dorsey,
dissented from the opinion of his associ
ates, and stated it to be his opinion that
the conspiracy charged in the indict
ment, is a criminal offence against the i
laws of this state. The decision on the
question of conspiracy, rendered it un
necessary to give any opinion on the
question of jurisdiction, and is consider
ed as settling the cases against all the i
Bank officers but four.

REPORT—
That as Massachusetts now has a valuable
interest in the lands within the territory of
Maine; and as this State has property to a
considerable amount in the possession of that
Commonwealth; and as the only mode by
which an equitable division can be made must
be attended with much delay and great ex
pense, it is evident that an exchange may be
effected which shall be mutually beneficial.
The Committee most cordially reciprocate
the wishes expressed by a Committee of the
Legislature of Massachusetts, that the harmo
ny and good will which have hitherto existed,
in so eminent a degree, between this and our
parent State, may continue undiminished; and
they also believe that there is great reason to
apprehend that the mutnal claims of indepen
dent Sovereignties may produce collision and
contention, if not brought to a speedy termi
nation, especially when we consider how pe
culiarly . desirable it is tha‘ this State should
have the exclusive ownership and centred of
all its territory.
The Committee are therefore of opinion that
the enlightened views of the Legislature of
Massachusetts ought to be met with corres
ponding libenftty on the part of this State,
and that no time should be lost in entering up
on the proposed negocia’ions; for which pur
pose the Resolves acompanying this Report
are recommended for adoption.—All which is
submitted.

The Sea-Serpent was seen by Capt-
Grows, master of the' brig Minerva,
bound from Martinique, to Bath, (Me.)
on Friday, the 30th of March. It was
between 5 and 6 o’clock in the after
noon, Cape Ann bearing W. S. W. and
distant 45 miles. The sea was quite
smooth, there being a very light breeze,
and the Serpent taking a south course
was distinctly observed, at about -40
yards from the vessel. Capt. Grows’s
description of the monster agrees with
the previous accounts. He was a stur
dy disbeliever in the existence of the
animal, in common with Mr. Lang, the
editor of the New-York Gazette; but
to see is to believe— and Capt- Grows, is
now fully convinced of the errour of
his old opinion. Some people can nev
er be satisfied of any truth, that does
not come in contact with one of the
senses.

It is the custom in Boston, with both politi
cal parties, to hold a general caucus on the
evening preceding the April Election. At the
federal caucus, in Fanueil Hall, four or five
thousand persdns are sometimes present; and
the assembly is usually addressed by some of
the most distinguished citizens.
It may be recollected that, a year since,
some new arrangements were made in Boston,
as to the mode of making their nominations :
a general committee was appointed, and ward
committees chosen, whose duty it was to se
lect candidates in the first instance, and then
to report them to the general caucus to be
holden on the evening preceding the election.
By the operation of this arrangement it so hap
pened that Mr. Quincy, who had, for several
years, been on the list of Senators, was last
year excluded from it, without any publick
explanation of the matter. Mr. Quincy, nev
ertheless, who was present when this was done,
magnanimously advocated the acceptance of
the new list. His fellow-townsmen, perhaps
ashamed of their unworthy treatment of him,
elected him, in May, as one of their Repre
sentatives. He now fills the Speaker’s chair :
so that this freak of the town has been of ser
vice to the State.
We have given this little narrative (put of
the way as it may seem,) in order that our read
ers may the better understand the allusions
contained in the extract, which is below, from
the Speech of Mr. Quincy, at the general cau
cus of this year. A sketch of his Speech is
given in the last Galaxy, and we select a pas
sage from it, not to show what every body al
ready knows, that Mr. Quincy is open, undis
guised, independent and honest in his politicks,
but to give our readers a specimen of his good
nature and sportive humour, upon a subject too,
which, in men of smaller minds, often excites
the most bitter feelings.

ba accused of pride qnd arrogance—it

This traveller has shown an indefati
gable boldness and perseverance in
.searching for remqants of antiquity, a
midst the burning and blinding sands of
the Egyptian deserts, seldom, and per
haps never surpassed. Let us transport
ourselves for a moment with this patient
son of science into the midst of those
scorching sands—a region never water
ed by Heaven’s refreshing rains. Hun
ger and thirst, and penury and assassi
nation, scowl with their haggard features
around him, from the midst of those
suffocating clouds of sand, while he,
with his attendant Arabs, is patiently
employed in removing those arid billows
from the base of some superb and mag
nificent monument of human art, that
towers in solitary majesty above tbe des
ert. When the winds arise and agitate
the sands, no other chance of safety re
mains for the traveller but in flight; to
oppose them is inevitable death. But,
it may be asked, what should induce our
travellers to endure such sacrifices, to
bear hunger and thirst, and privation
and heat, and the ferocious and perse
cuting Arabs ? With these adventurers,
it is the love of science, tbe rapacious
curiosity of research ; for this, they
forsake comfort, family and friends, and
rush into the Very vortex of danger ;
but the result of these inquiries point
to an object of still more extended and
of still more awful importance. Let us
look at the Mosaick account of the his
tory of the Egyptians. We-behold in
that venerable record divine ciiraes de
nounced against Egypt—Egypt, tbe an
cient repository of the sciences and
arts, that formerly stood amongst all the
nations of the earth dazzling and pre
eminent. Where is all this splendour,
this ostentation, this magnificence now ?
Say, if you please, that the Egyptians
are degenerated, sunk, degraded—nay,
even brutalized from their ancestors !—
Say all this, and what then ? Where
are her monuments, her obelisks, her
pyramids, and all the marble records of
her ancient magnificence and grandeur ?
Where are they ? They are buried be
neath the sands of the desert.—The
pyramids still tower as the monuments
of human art, amidst the ruins of the
desect; but is any one mad enough to
believe that* these venerable relicks of
ancient art were built by the Egyptians
themselves, in a desert ? No. The
oldest authors speak of blooming fields,
and fertile rallies, of a rich and redun
dant climate, and of a prolifick soil,
maintained and matured by heaven’s
choicest deh-j ! What has produced a
revolution so awful and so tremendous?
What has converted these smiling fields
and pleasant rallies into a desert ? Let
us answer these interrogatories by one
short, simple, comprehensive sentence :
it is the curse of the Almighty that has ac
complished such wonders ; it is that very
curse which we shall find recorded in the
Mosaick account of the world. The
foot of the camel now tramples upon
those sands, that hide in their hoary bo
som all the relicks of Egyptian magnifi
cence. Amidst these burning sands, a
midst all the horrours of a climate and
of a country so accursed, we discern the
standing testimonials of the veracity of
Mosaick chronology. It is there seen
that not only the whole course of mor
al, but of physical nature, that not only
living man, but the insensible creation •
likewise, has partaken of the curse of.
its Almighty Author; that where hostile ।
armies, and all the pride and pomp and I
circumstance of war could not obliterate ;
Egypt, and all its marble memorials,
from the admiration of man, the sands
of the desert have been let loose.—
Where the waves of the ocean do not
roll, the waves of the desert accomplish
the ruin of man, and bury beneath their •
billows all the memorials of his art.<— !
Man steers his solitary way by a com
pass ever the once fertile and redundant
plains of Egypt. The camel tramples
on the palaces of princes.—Who, after
such discoveries as have been made by
Mr. Belzoni, will disbelieve jn the Mo
saick account of. the Red Sea ? Who
will disbelieve that Pharaoh and his
host were drowned in that place, when
Egypt affords such awful evidences at
the present hour of Divine indignation ?
The fertile soil, tbe rich and redundant
plains, loaded with all the blessings of
the season, have been converted into
biljows, not indeed of water—but of
sand !—We will not pursue this subject
further ; but merely remark that these
stupendous events only tend to admonish
us of the truth of that passage record
ed in holy writ, that it is a fearful thing
to fall into the hands of the living God.”

Commonwealth of Massachusetts.
The Committee of both branches of
the Legislature, ’appointed to meet a
Committee of the Legislature of the
State of Maine, for the purpose of mak
ing sale of the land, in the [atter State,
belonging to this Commonwealth—have
Attended to the duty assigned them, and
ask leave, respectfully, to offer the
following
REPORT:
’ The committees from the two States met,
for the first time, on the 3d instant. Since
that day, your committee have devoted as
rtuch time and attention to the important sub
ject referred to them, as their Legislative du
ties would permit.
W ith the limited knowledge which is had
Of this large, and, for the most part, unexplor
ed tract of country, no very accurate opinion
can of course be formed, as regards either'the
quantity, the quality, or the valtte. On one
quarter, the boundary line between the State
of Maine and thb British government re
mains unsettled.
In considering th* subject of a sale, to the
State of Maine, of that part of those lands
which belongs to Massachusetts, some very
interesting views presented themselves to both
committees, not only as respects their value,
but especially as to the continuance of that
harmony and good understanding, between
the two States, which has so happily prevail
ed, and which it is of such Vast importance
mutually to cherish and ehcourage. Id those
views the committees were well supported by
the resolves under which they have acted bn
this occasion.
Should the lands, instead of being sold, as
the resolves contemplate, be surveyed and di
vided by commissioners, agreeably to the act
separating Maine from Massachusetts, the ex
pense would necessarily be very great to both
States—much time would be consumed, and
all this, probably, without adding much if

THE CONSTITUTION.
Notwithstanding the prevalence of
the opinion that no amendment of the
Constitution is necessary, we hear, on
every side, expressions of surprize at
the appearance of the votes upon the
proposed amendments. Individuals who
thought a Convention unnecessary, and
have voted against all the most impor
tant amendments, on the ground that
the existing provisions of the Constitu
tion are wise, and capable of being still
carried into effect, have been astonished
to find that a large majority of the peo
ple, by their recent vote, have virtual
ly decided that the exigencies of the
State did not require a Convention —
By rejecting the Fifth Article, the peo
ple have decided that there is no diffi
culty in apportioning forty Senators, ac
cording to a fair construction of the
Constitution : and thus the supposed ne
cessity for a Convention, it is shown,
never existed.

As for the people of the County of
Worcester, we never believed they de
sired a Convention. The most of them
did not vote on the question, and they
probably suffered it to pass without op
position from a regard to the supposed
wishes of other parts of the State.
The Fifth and Tenth Articles of a
mendment, proposed by the Convention,
are unquestionably rejected by the
people ; and there is little doubt that
the First and Ninth have met with the
same fate. It is also very probable that
the Second has not been accepted, not
withstanding it passed the Convention
by a vote in the proportion of eight to
one. The Seventh, which proposes a
very desirable change in the mode of
appointing Notaries Publick, is not im
probably lost on account of an obnox
ious clause annexed to it, concerning the
removal from office of militia officers.
This is to be regretted, as the clause
alluded to has no proper connexion with
the principal subject of the Article.

Ardent feelings often lead their possessor
into errour. The Editor of the National iEgis,
in his last paper, in a long article not more
dispassionate than the times will warrant,
labours to excite or to cherish a prejudice
against Mr. Quincy, who was guilty of having
four or five votes, in this town, for Governour.
In doing this, he introduces a quotation, in
such a connexion, and under* such circum
stances, as to lead to the inference that it is
the language or the opinion of Mr. Quincy
—and that the latter has, upon some occasion,
actually said, it is “ unbecoming a moral and
religious people to rejoice in the victories of our
countrymen.”
I’o assert that Mr. Quincy ever uttered
such a sentiment, is quite an errour. It is, I
suppose, true that he, with many other good
men, believed the late war to be unjust ; and
I have always understood that he, therefore,
expressed an opinion that it was unbecoming
to rejoice at victories attained in its prosecu
tion : in other words, that it was wrong to re
joice in the success of injustice. This is the
real sentiment expressed'.
Now, whether Mr. Quincy was right in be
lieving the war to be unjust, may be a ques
tion ; but, if he was wrong in that belief, it
will hardly be imputed to him as a crime
Assuming, however, that opinion to have
been correct, the correctness of the senti
ment expressed by him will hardly be ques
tioned.
Perhaps, Messrs. Editors, you will think
this subject not unworthy of notice, when you
recollect that many individuals are probably
not aware that the sentiment imputed to Mr.
Quincy, in the JEgis, was never expressed by
him. FAIR PLAY.

Two Trials Jor Murder !
On Thursday last, before the Su
preme Judicial Court now sitting in this
town—preseht, Chief Justice Parker,
and Justices Jackson and Wilde, came
on the trial of Thomas Charles Bell
for the murder of Pamela Percy.—
The indictment charged him with strik
ing her with his hands, and beating her
with a large stick; indicting such vio
lent blows upon her body as to cause
her death. After numerous witnesses
had been examined, who proved that
Pamela wa|Hl girl of ill fame, that she
was in the constant habit of intoxica
tion, and was abused and beaten by the
defendant, very severely, who kept
her—it did not clearly appear that she
came by her death from the actual
bruises she received from Bell. The
fact being rendered doubtful by conflict
ing testimony, the prisoner was acquit
ted. The prosecution was conducted
for Government, by the Hon. D. Davis,
Solicitor-General; Messrs. Dunlap and
Moore were the prisoner’s counsel.
Next day, before the same Judges,
Martin Manuel was tried for the alleged
murder of Nancy Blackman, on the
14th of March last, by striking her with
an axe, on the left side of the head, giv
ing a mortal wound of the length of six
inches, the breadth of two inches, and
depth of one inch, of which she died.
It appeared, by the testimony, that,
on the above night, Mrs. Manuel came
to the chamber of Jackson Neal, the
principal witness, in great agitation, and
said her husband was attempting to mur
der her, that he appeared to be out of
his head, and she was airaid he would
kill Nancy Blackman. Mr. Neal hear
ing a shriek, went into Manuel’s cham
ber, saw the girl weltering in her blood
by a lamp on the table, and heard a
low groan. Manuel was in the room,
with an axe in his hand. Asked the
prisoner what was the matter, who said
nothing at all. He ran into the street,
and having obtained assistance, went
for a Doctor. Mrs. Manuel had been
afraid to remain alone with her ht»-
band; a Miss Blackman came to stay
with her on that account. The head of
the prisoner’s bed was towards the en
try, and the bed on which the girl slept
was on the floor. The prisoner had had
epileptick fits, and had been unwell for
several days before this affair.. The
prisoner and his wife went to bed at 9
o’clock—he afterwards got up, asked
for a light, dressed himself, and went
out into the yard—came in again, and
began to strike her with his fists, saying
you are the person I want to find ; she
shoved him back and made her escape
frogi the room. The testimony agreed
that the homicide had been committed
by Manuel, and the defence was, that
he was under the influence of insanity.
That he had been insane was pretty
fully proved by divers witnesses, and
the opinion of Doct. Reynolds, who had
been his physician was, that he was in
sane in consequence of repeated at
tacks of epilepsy. After a summing
up of the testimony by the Chief Jus
tice, who put it to the Jurors, whether
under the circumstances there was not
a violent presumption that the act was
committed in a moment of insanity, they
returned a verdict of not guilty, by
reason of insanity. The Attorney-Gen
eral was for Government. Messrs. Sim
mons and Peabody were counsel for the
defence. —«>♦&— •

FA NN Y.-~ A new edition of this pleasing
little Poem has lately been published. Some
additions have been made to the original, and
we copy from the Evening Post the following
extract from them. This style of versification
has been but lately adopted by our English
bards ; although it has been common, we are
told, for a long time, among both the French
and Italian poets. The easy negligence of
common parlance was thought to be incom
patible with the formal and regular movement
of English metre ; and Peter Pindar was the
first, we believe, who attempted to unite them.
Wordsworth and Hunt, with others of the
Lake School,” have imitated him in his so
ber vein ; and Lord Byron, in his “ Beppo”
and “ Don Juan,” has equalled, if not excel
led his humorous and lively satire. “ Fanny”
is an obvious imitation of the last-named work;
though it is free from the indecency and infi
delity of some parts of Don Juan, and lacks,
withal, a good degree of its attick seasoning.
But it will be seen, by the extract here given,
that the author is no common rhymer ; that
bis verse is flowing and harmonious ; his lan
guage equally happy in the expression of pa
thos and humour ; and his perception of the
tender and pathctick, the absurd and ludicrous,
equally nice and discriminating.

gan;

it.
If in my story of her woes, or plan
Or moral can be trac'd, 'twas not intended;
And if I’ve wrong’d her, I can only tell her
I’m sorry for it—so is my bookseller.
1 met her yesterday—her eyes were wet—
She faintly smil’d, and said she had been
reading
The Treasurer’s Report, in the Gazette,

Um bleeding.
She had a shawl on, ’tWas not a cashmere one;
And, if it cost five dollars, ’twas a dear one.
Her father sent to Albany a prayer
For office —told- how fortune bad abus’d
him—
And modestly requested to be Mayor.
The Council very civilly refus’d him,
Because, however much he might desire it,
The publid: good, it seems, did not require it.
Some evenings since, he took a lonely stroll
Along Broadway, scene of past joys and
evils:
He felt that withering bitterness of soul,
Quaintly denominated the blue d tills ;
And thought of Buonaparte and Bellisarius,
Pompey, and Col. Burr, and Caius Marius.
And, envying the loud playfulness and mirth
Qi' those who pass’d him, gay in youth and
hope,
He took, at Jupiter’s, a shilling’s worth
Of gazing through the show-man’s telescope.
Sounds as of far-off bells came on his ears—
He fancied ’twas the musick of the spheres.
He was mistaken, it was no such thing—
• Twas yankee doodle, play’d by Scudder’s
band.
He mutter’d, as he linger’d listening,
Something of freedom, and our happy land:
Then sketch’d, as to his home he hurried feist,
This sentimental his saddest and his last.
Young thoughts have musick in them, love
And happiness their theme :
And musick wanders in the wind
That lulls a morning dream.
And there are angel voices heard.
In childhood's frolick hours,
When life is but an April day
Of sunshine and of showers.
There’s musick in the forest leaves
When sumufer winds are there ;
And in the laugh of forest girls,
That braid their sunny hair.
The first wild bird that drinks the dew,
From violets of the spring,
Has musick in his song, and in
The fluttering of his wing.
There’s musick m the dash of waves,
When the swift bark cleaves their foam ;
There’s musick heard upon her deck,
The mariner’s song of home,
When moon and star beams smiling meet,
At midnight, on the sea—
And there is musick, once a week,
In Scudder’s balcony.
But the musick of young thoughts too soon
Is faint, and dies away ; '
And from oar morning dream we wake
To curse the coming day.
And childhood’s frolick hours are brief;
And oft, in after years,
Their memory comes to chill the heart, a
-And dim the eye with tears.
To-day the forest leaves are green,
They’ll wither on the morrow,
And the maidens laugh be chang’d, ere long,
To the widow’s wail of sorrow.
Come with the winter snows, and a#k
Where are the forest birds ?
The answer i» a silent one,
More eloquent than words.
The moonlight musick of the wares
In storms is heard no more,
When the living lightning mocks the wreck
At midnight on the shore.
And the mariner’s song of home has ceas’d,
His corse is on the sea—
And musick ceases when it rains
In Scudder’s baltony.

It is false that the principle of Chris
tian sanctification possesses no influence
over the familiarities of civil and ordi
nary life. It is altogether false that god
liness is a virtue of such a lofty and mo
nastick order, as to hold its dominion
only over the solemnities of worship, or
over the solitude of prayer and spiritu
al contemplation. If it be substantially
a grace within us at all, it will give a
direction and colour to the whole of ovr
path in society. There is not one con
ceivable transaction, amongst all the
manitbld varieties of human employ
ment, which it is not fitted to animate by
its spirit Thore is nothing' that meets
us too homely to be beyond the reach
of obtaining from its influence the stamp

of something celestial. It offers to take
the whole man under its ascendancy,
and to subordinate ell his movements,
nor does it hold the place which right
fully belongs to it till it be vested with
a presiding authority over the entire
system of human affairs ; and therefore
it is that the preacher is not bringing
down Christianity; he is only sending
it abroad over the field of its legitimate
operation, when he goes with it to your
counting-houses, and there rebukes eve
ry selfish inclination that would carry
you ever so little within the limits of
fraudulency. When he enters into your
chambers of agency, and there detects
the character of falsehood, which lurks
under all the plausibility of your multi
plied and excessive charges ; when he
repairs to the crowded market-place,
and pronounces of every bargain, over
which truth, in all the strictness of Qua
kerism, has not presided, that it is taint
ed with moral evil ; when he looks in
to your shops, and, in listening to the
contest of argument between him who
magnifies his article, and him who pre
tends to undervalue it, he calls it the
contest of avarice broken loose from
the restraints of integrity. He is not,
by all this, vulgarizing religion, or giv
ing it the hue and character of earthli
ness. He is only asserting the might
and the universality of its sole pre-em
inence over man. And therefore it is
that, if possible to solemnize his hear
ers to the practice of simplicity and
godly sincerity in his dealings, he would
try to make the odiousness of sin stand
visibly out on every shade and modifica
tion of dishonesty ; and to assure them
that if there be a place in our world,
where the subtle evasion, and the dex
terous imposition, and the sly but gain
ful concealment, and the report which
misleads an inquirer, and the gloss which
tempts the unwary purchaser, are not
only concurrently practised in the walks
of merchandize, but, when not carried
forward to the glare and the literality of
falsehood, are beheld with general con
nivance ; if there be a place where the
sense of morality has thus fallen, and all
the nicer delicacies of conscience are o
verborne in the keen and ambitious ri
valry of men hasting to be rich, and
wholly given over to the idolatrous ser
vice of this world—then that is the
place, the smoke of whose iniquity rises
before Him who sitteth on the throne,
in a tide of the deepest and most revolt
ing abomination.

“ It is foul weather, so that we cannot
stand without."
Then, ve Dunv insects, who shiver at
a breeze, it presents an admirable op
portunity to remain advantageously
within.
One of the early British poets has
aptly characterized the present hutnid
month by the epithet ‘spongy.’ It is
certainly an anfavourable season to the
restless and the rover. The coxcomb
dreads being surprized in the shower,
the invalid trembles lest he wet his feet,
and the fine lady shudders lest she spoil
a silk shoe, or mar a muslin robe.
But, though men are not yet permit
ted to bask under serene skies, or to
walk through the clean street or the
dry pasture, they need not fancy April a
November, and hang or drown them
selves. If the ways be dank and the
roads mire, like those Milton describes,
still the carpet and the fireside may be
kept clean ; and he who can frolick with
his children on the first, or read or chat
at the other, may abate the desire of be
ing abroad, and be abundantly good-hu
moured at
Among the many miseries with which
the splenetick and the lazy imagine
themselves tormented, the wo of lone
liness and a drizzling day is not the
least. Cards, pipes, gaping, sndring, are
all ineffectual to cure the malady which
bad weather creates. I am persuaded
it was under a cloudy atmosphere that
the muse of Pope marked the vacant
face- and resourceless fate of Paridel.
“ Thee too, my Paridel, she saw thee there,
Stretch'd on the rack of a too easy chair,
And heard thy everlasting yawn confess
The pains and penalties of idleness.”
But nothing is more irksome than such
slavery to the seasons ; and it behoves a
man to strenuously burst such shameful
chains. Are we to intermit duty because
the day is dark, and to lose our hours
because we cannot clearly discern the
sun that makes them ? Whether it is
genial June or howling March, whether
rays dart or rain patters on our roofs,
let it be remembered that every day
alike has its task to fulfil.
How many mournful voices I hear in
my parish exclaiming, ‘ it is foul weaih
er, so that we cannot stand without.’
The weeping clouds, the driving gale,
and the muddy road, are al! considered
as so many manacles, restraining the
restless to hated home. They resemble
certain capricious birds, ever impatient
of a perch, and striving to be eternally
on the wing. These mutterers against
the order of the seasons are never at a
loss for querulous complaint. Evety
transient shower and every morning fog
are plentiful sources of vexation ; and a
storm, like the hags of popular supersti
tion, has the magick power to change
nature into the most terrifick and tre
mendous forms.

The wisest moralists have always en
joined upon men that they should not
only bear, but seek occasional solitude.
This thought was once carried so far by
a Certain philosophick state prisoner,
that he rejoiced he was inclosed by
walls, which kept vice out and kept him
in. Abroad, the mind, contemplating an
infinitude of objects, is distracted with
variety, and grows giddy by dissipation.
It is at home we read with system, we
think to purpose, and, by the aid of the
pen, embody our speculations.
To those who hold the fretful lan
guage of the text, and impatiently wish
moist April away, the ensuing modes of
passing early spring time are suggested.
For the Lay Preacher thinks it possible
to provide useful and agreeable occu
pation, whether it rains or snows.
In the first place, he who in earnest
devotes any of his days to the culture of
his mind, will soon discover that, to search
into his boolt, andto examine his thoughts,
it is not necessary to look out of the win
dow. The company of the Muse is so
enchanting,that we cease to think of the
mere accidents of the day. Of such a
visitant, the student may justly exclaim,
“ With thee conversing, I forget all time,
All seasons, and their change."
Let him repair to hi& shelves for a book,
or traee his ideas on paper, and he will
not once ask the servant if the wind is
east.
Again—wet days do not, necessarily,
damp the generous and social affections.
The distressed may be relieved, the cu
rious may be informed, and the stranger
courteously entreated, as w’ell in bad as
good weather.
If they look eagerly even within
doors, many will discover objects more
interesting than the state of the atmos
phere, or the colour of the cloxds. If,
sometimes, they cannot stand without,
they may enjoy many brilliant prospects,
at home—a blooming progeny, affec
tionate friends, and faithful domesticks.
These are fine sights, and shew to the
same advantage in gloom as in sun
shine.
Lastly—one may pass a dull day, sup
pose it should be a Sunday, in moral and
even devotional exercises. I have seen,
under a frowning sky, many happy faces
at church ; and have witnessed, both in
the storms of January and March, the
smiles of piety at her prayers. In hom
age to the Creator, and in benevolence
to his creatures, our hours, whether
gilded or gloomy, may most usefully be
employed.

ANECDOTE OF BURKE.
On one occasion, Mr. Burke’s quick
Sense of indignity discovered itself by
flight. He had just risen in the House
of Commons, with some papers in his
hand, on the subject of which he intend
ed to make a motion, when a rough-hewn
member, who had no ear for the charms
of eloquence, rudely started up and said,
“Mr. Speaker, I hope the honourable
gentleman does not mean to read that
large bundle of papers, and to bore us
with a long speech into the bargain.”—
Mr. B. was so swoln, or rather so nearly
suffocated with rage, as to be incapable
of utterance, and absolutely ran out of
the House. On this occasion, George
Selwyn remarked, that it was the only
time he ever saw the fable realized, a
lion put to fight by the braying of an ass.
