One amiable female is rendered mis
erable for the evening, by seeing anoth
er, whom she intended to outshine, in a
more attractive dress than her own ;
while the other omits no methods of giv
ing stings to her triumph, which she
enjoys with all the secret arrogance of
an oriental sultana. Another is compell
ed to dance with a monster she abhors.
A third has set her heart on dancing
with a particular partner, perhaps for
the amiable motive of annoying one of
her dear friends; not only he does not
ask her, but she sees him dancing with
that identical dear friend, whom, from
that moment, she hates more cordially
than ever. Perhaps, what is worse than
all, she has set her heart on refusing
some impertinent fop, who does not give
her the opportunity.

FEDERAL GOVERNMENT,
rHZRTY-THJRD YEAR.

[Whole No. 2510.

POLITICAL economy.
' • ««<*
Extract from the Message of Govern
nour Wolcott, to the Legislature of
Connecticut, at its present session.
ALL our national distrevses proceed, in
my opinion, frpm a defective system of finance,
which will, I am persuaded, more and more
weaken and impoverish the country, until it is
changed. The low rate of interest, and the
decreasing value of labour, are sure signs of
the Stagnation of every kind of active em-'
ployment; and the high prices of our publick
stocks in England, in connexion with the rate
of exchange, are infallible indications that the
representatives of our wealth are rapidly trans
ferring to that country. The produce of our
farms being refused, these transfers' are made
in payment for fabricks of wool, cotton, linen,
and metals, which our soil and our arts might
produce in abundance, not merely for home
consumption, but for the support of our com
merce, which can only revive through manu
factures, or during European wars in which we
remain neutral. The fabricks which we im
port, we yearly consume, thereby constantly
destroying the capital applied in payment, and.
leaving our accumulating debt as mortgages
upon our remaining resources.
There is now no civilized independent na
tion but ourselves which has not become a
wakened to the necessity of protecting its in
ternal industry. From the Baltick to the Me
diterranean, the effort is universal, and we
cannot, with impunity, disregard the admoni
tions which their examples inculcate. A com
parison between the condition of France and
this country win illustrate the difference be
tween wise and inefficient systems of political
economy. For more than £5 ytears, France
harassed by desolating wars—and within
five years, she was oppress- d by foreign ar
mies, excited to acts of extortion by vindic
tive resentments. Now she supports a circu
lating medium in gold and silver coins ; her
agriculture, arts and manufactures are flour
i*hing ; her commerce is reviving, and both
excite the jealousy of her neighbours and ri
vals ; h»T revenue exceeds her expenditures,
and her taxes are diminishing. Excepting the
short period of the last war, we have enjoyed
peace, and for most of the time have supposed
ourselves to be prosperous; but the acquish
tions of which we have boasted, for twenty
years, have vanished, or are invested in un
productive property, which is daily diminish
ing in value. Our industry is becoming lan
guid ; our currency consists of notes which,
are representatives of our debts due to banks ;
even usury is less profitable than heretofore ;
our national debt exceeds what it did when
Die present government was first organized,
including the debt of the revolutionary war,
and the State debts which were then assumed,
while our revenue is unequal to our annual
expenses, on the most reduced establishment
which we <ian make.
No man will deny that this contrast is true,
or affirm that it is too highly coloured ; and I
deem it my indispensable duty to present it to
your consideration, in consequence of the un
expected crisis at which our affairs have ar
rived. Congress are exclusively vested with
powers to regulate commerce with foreign na
tions and between the States, and yet find
themselves unable to adopt regulations which
would protect those industrious pursuits of
the people, to which they were invited during
a period of great difficulty and danger. For
want of uniform laws on the subject of bank
ruptcy, and in consequence of decisions in the
Supreme Court of the United States, local
frauds can be committed with impunity, and
yet no man, whatever may have been his pre
vious character and conduct, can, on the sur
render of all his property, be discharged from
liability for his debts. Thus it has happened
practically, that the non-observance of a Con
stitution, which was designed to protect the
rights of the people of all the States, and to
harmonize all their institutions, has, in effect
suspended two of the most important powers
of government in every State—has annihilated
many branches of industry—indirectly en
couraged fraud ; and condemned great num
bers, throughout this extensive country, to
hopeless poverty and indolence.
Man in a solitary and insulated condition,
is the most defenceless and wretched being
with which we are acquainted ; but in a state
of society, and with a mind illuminated by
science, he holds dominion over the earth,
the air and the sea, and renders all nature
tributary to his ease and conduit. The an
cient allegories of Prometheus and Hercules
are illustrations of the degradations of science
and human labour, during the early ages oC
mankind, and of the subsequent effects which
were produced by their emancipation and
united energy. These effects survive in the
literature, histories and monuments of the
microscopick republicks of Greece, as proofs
of the elevation which free states may attain
by concord, while their ruins are admonitory
tokens of the fatal consequences of disunion
and faction. It is a law of human nature,
that man never can exert his powers to the
injury of his associates, without harm to him
self. Selfishness is never profitable.
The preceding observations are not made
under the influence of any suspicion that the
interests of this state have been particularly
neglected, or that injuries to us are meditat
ed from any quarter : on the contraiy, I be
lieve that we have no reason to be dissatisfied
with our relative condition, and that ’ there ia
no state in the union to which our citizens can
migrate, with any prospect of advantage.—
We, at least, are not perplexed with contro
versies arising from any supposed opposition of
interests between different occupations and*
professions. Our agriculture, commerce and
manufactures are equally doptessed, an<l we
perceive that no branch of industry can flour
ish, but in consequence of events and meas
ures, which will be beneficial to every em-ployment. vicinity
to the best markets, our fertile toil, flocks and
herds, our manufactures, the vigour
of our institutions, thejSwKiity, concord and
energy of tho*eople will, with a divine bles
sing, sustain 'S under toy trials, which, in
common with.our neighbours, we may be re
quired to endure. ( »e ktow that the world
is open before us, and that we can share in
any contingent advantages, which foreign mar
kets may present, and that no export duty or

der, in 34’days from Liverpool, the editors of

The most interesting intelligence by these
vessels is the termination of .Austrian hostili
ties against Naples. It seems that the resist
ance on the part of the Neapolitans was feeble
as well as ineffectual; the troops being almost
all undisciplined militia, could not be brought
to withstand any serious onset from, their ene
mies, but fled immediately upon the first seri
ous exhibitions of danger. The Austrians ad
vanced with trifling opposition towards the
capital until the 20th of March, when they
had reached the neighbourhood of Capua, less
than 20 miles from Naples, when an armistice
occurred, and a convention was entered into
Which will be found in our paper this morning.
To say we regret this issue of a struggle
which certainly deserved a more rigorous sup
port on the side of the Neapolitans, would be
using but feeble language. We consider it
one of the most unjustifiable attempts, on the
part of the Austrians, to intermeddle with the
affairs of an independent nation, that has at
any time taken place. Even the French, du
ring the bloody days of their revolutionary ca
reer, had in many instances more plausible rea
sons to urge in favour of their aggressions upon
other nations, than the Austrians have in ex
cuse of their attack upon Naples.
After’all, there is reason to fear that a peo
ple who could make no greater efforts in de
fence of their country and its independence,
would not have had energy or virtue enough
to carry on- a free and representative system
of government. The probability is, that when
not urged to unanimity bf external pressure
and danger, they would have quarrelled a
mong themselves, and in that way have lost
the benefit of all they had apparently gained.
Disturbances still continued to exist in Sa
voy ; but they will probably prove as short
lived as the Neapolitan war.
A Liverpool paper, of April 3, states that
recent accounts, from the Italian seat of war,
state that an engagement had taken place be
tween Baron Frimont and the Neapolitan
General Carrascosa, in which the latter was
defeated, and had in consequence fallen back
to Aversa, which is within 10 miles of Naples;
but neither place nor date is given for the
scene or time of this rtimoured engagement,
and the probability is that the rumour has
originated in the advance of the Austrian ar
my, which, according to the last accounts,
was, at the date of the 18th, at San Germano,
a town within the Neapolitan frontier, on the
main road between Rome and Naples, from
the latter of which cities it is distant about
fifty British miles. The near approach of the
Austrians to the capital is- represented to have
produced the most dispiriting effects at Naples;
and; according to accounts from Florence and
Turin, of the date of 24th and 25th ult. and
from Paris of the 28th, the Neapolitan Parlia
ment has been finally closed ; the army has
been dissolved ; and the Prince Regent has
submitted to his father, King Ferdinand. The
same account states that' the ancient order of
things has been restored in Piedmont; that
Gen. Latour, who commands in Novara, as
Generalissimo of the Piedmontese troops, in
the name of the abdicated King, Victor Em
manuel, has rallied a great part of the forces
to the Royal standard ; that the Prince, Carig
nan, has, by proclamation, divested himself
of the regency, and joined the army at Nova
ra, placing himself under General Latour’s or
ders as a junior officer ; and that Piedmont is
replaced under the authority of the King,
with the exception only of the citadel of Tu
rin and Alexandria. These mighty and sud
den changes are as astonishing as were the
revolutions at Naples and Turin, and we have
no doubt but they will be hailed by the mem
bers of the Holy Alliance as the triumph of
their cause over the infant liberties of Italy ;
but our belief is, that the struggle for inde
pendence, in that fine region of the world, is
not yet at an end, and that when the end comes,
a government by delegation from the people
will be as certainly established in the States
of Italy, as that it now exists in Spain and
Portugal.}

LIVERPOOL, APRIL 6.
We have, in our columns, given an account
of the failure of the attempt of the Neapoli
tans to establish for themselves a free form of
government. This failure will be seriously la
mented by all men of liberal sentiments, par
ticularly at a moment when, as a confirmation
of the beautiful theories ot liberty, we present
them with the inaugural speech of the Presi
dent of a great nation, which shows how bene
ficially to the human race those theories may
be rendered practical. The Holy Alliance
may triumph over Naples ; but America re
mains a great and inextinguishable beacon, to
direct our hopes and our endeavours to the
safe harbour of constitutional government.—
While America remains free, (and what pow
er on earth can enslave her ?) Europe cannot
be wholly enslaved. Nor do we think that
the friends of freedom have cause to despair,
even of Naples. In this successful
Austria'has added to the catalogue of her own
crimes, and thereby afforded further cause for
the hatred and vengeance of those whom she
dares to oppress. It is not by soldiers that the
ideas and sentiments of men can be extirpat--
ed ; and she has been taught by the events of
the last year, that even soldiers have their pe
riods of reflection ; that even those well-prac
tised machines of vfrar may sometimes assert
their share of humanity, and may turn weap
ons to other purposes than that of defending
the thrones of despots, or that of executing
the sanguinary behests ot greedy and ambitious
tyrants. Spain and Portugal still remain in
the enjoyment of their newly-acquired liber
ties ; and it is- impossible that France and En
gland can long»continue to behold with indif
ference the westward progress of that oriental
despotism, which, while it pretends to preach
the safety of thrones, is manifestly aiming at'
the destruction of all'the commerce, all the
power, and all the independence of the west
ern nations. The despotick spirit must be
driven beyond the Wolga, or Europe will be
to Russia what Egypt and Persia were in an
cient days to Assyria. Even now, the smaller
kingdoms; and even France, under the misera
ble government of the feeble Bourbons, are
little better than the satraps of a great three
headed empire, which,-alter the manner of
the eastern tyrannies, has denominated itselF
Holy. leis time, therefore, for the west of
Europe (as Sir R. Wilson emphatically declar
ed) to raise its own defence. It must do so
in the spirit of freedom, and with the strength
which true representative governments neces
sarily possess.

known that the orders given were to form im- I
mediately a new Austrian army of 70,000 men ;
in Lombardy, independently of the expedi- J

risons which, at this moment, occupy the 1
whole of the Lombardo-Vcnetian territory.— '

men, which had already been directed to hold

Never were hopes more completely disap
pointed than they have been by the issue of
the Neapolitan struggle for independence.— j
The foreign intelligence, with which we fur*
taish our readers, this week, is a sad comment
upon the Manifesto of the Neapolitans, in
serted on the preceding page. Austria has ef
fected her purpose, and Naples has submitted
-*-almost without an effort! The large bodies
of troops collected by the Neapolitans, prove
to have been altogether inefficient; and the
victory which, last week, there was reason to
believe they had obtained over the Austrians,
Was, it seems, an unimportant affair, in which
the latter claim the advantage.
It is not to be concealed that all this is a se
rious disappointment of our expectations. But
still, we believe, the end has not yet come.
The allied powers, though they have over
come Naples, have not conquered the spirit
that has gone abroad in Europe. The ancient
order of things they have by no means firmly
established; and if they have put off the evil
day, they cannot defer it forever.
It is now a very obvious inquiry—What step
will the allies next take ? The same princi
ples by which they have been governed in
their conduct towards Naples, will lead them
to interfere in the affairs of Spain and of Portu
gal. But will the rest of Europe, will France
and England, submit to see the independence
of those nations violated ? Will the allies dare
attempt it ? Time will show whether Europe
has, at so much expense of blood, rid herself
of the domination of Napoleon, to submit to the
control of the “ Holy Alliance”—whether the
power of Cusar was overthrown merely to
make room for a no less domineering trium
virate.

Samuel P. P. Fay, Of Cambridge, is ap
pointed by the Governour and Council Judge
of Probate of Middlesex—vice James Fres
co tt, removed.—Front the slight knowledge
we have of the character of Mr. Fay, we deem
this it very judicious appointment: Many of
the suitors in Probate Courts are Widows and
Orphan*, just bereaved of a husband or a fath- '
er, and whose feelings require that kind and
deligate ti'eatnient which some men more thin
others are in the habit of awarding to all with
whom they have intercourse.
We have not yet sebn a report of thfe trial
of Judge Prescott, and it is therefore that we
have abstained from any comment upon the
result. Our readers know that he was con- '
victed upon two out of fifteen charges. Al
though there is no reason to doubt that this
decision is just, we have no disposition to ex
ult at the disgrace of the individual convicted.
We do rejoice, however, that justice has had
its course—that effect lias been given to that
principle of our government Which subjects
the high as well as the low, the magistrate as
well as the mere citizen, to the scrutiny of the
laws, and to the punishment provided for their
Violation.
A New-York paper remarks that it is hon
ourable to Massachusetts that Judge Prescott,
being a Federalist, has been impeached by a
federal House of Representatives, and con
victed by a federal Senate ! What must be
the effect of political parties upon that com
munity where such a circumstance is thought
worthy of notice ! Who would think of re
marking upon the circumstance of a man’s be
ing indicted for a crime by a grand jury, and
convicted by a traverse jury, all being of the
same political party ? The very remark would
be an implied reproach upon the administra
tion of justice. The case of Judge Prescott
is not dissimilar in principle. The House of
Representatives is the Grand Inquest of the
State ; and the Senate, when organized as a

Court, is the most dignified judicial tribunal in
the Commonwealth. Neither the one nor the
other can be supposed to have any more sym
pathy with the individual Impeached, than
the several branches of any other Court, with
any person charged with a crime. The com-,
pliment, therefore, of the New-York paper is
a very cheap one, and rather unfortunate for
the credit of the State from which it proceeds.

“ Gen. Pepe had several days since
collected the greater part of his forces
between Civita Ducale and Aquilla.—
On the 7th, he advanced with a body
of 10,000 men upon Rieti. Two col
umns of this corps manoeuvred on the
heights which form the valley of Rieti,
and threatened to turn our advance
guard, which was posted there under
the orders of Gen. Geppert, whilst a
third column moved straight forward on
the road from Civita Ducale to Rieti.—
These movements were judiciously con
ducted, and the points of attack well
chosen. Our light troops suffered them
selves to be approached, net yet believ
ing that they were enemies who were
marching towards them. We had ex
pressed to them only the words of peace.
A very brisk fire soon convinced us that
we had mistaken their The
battle then commenced: it was near the
hour of noon: the enemyk attack be
came serious. And Lieut. Gen. Wal
moden ordered his reserve, which was
at Casa Vicentini, in the rear of Rieti,
to march to the support of Gen. Gep
pert. He directed an attack with a
very inferiour force, upon the two col
umns which formed the enemy’s wings,
and they were driven back into the
mountains, notwithstanding all the ad
vantage of the ground being in their fa
vour. The centre column fell back
upon Civita Ducale.
“ The enemy abandoned that city at
ten o’clock at night, after having pillag
ed it. Our advanced guard immediately
occupied it, and our soldiers were re
ceived as deliverers.
u We lost in this action about fifty men
killed or wounded. Capt. Schmidt, of
the 7th battalion of Chasseurs, was kill
ed. Capt. Pfield, of the Hussars of the
King of England, and Lieut. Braun, of
the Ist battalion of Chasseurs, were
wounded.
“ During the battle of Rieti, a body
of 3000 men that had assembled at
Leonessa, advanced upon Pie-di-Lugo,
and attacked Col; Schneider, who was
posted there. He repulsed them with
the loss of several killed or wounded.—
In the course of the day, we took seve
ral prisoners, and among them a Captain
of Gen. Pepe’s staff.”

LITERARY.
A manuscript Bbem has lately been put into
our hands with a request, that we would ex
amine it and give our opinion of its merits.—
We have read it over with care, and its pe
rusal has afforded us so much pleasure, that it
was believed a concise review of it might
gratify some of our readers.
The Poem is entitled “ Escalala ; an
Thie”—by Samuel B. Beach, of
Oswego County, in this state. In his choke
of a subject, we think the author has been
peculiarly judicious and happy, since he has
selected one, which, in the language of crit
icks, possesses great poetick capabilities, and
opens a wide field for descriptive imagery and
the flights of fancy. The story on which the
Poem is founded, is semi-historical, authen
tick enough to render the event* probable,
and sufficiently involved in doubt and uncer
tainty, to leave ample room for poetick inven
tion, and a free range to the imagination.—
It is very probable the author's plan might
have been suggested by reading Mudock, to
which at any rate it is in .subject nearly allied.
In a prefatory note to the Poem, Mr. Beach
gives the following outlines of his story ? —
“ The ruins of fortifications and other traces
of civilisation, discernible in the interiour of
North-America, and particularly along the
Oldo, and between that and the lakes, remain
to this day, and probably ever will remain,
totally unaccounted for. From this I have
taken my hint. In the ninth century, Harold
Houfagre conquered twelve of the petty
chieftains of Norway, and united their terri
tories into a kingdom. Naddhr, one of these
petty chieftains, fleeing from Harold, turned
pirate, discovered and colonized Greenland ;
and in one of his voyages from Norway to
that country, with colonists, he is supposed
to have perished by shipwreck—so says histo
ry : But I have taken the liberty, continues.
Mr. Beach, to altek his supposed fate, and to
make him the founder of a Norwegian colony,
at the junction of the Ohio and Missisippi—
Of course, this colony retains the superstitious
ceremonies and observances of its Scandina
vian ancestors, who at that period were not
Converted to Christianity.
“ The poem opens with a grand feast, in
troductory to a splendid hunting-match, and
preparatory to the annual religious rites in
honour of Odin—the time about 300 years
after Naddhr's first landing on the continent,
and when the colony had become powerful.
Phen follows the grand hunting-match of the
King and Nobles, in the course of which,
Ruric, the King's son, carries off by force
Fiscalala, the daughter of a powerful Indian
:hicf, and the heroine of the poem. This
produces a destructive war between the
Aborigines and Colonists, ending in the utter
>xtennination of the latter; and this result is
winced by the energy, skill, and implaca
jle revenge of Escalala.”
The reader will see at a glance, that such
i story opens to the poet an almost boundless
ange, rich in the grandest scenery of nature,
md fertile in topicks for poetick fiction. In
nany respects the author has the advantage
n the choice of a subject, of Southey, in his
Viadock, or Campbell, in his Gertrude of
Wyoming; since his design embraces, not only
the native grandeur of American scenery
■--mountains, rocks and solitudes, which the
nuses have never haunted —lakes and rivers
4 unknown to song,” and the exhaustless
opicks of Indian character, manners, and cus
ums, but also the awful sublimity of arctick
scenery, as well as the pagan mythology and
superstitious lore of Scandinavia. Besides,
here is more of romantick adventure in the
iharacter of the Norwegians, than in that of
he Welch, from whom Southey selected his
»ero; and our author is less trammelled by
ibtorick records, than Campbell was in his
Gertrude.
It remains to be seen, 1 with what talents,
(enius, and taste, Mr. Beach has availed
limself of the advantages, whieft his subject
presents. The first part of the poem, com
prising three cantos, which is all we have
cen, and all, it is believed, which the au
thor has finished, embraces a great variety of
topicks, and several kinds of versification ••
md to enable the reader to judge for himself
if the merit of the work, our extracts shall
oe as copious and diversified, as our limits
will permit.
As a specimen.-of the author’s talent at
Sescription, we select the following lines* from
he first canto :—
‘ Long was their wanderiqg—but at last,
Fhrough many a wild and trachJMi waste,.
By Missisippi’s hoary flood,
rhe homeless, houseless wanderens stood,
And found them there a place of rest,
Richer than Araby the blest.
Wild was the scene—but all as fair
As fancy’s fondest visions are,
And seem’d to those its haunts who trod,
4 paradise without its god.
Here, on the right, Ohio roll’d
His tribute waters, swift and bold ;
Like some rich vassal proud to bring
rhe wealthiest off’ring. to his King—
While there, broad, deep, impetuous, strong,
Old Missisippi swept along,
As tho’ be scorn’d the needless tide
His vassal’s feeble founts supplied.
And on its surface all the pride
Of plumage, that e’er deck’d the tide
Of sylvan stream, in eddying play,
Wheel’d lightly in the summer ray.
The deep embow’ring woods around,
With vines and mantling ivy crown’d,
And thousand flowers of varied hue,
Fresh from their birth and moist with dew,
Shed fragrance, rich as poets sing, y
Elysian gales were wont to fling
Round those blest souls, by Minos given
On earth an antepast of heaveu—
Seem’d that of nature’s birth the fairest,
Of nature’s boons, the richest, rarest,
Some fairy band had cull’d with care,
Spell bound them all, and plac’d them there.”
The Tollowing extract from the same canto
will afford a fair specimen of the author’s abil
ity in the delineation of character. Gondibert,
King of the colonists, and Ruric, hi* son, a
young, passionate and heedless Prince, are
thus described-
“ His form was of that giant mould,
So common in the days of old,
Ere luxury, and ease, and art,
Curdliug’the liferblood at the heart,
perverted nature’s gen’rous plan,
And made a pigmy race of man :
And on his front, and in his cm,
Sat stern resolve and purpose nigh,
And noble daring, tbit became
His rank, his lineage, and his fame ;

And kingly pride, that ill could brook
Or opposition or rebuke—
Yet would he sqpetimes, when the tide
.Of genial wiue had open’d wide
The gates of prudence, condescend
From such high bearing to descend,
And mid a chosen festive ring.
Play any part but that of King—
Nor forfeit by such frolick mirth,
Such fooTries of ephemeral birth.
Aught of respect, or influence, due
To his high rank and merit true.
Next to the King, bis only son.
Heir to his honours and his throne,
Sat Ruric, ardent, bold and young.
Ready of hand and free of tongue,
Advewt’rous, heedless, rashly brave.
Bom to command, and yet a slave
To ev’Ty upstart passion’s sway
That chanc’d to seize him for the day-
Fortune’s spoil’d child, his sole employ
Had been to wish and t’ enjoy ;
And manhood came, and saw his frame.
Such as Apollo’s seif might claim,
Graceful and vigorous, light and free,
While his mind slept in infancy :—
Yet Ruric was his father’s pride,
Who, like most fathers, seldom spied
' A fault in one so dearly lov’d ;
Or, if he spied it, half approv’d.”
The first canto contains two episodes, which
are sung at the feast for the entertainment of
the King and his guests, by rival scalds, or
minstrels. One of the ballads is entitled The
Witch of Hetleggen, and the other The Mer
maid. Both are full of the terrifick supersti
tion and legendary lore of the north.—From
the former of these pieces, we select the two
following stanzas, as containing a more elevat
ed flight of the author’s muse, and a different
and a more difficult kind of versification :—
“ A twelve-month had pass’d, when a galliot
brave,
From the island of Ver, bounded light o’er the
wave r
' On its deck sat fair Ella, Lord Harold’s young I
bride,
And Dermid, his first-born, his heir and his
pride,
Enjoying the zephyr, that balmy and free
Just kiss’d, without moving, the face of the sea:
Lord Harold impatiently watch’d, from the
strand,
Near the base of Hesleggen, that galliot ca
reering ; —
The rowers were strong —scarce a bow-shot
from land—
They plied to the shore they were rapidly
nearing—
When sudden and black, from Hesleggen’s
high brow,
Shot a tempest-fraught cloud to the ocean be
low :
It swept past Lord Harold, all angry and dark,
And in whirlwind it burst o’er the sea-circl’d
bark
While borne on its pinions, the demon-like
form
Of the witch of Hesleggen directed the storm :
From the galliot's deck, a short death-shriek
was heard
With soul-piercing shrillness, one moment to
quiver:
One moment aloft that brave galliot appear’d—
Then sunk to its grave in the billows fore, ”
From these extracts our readers will be able
to form an opinion of Escalala ; and we doubt
not they will coincide with us in thinking it a
poem of no ordinary merit, and creditable to
the genius and taste of the author. If it has
some blemishes, it has also many beauties ;
and, iu our opinion, the latter more than bal
ance the former. We understand Mr. Beach
has not yet decided whether to publish or not.
There is as much truth as poetry in the follow
ing lines from the close of his introduction ;
and if he shall determine to publish, under
circumstances so inauspicious to the most cred
itable efforts of the American muse, we can
only express a hope that he may be more for
tunate than his predecessors, and that his poem
may meet with a patronage proportioned to its
merits :—
“ Distinguish’d thus for every gen’rotif art
That can expand the mind, or mend the heart,
Born with man’s rarest blessing—to be free,
And freedom's richest gift, a soul of energy ;
Why shun Columbia’s sons to wake the lyre,
With all the fervour of poetick fire ?
Why gaze on charms the stranger muse hath
shown,
Nor make such charms, such beauties all their
own ?
I blush the seeming riddle to unfold ;
But truth demands the tale—and truth must
aye be told.
If British genius woo the tuneful nhy,
Shape the smooth verse, and point the polish’d
line,
With prompt acclaim we hail the heavenly
lays,
lavish unscann’d applause and heedless praise.
But if some luckless native-minstrel twine
A votive chaplet for Apollo’s shrine,
Tho’ every flow’r on high Parnassus grew,
Hearv’n-bom, and nourish’d with Castalian
‘ dew,
Tho’ harmony hath breath’d her soul around
The mystick zone in which their stems art
bound,
We catch no fragrance, proffer no regard,
And cold disdain repels tire hapless bard.
Oh ! my soul sickens at the niggard meed,
By apathy, to native worth decreed—
Scorns the perverted taste that still must roam
In quest of dainties which abound at home—
Longs for the days to come—and come they
i must—
To others lib’ral, to ourselves more just—
‘When my lov’d countrymen shall learn to
prize
The wild wood flowers that bloom beneath
their native skies..
Meantime, unknown to fame, unskill’d to
guide
My slender bark across the stormy tide—
I launch, advent’rous, on the fickle sea,
Where those who seek renown oft find obscurity,
if genius guide the helm and trim the sail,
The voyage is glorious, e’en to those who fail;
Cheer’d with the tho’t I dare the high emprise,
And tempt my fate—perchance more valiant
far than wise,”

DAVID HARTLEY.
Mr. Burke was not the only tiresome speaker
of his day—at will be tun from the following
anecdote, which, Lord North used to relate,
at containing the but specimen of wit he
ever heard in the House, of Commons :—
One afternoon, the Opposition had
come down to the House to give the
Ministers battle, on a very, important
point. The business was opened by

one of the ministerial party. Mr? Burke
was ready to rise the moment his an
tagonist sat down ; but behold 'David
Hartley, who sat a few benches behind
Mr. Burke, was on his legs before him.
Mr. Hartley received the usual nod
from the Speaker, and began his oration.
The wilderness style of Mr. Hartley’s
eloquence is well known. In the course
of three hours, almost every member
who could possibly get away, had left
the House. Mr. Burke sat writhing on
the tenter-hooks of impatience, till, at
at length, Mr. Hartley stumbled on
some idea, which made him call for the
reading of the Riot Act. “ The Riot
Act I” said Burke, starting up, “ what
does the gentleman mean ? why they
are all dispersed already.”
[From the Hartford Mirror.]
EXHIBITION OF THE DEAF AND
DUMB.
On Tuesday zftemoon, (the Ist mst.) the
pupils of the Deaf and Dumb Asylum gave
a publick exhibition of jtheir progress under
the course of instruction pursued in that hu
mane institution. An occasion so interesting
drew together a large concourse of our citi
zens ; and the singular and universal attention
which the audience paid to the exercise, ex
’hibited a proof that the growing knowledge
of this unfortunate class of our species is not
without pleasure.
In addition to the neatness which we observ
ed in the dress of the pupils, we were partic
ularly struck with tlie perfect order and gen
teel deportment with which every thing was
done ; and we believs it but justice to the of
ficers of the institution to state, that in gen
eral, the pupils, in every respect, exhibited
proof of the constant and unwearied pains
which had been taken in their instruction.
The exercises of the day began by prayer,
followed by an elegant and appropriate ad
dress by Mr. Gallaudet, the principal, and by
an address by signs by a pupil—here followed
the exhibition of the several classes, under
the direction of their instructers, beginning
with the fourth class, consisting of such pupils
as had been the shortest time in the Asylum.
This class, at present under the care of
Mr. Turner, who, we understand, has been
in the Asylum only about two months, first
wrote single words from signs, to illustrate
their knowledge of the distinctive use between
the articles a and an. Then followed a set of
verbs and substantives from signs, with sever
al short phrases and answers to a few ques
tions..
The third class were under the instruction
of Mr. Orr.
This class gave proofs of their knowledge
of language, by supplying the connectives,
when the nominative and objective cases, and
verbs, were given them. Also, by supplying
the verb in its proper tense, when only the
nominative was given them. This class also '
displayed a knowledge of the meaning of words,
as well as of grammatical distinction, by mak
ing an original sentence, by being merely
supplied with a verb from the instruett r.
The second class was under the direction
of Mr. Weld.
The first object- was to show that the lan
guage of signs was applicable to the gram
matical part of our language. This was il
lustrated by dictating the various senses of the
verbs to the pupils. Thus, ‘ I shall hare sail
ed from England before you arrive there.’—
1 his sentence was immediately written down
by the pupils, and is a proof that the distinc
tion of complex tenses is as easily conveyed
to the mind by the language of signs, as in
any other manner. "
This class gave further illustration of their
knowledge of grammar, by making the proper
distinction between active and neuter verbs,
and of their knowledge of words, by deriv
ing from the same root the different parts of
speech, and different meanings to which the
words are applicable ; as from the root to ad
mire, the derivations, admiration, admirer,
admirable, &c. were properly used in differ
ent phrases.
The construction of a sentence, where sev
eral relatives are used,-is well known to be
attended with difficulty, even to those who
are in possession of all the senses. We
however, astonished to see the fol lowing sen
tence written down by the pupils with the
utmost readiness.: ‘ A King who was powerful,’
had a palace which, was elegant, and a crown
that was costly.’
Now that the pupil should be made to under
stand by a sign, aud without spelling, the prop
er use of each of these relatives, where they
fill occur in the sentence, will give our read
ers some proof of what the deaf and dumb
language is capable; and particularly, when
it is understood, that the pupils, previous -to
the moment, did not know a single phrase
which was to be dictated to them. • SeverAl
questions were now put, and the answers
given by the pupils.
The First Class, under the immediate in
struction of Mr. Gallaudet, were brought for
ward last. The first thing in their exercise
was to show in what manner it was practica
ble, by mere signs, to designate proper names;
and those of the Scriptures were taken as an
example. The signs were all an actual analy
sis of the most striking traits of the subject jlq-..
noted by the name. Thus when the instructer
made the appropriate signs, the Class immedi
ately wrote the names—Paradise, Canaan,
Sodom, Sinai, &e. While Mr. Gallaudet was
■ making these signs to the pupils, he at the
same time explained to the spectators their
various meanings and combinations. Thus he
made the sign which he explained to us as sig
nifying mountain, then Moses, then the com
mandments, and the Class immediately wrote-
Sinai. It was striking to see the rapidity with
which these- combinations were made, the ex
tent of their application, and the quickness
with which, among a considerable number of
proper names, each was known by its analysis*
and written by the pupils. Phrases were also
dictated by signa, including proper names, and
the Class were directed to write original sen
tences, chosen at the time, without their pre
vious knowledges.' To these succeeded a se
lection of various synonomes, the mode of dis
tinguishing which by signs, was explained,
and the pupils wrote original phrases involving
such synonomes. We should have scarcely
thought it possible, had we not observed the
fact, that by a sign the pupils were made to
understand the difference between the verbs
to perceive and to observe—to discern and to
distinguish—to contrast and to compare ; and
yet this seemed to be easily done, and the
words were written down without hesitation.
The exercises of this Class were concluded
by an illustration of a mode lately invented by
Mr. Gallaudet, of dictating by grammatical

ug»t on the fingers and arm a complete sen
tence involving some of the most difficult
tenses of the verbs ; so that the? pupil, who.was
quite a youth, would compose bis own phrase
by making use of the parts of speech and
tenses of the verbs as dictated by the instruct
er. In this case, the signs for words were en
tirely omitted. Thus -the instructor made a
sign on his finger which the pupil understood
to mean personal pronoun ; then for the sec
ond future tense—then for the present partici
ple of an active verb—for an article—an ad
jective—and an objective case; and the pupil
immediately wrote a phrase of his own con
struction, similar to the following—“ I shall
have been eating the sweet apple.” These
signs were varied through several combina
tions ; and it was surprizing to observe with
what promptness the pupil wrote a sentence
involving all the parts of speech and tenses
of which had been dictated to him—the in
vention and meaning of the phrase being en
tirely his own.
We cannot close this article without one re
m^rk—When we compare the present condi
tion of these unfortunate beings with what
they were only three or four years ago, or
what they would have been at this time, had
not humanity dictated this mode of convey
ing ideas to their mind, we must consider this
Institution as one of the most noble in design,
and successful in its execution, that was ever
founded by the benevoleilce of man. Four
years ago most of these pupils knew nothing
of a God, or his attributes. They now can
converse with fluency on any common subject.

AGRICULTURAL.
Remarks on the late Callie Procession in Phila
delphia, with directions how to effectually
’ promote the breed of Cattle, by Jamis Mease,
M. D. Vtte-Presidbni of the Philadelphia
Society for promoting Agriculture.
Now that the recent ‘ splendid show’ of fat
Cattle has passed, it may be Well to reflect
upon the exhibition • to examine the justness
bi the claims it had to the imposing Ltle-of its
alleged objedt arid utility* to ask ourselves
whether that object find that end will be in
the least promoted by such a procedure, first
and last, as we have witnessed ; and whether
there are not other measures more calculated
to attain both, at a much cheaper rate than
those which have been adopted.
The exhibition was entitled, u Pennsylvania
against.the world;" 65oxen, 4 hogs, 19 sheep,
M) kids, 3 deer, 4 bears; had been kept for
different periods at an extra allowance of pas
ture and short feed, for the purpose of seeing
how much flesh and fat could be put on their
bodies, and how much fat be made to cover
their intestines. The object, as alleged, is the
“ improving the breed of cattle.”’ Let us re
flect a moment, and ask how such an end can
be obtained by the measure.’ pursued I
It is apprehended that it Will not be difficult
to prove that the desirable objects contemplat
ed will not be effected ; that the Zealand spir
it of the concerned have been most egregious
ly misapplied ; that the exhibition was calcu
lated to keep up a bad fashion and ruinous
practice among graziers, and that a more ra
tional plan must be adopted before the desira
ble end of the “ improvement of the breed of
cattle,” can be effected.

The same principles Which Are so well es
tablished with regard to the human race, ap
ply with full force to the brute creation. How
then, it may be asked, is the form of mankind
improved ? Is it by long continued overfeed
ing them, when in the decline of life, to clothe
their bodies and line their interiours with loads
of fat ? What would be thought of a people
who avowed that such means were the best to
mend the shapes of a badly formed communi
ty ? And yet the fashionable practice among
graziers, with their cattle, is hot less absurd.—
Excluding the bears, deer, and kids, from con
sideration, let us confine our remark to cattle,
sheep and hogs. A number of large framed
oxen, with caj/fcious bodies, some of them 8
or 9 years old, are selected, and after the full
est allowance of the finest pasture, either
hired or given to them to the exclusion of the
rest of the stock on the farm, are put up in the
winter, and fed at regular hours with as much
Indian corn-meal, ground oats, potatoes,
pumpkins, and hay, as they can possibly di
gest, and until they groan from the oppression
they suffer, and their hides carded and rubbed
with as much attention as is bestowed upon a
southern race-horse. Sometimes corn-meal
and the other articles arc given to the animal
while at pasture, f rom one to even lour years
of such treatment are required to bring the
animal to the “ sticking point.” Sheep, ot the
New-Leicester or Bakewell breeds are also se
lected for similar experiments. This breed,
from its admirable form, is known to take on
fat with great ease, and individuals of it, with
good pasture, will always in one season become
as fat as any reasonable man ought to desire ;
but by the treatment mentioned, they are So
overloaded with fat as scarcely to be eatable.
The same remark is applicable to hogs,
some of which, upon the late occasion, were
absolutely blind from the projection of fat over
their eyes, and required to be taised from their
beds of straw to take food; None of them
could walk without difficulty. Let us ask
how these ope rations will improve the breed
of cattle ? Did any of these crammed beasts
leave their progeny behind them ? The ab
surdity of naming the object to be effected by
this excessive feeding, ‘ the improvement of
the breed of cattle,’ is evident. Where, more
over, is the utility of such over-feeding ? If it
be said that it furnishes a market for grain and
hay, why not apply the extra feed consumed
by the show cattle, sheep and hogs, to the fat
tening thrice the number of head, all of which
by it would have been turned off in as excel
lent order as Is required for human stomachs of
ordinary powe rs of diges- ion. The difficulty
is to find lean enough in the cattle and sheep
to eat: as to the hogs, nineteen-twentieths of
their weight will be consigned to the manu
facturers of soap.
Any animal, however badly shaped, can be
made inordinately fat, sooner or later, by ex
tra quantities of nourishing food; but this is
not the way to improve the farm stock of a
country. Plain reason and Common sense dic
tate that what we require is a breed that will
soonest furnish the greatest quantity of good
meat or milk at the least expense. It is only
in this way that the advances of the grazier
will be returned to him ; and it is the quick re
turn and circulation of capital that enriches a
nation. 7he money expended and even lost
by heavy Show beef cattle, impoverish
more or less a country, by diminishing the
means which the leeders would have had with
out such expenditure, of bringing to market a
greater number of cattle in future.
Two methods, and two only, exist by which
farm stock can be improved. The first it by
breeding from those native individuals of a
kind, possessing the forms known to take cn
most easily flesh and fat, and by occasionally
crossing their progeny with others having
points in which those resulting from former ex
periments may be deficient. If milk be the j
object, subjects should be selected wh’ichyii Id |
great quantities of it, and of a good quality, ’
and retain it longest ; and crosses may be '
made with those mules within our reach hav
ing the best forms and least offal. Materials
for such experiments are by no means deficient
among us; but, unfortuLately, the spirit for
slow improvement does not sufficiently prevail
among our intelligent cultivators. In this way
a mail may in a few yean obtain a breed, from I

The peculiar marks which designate this

LATEST FROM ENGLAND.
By the regular trading ship Martha,
Capt. Sketchley, in 38 days from Liver
pool, we have received our files of Lon
don papers to the 22d Liverpool, to
the 24th; and Lloyd’s and the London

The most interesting and gratifying
intelligence by this arrival, is an account
of the result of the commencement of
hostilities between the Austrians and Ne
apolitans. It would seem, though there
is not, as we have seen, any official in
telligence concerning it, that a body of
the Austrian forces were at a place call-
Rieti, a town about forty miles north
east from Rome. The Neapolitans-are
stated to have advanced to that place,
and on the 9th of March io have attack
ed the Austrians, and after a smart en
gagement to have gained the victory.—
It is, however, stated that the battle
cost them their principal officer,. Gen.
Pepe. These accounts' come by the
way of Paris. The time and place when,
and where the engagement took place
agree in all the accounts we have seen,
which are circumstances in favour of its
correctness. Still there appears to be
some ground for doubt. The first ac
count of the commencement of hostil
ities was published ire London on the
20th of March- The Statesman,, of 3
o’clock, the same day, says—“ We are
this moment informed that an express
arrived this morning from Paris, which
has brought the confirmation of the san
guinary conflict, on the 9th fast, between
the Austrians and Neapolitans, in which
the Austrians were defeated.” The
Courier, on the other side, states, “that
accounts have been received from Par
is, dated on Monday morning, (the 19th;)
but they do not furnish any details of a
battle having been fought. If any affair
haff taken place (add these accounts) it
was only a very partial one.”—lt would
certainly be strange if the story could
be wholly without foundation. All ac
counts agree that it took place at Rieti,
on the 9th.of March, and that General
Pepe was killed..
If reliance can be placed upon it, the
event is highly creditable to the Nea
politans. The plan of marching to
meet, instead of waiting to receive, their
adversary, does them credit; and the
spirit and enthusiasm with which they
attacked and defeated them is very hon
ourable to their courage and conduct.—
We shall wait with a good deal of solici-

t ude for more certain intelligence em
cerning this event. Should the Nea
politans, at the onset, have gained a seri
ous advantage over the Austrians, the
effect of it can scarcely fail toexcite new
zeal and courage in the defenders of
their country and its independence.

EUROPE.
The drama which has opened in the South
of Europe, is rapidly unfolding—new scenes
are fast meeting the eye, and fresh actors are
crowding upon the stage. The cry of free
dom, which burst forth in Spain and was re
echoed in the South of Italy, now reverbe
rates from the North; and amid the very
flashing of fifty thousand Austrian bayonets,
the Piedmontese join their shouts to those of
the proscribed Neapolitans. In the mean
time, the latter have bravely met a detach
ment of their invaders, and have conquered
them—thus gathering strength and confidence
from their very first effort. With an enemy in
front, flushed with success, and with foes eve
ry moment starting up in the rear, the Austri
An army may ere long find itself, like the
French army at Moscow, obliged to fight its
way out of the country which it entered to
conquer. Nor is it very extravagant to sup
pose that, having driven back her invaders,
Italy may herself strike a blow that shall shake
Germany to its centre.—The despotism of one
man was not prostrated in order to strengthen
the iron thrones of three or four despots.—
Prussia and Austria, and Russia perhaps, are
now kindling a fire, which may light their own
subjects on to liberty; and while Frederick, and
Francis, and Alexander are crusading against
Constitutions abroad, they may be forced, at
home, tq drink of the very cup which they
are so solicitous to dash from others' lips.
Perhaps this is all very extravagant for so
ber journalists; but, if it be so, it is a sub
ject on which a little enthusiasm is excusable.
In sober seriousness, however, our readers will
find, in the intelligence from Italy, matter for
much interesting reflection. The revolution
in Piedmont is a serious affair for Austria, and
a very timely and efficient aid to Naples. The
Austrian army, unless speedily and power
fully reinforced, must be destroyed.

selves against Naples, and Spain, and Portugal ;

The celebrated Elegy in a Church-yard, by
Gray, is well known and justly admired by
every one who has the least pretensions to
taste. But with all its polish and deep
poetick beauty and feeling, it always ap
peared to me to be defective, and 1 have
met with a remark in Cecil’s Remains to
the same effect. Amid a scene so well cal
culated to awaken in a pious mind reflec
tions on the sublime truths and inspiring
hopes of Christianity, Gray, with the ex
ception of two or three somewhat equivo
cal expressions, says scarcely a word
which mizht not have been said by one
Who believed that “ dßnth was an eternal
sleep,” and who was disposed to regard
the humble tenants of those tombs as in
deed “ each in his narrow cell forever laid.”
With these views, I have regretted that
sentiments similar to the following had not
sprung up in the heart, and received the
exquisite touches of the classick pen of
Gray. 1 do not offer them to supply the
deficiency. This would be as presumptu
ous and hopeloss an attempt as that of the
English artists to repair the mutilations
which time or accident had occasioned a
mong the inimitable relicks of Grecian ge
nius. They might, with great propriety,
have followed the stanza, begininng “ Far
from the madding crowd’s ignoble strife.”
NO airy dreams tbeir simple fancies fir’d,
No thirst for wealth, nor panting after fame ;
But truth divine sublimer hopes inspir'd,
And lur’d them onward to a nobler aim.
From every cottage, with the day arose
The hallow’d voice of spirit-breathing pray
er;
And artless anthems, at its peaceful close,
Like holy incense, charm’d the evening air.
Though they, each tome of human lore un
known,
The brilliant path of science never trod,
The sacred volume claim’d their hearts alone,.
Which taught the way to glory and to God.
Here they from truth’s eternal fountain drew
The pure and gladdening Waters day by day;
Leam’d, since our days are evil, fleet and few,
To walk in wisdom’s bright and peaceful
way.
In yon lone pile, o’er which hath sternly pass’d
The heavy hand of ail-destroying'time,
Through whose low mouldering aisles now sighs
the blast,
And round whose altars grass and ivy climb—
They gladly throng’d, their grateful hymns to
• raise,
Oft as the calm and holy Sabbath shone ;
The mingled tribute of their prayers and
praise
In sweet communion rose before the throne.
Here, from those honour’d lips which sacred
fire
From heaven’s high chancery hath touch’d,
they hear
Truths which their real inflame, their hopes
inspire,
Give wings to faith, and check affliction’s
tear.
When life flow'd by, and. like an angel, Death
Came to release them to the world on high,
Praise trembled still on each expiring breath,
And holy triumph-beam’d from every eye.
Then gentle hands their “ dust to dust" con*'
sign ;
With quiet tears the simple rites are said ;
And here they sleep, till, at the tnnnp divine,
The earth and ocean render up their dead.-
Philadtlphia, April 14.

MISCELLANY.
MR. BURKE.
When the trial of Mr. Hastings com
menced in Westminster-Hail., the first
two days were taken up in reading the
articles of impeachment against him ;
and four more were occupied’ by Mr.
Burke in opening the case, and stating
the grounds of the accusation. Never
were the powers of that great man dis
played to such advantage as on this oc
casion. The contrast which he drew
between the ancient and the modern
state of Hindostan was sketched with
the hand of a master, and wrought up
in a manner that could not fail to fix the
attention, and to command admiration ;
when at length he came to speak of Mr.
Hastings, no terms can describe the
more than mortal vehemence with which
he hurled h s manifold accusations a
gainst him. He seemed for the moment
as if armed to destroy with all the light
ning of all the passions. The whole
annals of judicial or contain noth
ing finer than his conclusion.
“1 impeach Warren Hastings,” said
he. “in the name of the Commons of
Great-Britain in Parliament assembled,
whose parliamentary trust he has abus
ed.
“ I impeach him in the name of the
Commons of Great-Britain, whose na
tional character he has dishonoured.
“ I impeach him in the name of the
people of India, whose laws, rights, and
liberties, he has subverted; whose prop
erties he has destroyed; whose country
be has laid waste and desolate.
W I impeach him in the name of hu
man nature itself, which he has so cruel
ly outraged, injured and oppressed. And
I impeach him in the name and by the
virtue of those eternal laws of justice,
which ought equally to pervade in both
sexes, every age, condition, rank, and
situation, in the world.”
The agitation produced by this speech
was such that the whole audience ap
peared to have felt one convulsive emo
tion; and when it was over, it was some
time before Mr. Fox could obtain a hear
ing.
Amidst the assemblage of concurring
praises which this speech excited, none
was more remarkable than the tribute
of Mr. Hastings himself. u For a half an
hour,” said that gentleman, “I looked
up at the orator in a reverie of won-

det; and during that apace I actually
felt myself the most culpable man on
earth.” Had the sentiment concluded
here, our readers would not believe that
it was in the language or manner of Mr.
Hastings. M But,” continued he, M I re
curred to my own bosom, and there
found a conscience which consoled me
under all I heard and all 1 suffered.”

On Wednesday night, Monsieur Alexandre,
whose fame had already reached this country
from the Continent, gave his first publick ex
hibition at these rooms, as ventriloquist; and
we are happy to say that his success fully
confirmed the high reputation which he had
acquired abroad. •
The performance commenced between
Mons. Alexandre, in the character of a wait
er, and an imaginary old and infirm bon vivant,
hi which the former is compelled much against
his will to prepare an omelet. This entails
upon him the necessity of plaining and saw
ing wood, striking a light, and frying the eggs
over a. candle ; these different sounds he imi
tated in the happiest and most astonishing man
ner. After this, followed a dialogue between
a chimney sweep and Mons. Alexandre. In
this the voice of the sweep, modulated in his
descent down the chimney, was so exactly
imitated, that a slight suspicion of confederacy
pervaded the minds of several of the audience.
This doubt, however, so creditable to the rare
talents of the Ventriloquist, was most happily
removed in the progress of the representation.
We have not leisure to follow him through the
various humorous dialogues which took place ;
we will, therefore, simply enumerate them.—
A conversation between Mons. Alexandre,
some one shut np in a room, and a servant
in the cellar—a dialogue with a man enclosed
in a trunk—a conversation between a game
keeper, a countryman and his wife, illustrat
ing the effects of an alarm in a house guards
ed by several dogs—the quarrel between these
last and some cats, followed by the cries of an
infant awakened by the uproar; and tire vain
attempts of the game-keeper’s young wife to
pacify the child, were delineated with such
truth, that doubts might have again arisen, as
6o the existence of a confederacy, had not
the removal of the screen revealed to our
astonished senses Mons. Alexandre solus,
who m conclusion, caused a voice to issue
from stomach of one of the spectators,
singing the French air Malbrduk. The Duke
of Clarence wa« present, and expressed him
self most highly gratified with the perform
ance. The company was numerous and of
the most fashionable nature; we observed
most of the foreign Ambassadors present.
BOSTON-, APRIL 28.
YANKEE BET.
A bet was made in Providence, on
the late gubernatorial election, of a
Cuke of Gingerbread, to be of as large
dimensions as the winner should direct.
Accordingly, a cake was baked by a
Mr. William Barstow, under direction,
of the foilowing dimensions. It was
ten feet long, two feet two inches wide,
two inches thick, and contained 43 feet
four, inches, board measure. On Satur
day last, it was exhibited for distribu
tion, handsomely figured, and dressed
out with box. In “• eating the cake,”
all parties cordially united ; the recipi
ents hoping that it was a foretaste of
the racy, soft and refreshing adminis
tration of the successful candidate.

In SENATE, TUESDAY, APRIL 17, 1821.
A sufficient number of members ap
pearing in their seats, the Senate imme
diately proceeded to business; and, after
choosing a Committee to wait on his Ex
cellency the Governour, advising him
of their readiness to receive such com
munications as he might deem necessary
to make, took up the subject of the pro
posed sale of the State’s Land, in Maine,
which, after some conversation, was re
ferred to the Committee appointed at
the kst session, to consider and report
thereon. This Committee consists of
the Hon. Messrs. Brooks, Welles, and
Sullivan.
The Senate, desirous of some ftirther
deliberation on the course necessary to
be pursued, on the pending trial of Judge
Prescott, the floor was cleared of stran
gers, and the Senate, after sitting some
time with closed doors, adjourned to to
morrow. '
WEDNESDAY, APRIL iff——Twenty-six
members were present this day.
a Message w<teTeceived ibom bis Ex
cellency the Governour, accompanied
with sundry’ document*, the most materi
al of which was a Resolve of the Leg
islature of Maine, ratifying and confirm
ing the agreement made and concluded
by the Commissioners appointed by that
State, and the State of Massachusetts,
for the disposal of the publick land in
the former, belonging to the latter State.
The Hon. Messrs. Welles was charg
ed with a message to the House of Rep
resentatives, notifying that the Senate
were about to proceed on the trial of
Judge Prescott
Mr. Sturgis, of Boston, came up with
a message, that the House, accompani
ed by the Managers of the Impeachment,
would immediately attend the Senate.
The time assigned for the trial of
James Prescott, Esq. Judge of Probate
f--- the County of Middlesex, having ar
rived, at 11 o’clock the Senate proceed
ed to resolve itself into a
Court of Impeachment.
The members of the Hoose of Rep
resentatives, preceded by their Speak
er, came in and took the seats assigned
them.
The Hon. Mr. Hyde, who was not
present at the former organization of
this Cburt, took the oath prescribed for
its members. ■
The respondent having been called,
came into Court, attended by Messrs.
W. Prescott, Blake, Webster, Hoar,
Hubbard, and Peabody, as his Counsel.
The President of the Court having
informed the respondent that the time
assigned for his trial had now arrived,
and that the Court were ready to pro
ceed in that trial, asked him if he was
prepared to answer the Articles of Im
peachment alleged against him.
Mr. Webster rose and informed the
Hon. President that he had come here,
in company with his learned associates,
to act as Counsel for the respondent.—
Having received a copy of the charges
exhibited against him, his honourable
client had prepared his answers to them,
and had directed him, with permission
of this Hon. Court, to read them. He
then proceeded to read the answer,
which is very elaborate —the reading
occupying more than an hour.
The answer having been concluded,
the .President asked the Managers, on
the part of the House of Representa
tives, if they were ready to reply.
on the part of the Managers,
informed the Court that they were ready
to reply at such time as the Court may
see fit to assign. Four o’clock, this after
noon, having been assigned, with con
sent of the Counsel on both sides, the
Court adjourned to that time.
Mjoumed to 3 o'clock.
Afternoon Session.
At 3 o’clock, the Senate again met
and proceeded to the consideration of
legislative business, until 4 o’clock, when
it again resolved itself into a
....Court of Impeachment.
The members of the House of Rep
resentatives came in, and
Mr. King, on behalf of the House of
Representatives, offered a Replication to ’
the Answer presented by James Pres
cott, Esq. Mr. K. then opened the cause
on the part of the prosecution, in a very
eloquent address to the Court, of near
an hour’s length. He then proceeded
to call the witnesses, who were ques
tioned by the Managers, and cross-ex
amined by the Counsel, for the defend
ant.

opened at 9 o’clock.

athan Loring, Samuel Whiting, Esq. Jo
siah Crosby, Esq. Benjamin Wyman, Al
pheus Ware, Abner Bartlett, Esq. John

Mr. Shaw, one of the Managers, op

agers, also opposed, at considerable

spondent's Counsel, replied to them, also,

morning.

BY THE MAILS.
NEW-YORK, APRIL 18.
Latest from England.
Yesterday the regular packet ship,
James Monroe, Capt. Rogers, arrived
at this port, in 45 days from Liverpool,
which place she left on the 2d of March—
seven days later than the last arrival.
By this vessel we have received our
regular files of London papers to the
evening of the 28th of February.
The affairs of Naples, and the move
ments of the Austrian forces, are among
the most interesting subjects mentioned
in the papers. The London Courier,
of the 27th of February, contains the
Austrian Manifesto, which will be found
in our paper this morning. The Cou
rier says, it makes out a case which
justifies a course pursued under the alli
ed Sovereigns. Mr. Wilberforce seems
to entertain a different opinion with re
gard to their conduct. In a debate in the
House of Commons, on the 21st of Feb
ruary, on a motion by Sir James Mack
intosh for the papers referred to in the
Circular of the British government,
Mr. Wilberforce said, “he conceived
the principle of the allied powers to be
odious, unjust and abominable. To him
it appeared likely that Europe would
be, lor some time to come, involved in
trouble, because free constitutions were
every where expected by the people. Such
an expectation naturally called into ac
tion a high and generous spirit which
could not be subdued.”
The Manifesto is certainly a well-writ
ten document; but according to our judg
ment, contains nothing more than a
plausible statement of the reasons for
the interference of those powers in the
affairs of an independent nation. The
amount of the reasoning is, what has
been all along considered would prove
to be the fact, that the example of Na
ples is, in the opinion of their Imperial
and Royal Majesties, dangerous to what
they are pleased to denominate “• legit
imate governments,” and therefore
must not be suffered to continue and
spread its contagion. Much, indeed, is
said of the Carbonari, and of the sol
diers ; but it is apparent that it is the ex
ample of the people and of the army,
that the Sovereigns most emphatically
dread.
That much stress would be laid upon
the interest and activity which the sol
diery has had in the various recent rev
olutions in the South of Europe, we
have never had a doubt- In the answer
of Lord Castlereagh to the above-men
tioned motion of Sir James Mackiatosh,
he remarked, that “it was much to be
regretted that the troops had been induc
ed to depart from their allegiance to the
crown, and that soldiers had asserted their
opinions as to the forms of government
which ought to be established.” In the
great revolution of 1688, in England,
the soldiers very generally departed
from their allegiance to James, and unit
ed with William, very much to the sat
isfaction of the great body of the na
tion ; and they rendered much aid in the
establishment of the government in the
hands of William and Mary. It is, how
ever, not to be wondered at, that Aus
tria, Prussia and Russia, situated as they
are, and forced by circumstances to
maintain large standing armies, even in
time of peace, should stand in fearful
apprehension of the consequences that
might easily follow a disposition on the
part of their troops, to assert their opin
ions as to the form of government, which
ought to be established- Two or three
hundred thousand disciplined troops,
with arms in their hands, might shake
the throne even of the Emperour of all
the Russias.
It seems the Duke de Gallo was sent
forward to Naples, to inform the Par
liament of the ultimatum of the Allied
Sovereigns. He reached that city on
* the 9th of Feb. and proceeded immedi
, ately to the legislative body who were
| already assembled. Before he could
; finish reading his instructions, he was
interrupted by loud cries of “ War—
war—war,” from every side of the
assembly. It is stated that one propo
sition was, that the Neapolitans should
give up the form of the Spanish con
stitution, and adopt that of the British,
with modifications- This appears to
us so strange an idea, that we Can scarce
’ ly credit it. The British Constitution
has never bee» reduced to writing at
home, as we have heard, and we think
it would puzzle an Englishman, much
more an Austrian or a Russian, to put it
' down in black and white. But if they
had it, they would not know what to do
with it. It is as much as the British na
tion, with alt 4heir wisdbmi, learning,
and experience, can do, to keep steady
under it. The Carbonari would make
: wild steerage under it.
The Neapolitans make a shew of re
sistance.—We most cordially hope they
may persevere, and succeed, to their
complete emancipation. The attempt
to control them on the part of the
allied powers is flagitious in the ex
treme ; and if persevered in, may prob
ably in the end involve Europe in war,
and possibly cost some of her monarchs
tlieiir thrones.. [New-York Adv.
I ft appears that the Neapolitans have
; not been deficient in providing for their

defence. On the 11th of February',
two bodies of Neapolitans, (regular
troops) had advanced to the frontier.—
One ot these consists of 45,000 men, un
der General Carascora, who was ad
vancing by the usual Roman road, thro’
the Mola di Gaeta and Terracina.—The
other, of 40,000, under General W.
Pepe, on the line of the Abruzzi. The
former were pushing forward towards
Rome, arid were expected to arrive at
the Papal capital on the 15th tilt, long
before the enemy could advance to its
assistance. Accounts from Rome ac
tually state, that a corps of Neapoli
tans, 20,000 strong, had reached Velle
tri, on the 13th, within 26 miles of the
seat ot the Papal government. The
magazines, established at Rome for the
use of the Austrians, would consequent
ly tall into the hauds of (jarascora; and
the whole revolutionary spirit of the
Roman people would be roused and
encouraged by this decided movement-
Of the Austrian army, of 90,000 men,
which has passed the Po, it is not ex
pected that more than 60,000 will be at
liberty to act as a body—as there are*
numerous points, which in the present
unsettled state of the minds of the peo-'
pie south of the Po, it would be dan
gerous to leave unoccupied.—lt* was not
until the 15th ult.that the advanced guard
of the Austrians reached Fano, in the
Adriatick, about eight days’ march from
Rome.
The Pope, who is placed in a very
awkward predicament between the two ,
contending parties, has issued a proc
lamation, in which he expresses a hope,
that neither party will occupy Rome.—
His Holiness says, Ist, that he cannot
help the foreign troops passing througl*
his dominions—2d, that he receives
tbe Austrians as friends, who march
only out of pure regard to Italy—3d,
that he will maintain a strict neutrali
ty—4th, that the foreign regular troops
shall not be resisted in the passage ; but,
sth, that any of the “evil-disposed
class,” [meaning thereby the Neapoli- •
tans, whether regular or irregular]
who shall attempt the same friendly
freedom repassing through the Holy
territory, “ shall be opposed” with all
his might.

NAPLES, FEB. 11.
The Duke de Gallo arrived on the
9th with the ultimatum of the Allied
Sovereigns. On the outside of the city
gate he entered his private carriage,
and proceeded immediately to the Par
liament, who, according to the instruc
tions previously given by him, were al
ready assembled. Before he could fin
ish reading the ultimatum of the Con
gress at Laybach, he was interrupted by
reiterated cries of‘War! war! war!’
from all parts of the assembly. I have
not seen a copy of the ultimatum, but
learn that the following are the princi
pal points contained in it :—
1. That the Neapolitans shall aban
don the Spanish Constitution, and adopt
that of the British nation, with some
corrections and modifications suitable to
Naples.
2. That during the period while this
re-organizing shall be effecting, and for
six years afterwards, the capital of the
kingdom of the Two Sicilies, and all the
fortresses, shall be occupied by Austri
an garrisons.
3. On these conditions a general am
nesty will be accorded. And,
4. The pay and subsistence of the Aus
trian troops will not be at the charge of
the Neapolitan nation.
The circulation of the terms of the
ultimatum in Naples produced the high
est degree of excitement in the publick
mind. Every man is ready to die in de
fence of the liberties of the country.—
The military dispositions are proceed
' ing with the greatest activity. Gen.
Guglielmo Pepe commands in the Abruz
zi, Arcovito, in. San Germano ; Carasco
sa and Ambrosio are marching to Rome,
where they are expected to arrive on
the 15th. Filangieri will remain in Na
ples with the reserve. The Prince
Vicar-General will be at that point where
his presence shall be found most essen
tial. Bergani commands at Gaeta, The
regular troops at Naples amount to 60,
000 infantry, and 20,000 cavalry, with a
good supply of artillery. The militia
are estimated to amount to 100,000 men.
Finally, great reliance is placed on the
publick spirit and known courage of the
Nteapolitan citizens and' peasants, in the
event of its being found necessary to
have recourse to the system of Gueril
las.”

[The following notice of the late Mrs. Mary
Sutton, whose death was mentioned in our
paper of the 11th inst. was communicated

It is often said of those who die, that they
were resigned to the will of God : but in the
resignation of many, there is no convincing ev
idence of an interest in Christ. A long and
painful sickness often reconciles the sick to
death, as a release from their sufferings ; and
some are resigned to the will of God in their
distress merely because resistance would be
fruitless. Resignation, on either of these
grounds, is no proof of Christian character, or
of fitness for death But, in the case before us,
we have an instance of resignation from higher
motives, and not of resignation merely, but of
joy and peace in believing—that “ peace of
God which passeth understanding.” The de
ceased richly shared in the divine favour.—
God was graciously pleased to manifest him
self to her in an uncommon degree. In view
of the richness of the grace of God, and the
many wonderful tokens of his favour towards
her, she said, “ Why should I doubt ?” She en
joyed the presence and smiles of God to such
a degree that she seemed often to have arrived
at heaven, and to have commenced a partici
pation of the joys there reserved for the people
of God. Earthly objects had almost vanished
from her view, and her great desire was that
the hour of death might be hastened, that she
might be with Him whom her soul loved. No
murmur was heard to escape from her lips.—
Her sufferings she received as nothing in com
parison with those of Christ, and she was wil
ling to endure more, or to be released from all
her trials, as God saw best. When a friend
approached, and offered to converse or pray
with her, she often exclaimed—“ lam happy:
I cannot hear you now : my joy is so great that
my feeble body cannot support an increase.”—
When the hour of her dissolution had arrived,
she said—“ I have long been waiting for and
desiring this happy hour.” Among her last
words, she exclaimed—“ 1 feel the support of
Christ : lam happy lam willing to go :
death to me has no terrours.”—Such a great
and continued degree of joy has, probably,
rarely been witnessed : And we trust that she
has now gone where those joys Will be greatly
increased, and will never be interrupted. In
view of such a death-bed scene, who can but
exclaim—“ Let me die the death of the right
eous."

The soil of Florida is divisible info
three grand varieties : pine barrens,
savannahs, and marshes. Other varie
ties have been given by some authors,
but are mere shades of admixture, or
points and lines of contact between the
three foregoing. Pine forest-land here,
elsewhere, is remarkable for its ster
ility in the production of the domesti
cated species of plants, though produc
tive in an indefinite variety of indige
nous vegetables.. The syl of the pine
woods of Florida is, perhaps; as sandy as
in any other part of the United States.
A ridge of dry, and; in a great part, of
unwooded hills, or hiltocks, destitute of
water, extends from Eokefanoke Swamp
to an unknown distance southward, west
of St. John’s anti Nassau rivers. This
ridge, no doubt, sinks into the common
level of the country before reaching
the cape, or, perhaps, even the lati
tude of 27 deg.
Savannah, or prairie land, in Florida,
is, in strictness, mere varieties of swamp.
The former is, indeed, part of the lat
ter, with elevation sufficient to admit
culture without artificial drainage. The
prarie grounds of Florida, being com
posed of so great a part of animal exu
vi®, are generally productive, but are
confined in extent.
Swamps, or marshes, next to pine
woods cover the largest portion of Flor
ida. A small share of these flat re
gions may be reclaimed, but the far
greater part being morasses, arc beyond
the ordinary powers of human meliora
tion. On some points of consideration,
the Florida, swamps may be considered
valuable; they are, in many places,
covered with excellent timber, and
where of proper tenacity, would afford
good grazing for cattle.
Another variety of soil occurs in Flor
ida, called hammock land.. This species
forms, in most instances, an interval be
tween the pine tracts and the marshes,
or savannahs, and, indeed, in no respect
differs from the latter, except in being
covered with wood. The hammock
land, not only of Florida, but of all the
couthem section of the United States,
yields, next to river alluvion, the best
arable soil. In Alabama, Georgia, and
Missisippi, the hammock lands form
xnucti the largest part o<f Qio cujtivated

surface. The quality of the soil alter
nates from that of savannah and river al
luvion, to that of the most unproductive
pine barrens. Bay galls, or wet spongy
spots, very frequently deteriorate ham
mock land. This inconvenience is les
sened by a slight, and removed by a
considerable inclination of surface.
To those who visit Florida with high
raised opinions in favour of its natural
advantages, much disappointment is in
store ; but those who commence an ex
amination of this country with expecta
tions to meet with nothing but sterility,
will not be less, but more agreeably dis
appointed than the former class. In a
space so extensive, and with a climate
so mild, many spots have concentrated
all the rich features of a tropical physi
ognomy. When it is considered that,
when compared with the entire area, so
small a part of any equal surface in the
United States is actually cultivated, it
may be conceded, that if one twentieth
part of its superficies can be brought
under the dominion of the orchard, the
scythe, or the plough, that, even in an
agricultural point of view, Florida is an
invaluable acquisition to the people of
the United States.
It may be repeated that the whole
peninsula owes its existence to mineral
and animal deposition. As far as the
earth has been penetrated, this inference
is supported by facts. The entire fer
tility found on? detached spots is due to
animal matter. By means of this class
of substances, as the original sand banks
rose above the waves, a scanty vegeta
tion was formed, which, in the lapse of
countless ages, has clothed this recently
formed expanse with herbage. We
may, from what has been established,
safely form the induction, that the soil
oi Florida, like that of ail low, barren
regions, situated near the tropicks, is
much more favourable to the produc
tion of orchard fruit-trees, than to grass
es, esculent roots, or other animal or
short-lived field or garden vegetables.
