HORRIBLE TRANSACTION!
On the evening of the 4th inst. the
house of a poor widow, in Goffstown, by
the name of Ayer, was entered by a
ruffian, and an attempt made to murder
the family, at that time consisting of the
widow and her daughter, aged about 13.
The circumstances, as collected from
the sufferers, and the appearance of the
house, are somewhat as follows :—
Daniel D. Farmer came into the house
that evening with some biscuit and a bot
tle of rum, with which he was very
free—urging the widow to drink several
times, with which request she sometimes
complied. He then told her that he
was going to kill her, and immediately
knocked her down with a club ; upon
which the child began screaming for as
sistance. The ruffian then quit the
mother—knocked down the child—drag
ged her out of doors—took up a stone
weighing about six pounds, and pounded
her head until he supposed her dead.—
He then dragged her into the house,
leaving the blood as he drew her along
in considerable quantity, and threw her
under the bed. He then returned to
the mother, to finish her; took the tongs
and broke them over herheadr this not
dispatching her, he took the fire-shovel
and beat in her skull in several places,
one of which is open about 4 inches
long, and near half an inch wide, leav
ing the brain visible for the same space !
This was not sufficient; but, in order to
conceal the horrid deed, he took a roll
of cotton cloth which happened to be in
the way, tore it in pieces, set it on fire,
ams strewed it about the house ; then
scattered the fire round the room, throw
ing such quantity upon the child as to
burn her legs and thighs to a blister.—
The child is supposed to have been in a
state of insensibility at the time, - as she
does not know how she came to be so
burned.. zAfter doing all this, he left the
house, probably supposing it would burn
up and consume the bodies of its occu
pants ; but, strange to relate, the child,
notwithstanding her violent treatment,
recovered her senses, crawled from un
der the bed and found the house on fire
in several places. She looked for the
water-pail, but this was not to be found,
the villain having taken the precaution
to throw it out of the door. She then
thought of a pot of beer, with which
she extinguished the fire. She after
wards managed to get her mother upon
the bed, and got on by her side, where
they remained till morning ; when the
child had sufficient strength to get up
and go a quarter of a mile, to the near
est neighbour’s, and give information of
the horrid deed. The neighbours were
alarmed, proceeded to the house, and
found the woman alive, but in an insen
sible state
A physician was immediately called,
her wounds dressed, and she so far re
covered as to relate who the person was
that committed the act. The child, not
withstanding she performed all the above
mentioned services, is at this time una
ble to turn herself in bed without assist
ance. The woman’s head is literally
cut into checkers with the blade of the
shovel, which was very bloody, and hairs
were found upon it corresponding with
the woman’s hair; and the stone, with
which the child was beat, was known by

its being bloody, -and bairt upon it cor
responding with the child’s hair. In fine,
the appearance of the house and the
family was a most shocking spectacle.—
Physicians are of opinion that the wo
nlan cannot survive.
■ The person who committed this dia
bolical deed has been taken into custody
and committed to prison.
BOSTON, APRIL 14.
COURT OF IMPEACHMENT.
The Senate Chamber of the State
House, has been prepared for the
Court of Impeachment, to sit on the
trial of James Prescott, Judge of Pro
bate, in the County of Middlesex, on
Wednesday next. The circular seats
ot the Senate board, being found to
occupy too much room, have been re
moved ; and a new arrangement of the
places of members has taken place.—
The President of the Court will retain
his position in front; but his desk and
the tables of half the Senate are plac
ed in a range, round a semi-circular
platform, a little elevated from the
floor ot the room. In front, round a
corresponding semi-circle, the tables
and chairs oi the rest of the members
are disposed on a level with the floor,
immediately below the other seats.—
The Clerk’s desk is in the centre of
the second semi-circle, directly in front
of the President. By this disposition
the whole Senate will front the folding
doors and gallery. Along the line form
ing the chord of the semi-circle, are
the tables and seats for the managers
of the Impeachment on the part cf
the House of Representatives ; the ta
bles and chairs for the defendant and
his Counsel, and a stand, directly in the
centre, for the witnesses. Seats for
the officers and members of the House
will he arranged on the floor of the
Senate Chamber, whenever they at
tend the Court as a body.
The Court will probably be opened
on the 2d day oi the session, after no
tice has been given by a committee to
the Governour, of the re-assembling
of the two Houses, and their readiness
to act upon any communication he may
think proper to make. The defendant,
we hear, has engaged" numerous Coun
sel, (some of them quite eminent,) and
the trial, we suppose, will occupy more
than a week. Every article will form
a distinct subject of discussion, and the
sentence of the Court must be pro
nounced upon each separate charge.

Messrs. Editors,—
1 hope that my countrymen generally do not
possess that irascible temper which I fear by na
ture belongs to me. If they do, lam certain
they cannot relish for any length of time, the
reiterated, uncandid and brutal assaults which
• are made upon our common country by the
Edinburgh Reviewers. • For example, take the
following: “The Americans are intellectually
and morally savage, and in those parts where
learning is neglected, man is still a wild and
ferocious animal; and, consequently, dangerous
in proportion to the number of the, herd.”—
They remember the dire doings of’76.

I.
I WISH (by way of ornament or so)
We had the knack which Scottish bards pos-
•sess,
To hire some clever scavans whom they know,
To varnish verse before it goes to press.
They call them critickr, alias reviewers ;
A downright honest, scientifick pack,
Who kernel ’mong old Edinburgh sewers,
And prowl abroad by night to make attack ;
Who vainly boast they give to science law,
And hold the literary world in awe.
11.
These northern yelpers, with their learning
frantick,
Make sorry work with rhymes this side th’ At
lantick ;
They rend in tatters harmless songs to Cupid,

Contend pur dogs don’t bark, they are so stupid?
Our girls so clumsy, that they cannot dance.
How laudable, to love their race so well;
These snarlers do not mangle one another.
But wag their tails to all, save Peter Bell,*
And treat each chiming Scotchman as a broth-■
er.
111.
I wish we Yankees, like the Highland Scots,'

Call’d glens, where poets might invoke the
muse—
I wish we had a score of bonny lasses,
(I’d have the bonny lasses wear their shoes)
To teach our awkward girls some “ westlin '
dashes
To make an oaten cake, a barley rig,
And dance with ease the highland fling and jig.
We want a kirk, and priests to check the ;
sneerers,
And preach down lux’ry to their ragged hear
ers. •
IV.
Some haunted castle ruinous and old.
Among the western hills they have a plenty;
Some boorish landlord who his tales has told
To furnish stuff for novels more than twenty—
’Bout .Robin Hood, Rob Roy, and Lady Ma
rion,
And gangs of robbers who infest their moun
tains,
Where they their cursed machinations cany om,
Steal sheep, pollute their maids, and poison
fountains— ■ •
A few sagacious, highland shepherd dogs.
To huht bewilder’d flocks in fens and bogs.
V.
Alas r we Have no ruin’d monastery
For witless, love-sick lasses to get lost in I
Nor have we tender-hearted swains, who tarry
All night round fallen piles, because they’re
cross’d in
Love for pretty maids, who are so modest,
They lose themselves on purpose to be found
By those they seem to hate; which is the odd
est
And queerest caper on romantick ground.
We have no border tours nor border ravages— >
What then ? By way of set-off, we have sata
ger.t «
VI.
Had we such rich materials for novels,
And when our works were finish’d, such re
viewers
To puff our works—we’d lay aside our shovels,
Transform our cobblers, journeymen and hew
ers,
And make them over into story-writers
Of feats of old Scotch Baror.saud their fighters—
A proper civil, v/elhbred band of robbers.
Whose grand achievements, for the romance
jobbers,
Have furnish’d fragments, (say two hundred
bales)
Enough to make a wagon-load of tales.’
VII.
Then we could tune our harps oh “Moray
hills”—
Alas! we’ve no such hills, nor tuneful harpers
As Ramsay, Scott and Bums.—No rippling rills
To wake the muse.’—We are a horde of sharp
ers*
Pfedlars, pick-pockets, these North-Britons say.
Who have no skill to write a roundelay.
And then our savages are quite too frantick

run,

Remarks on Capt. Parry's
Expedition.
The expedition under the command
of Cupt. R jus, although very important
and interer.jng* from the numerous nau
tical' observations it made in Baffin’s
Bay, still did not satisfy the expect
lions of men of science and the pub-

lick, fa regard to the North-west Paa
sage, The Lords of the Adntiralfy, as
we are led to believe, from a statement*
(we think a harsh one,) in the Quarter
ly Review, were, on the whole, some
what dissatisfied with Capt. Rom’s in
vestigation of Sir James Lanctfster’s
Sound, and were of opinion, that if a
passage existed in Baffin’s Bay, it must
be somewhere in that quarter. In or
der to determine this important geo
graphical problem, an expedition was
fitted out last year, consisting of two
strong vessels, the Hecla and Griper,
which were placed under the command
of Lieut. Parry. This gentleman,
whose talents and feelings are wonhy
of the best and most glorious days of
nautical enterprise and discovery, was
accompanied by a chosen band of in
trepid and experienced officers; and
the vessels were manned by crews full
of zeal and enthusiasm, and in the high
est and most perfect state of discipline.
Government provided every comfort
and convenience for the crews embark
ed in this perilous undertaking—and it
was universally acknowledged, that no
discovery ships ever left the shores of
England in a higher state of equipment.
They left England on the Hth of
May, 1819, and reached Cape Farewell,
the most southern part of West Green
land, on the 14th of the succeeding June.
On the SOth of June, the ships were
in lat. 64, north.—On the 26th of June,
they were beset in the ice ; and, after
having endeavoured, but in vain, to urge
their way, during a painful detention of
• fourdays, were, at last, glad to get back
| again. Having reached lat. 74, north,
they determined to force a passage
through the barrier of ice, which they
found to be eighty miles broad. Having
succeeded in this, they reached Pos
session Bay on the 31st July; andon
the Ist of August, enured in safety Sir
James Lancaster’s Sound, where they
found the same open sea, which has been
described in the accounts of the former
expedition. They advanced to long.
89, west, meeting with but little ob
struction from the ice; and in long. 90,
west, discovered two considerable isl
ands, named Prince Leopold’s isles.—
But, at this point, their progress west
ward was interrupted by a strong bar
rier of ice, extending quite across from
these islands, to the north coast of what
Capt. Parry, we understand, named
Barrow Straits. Being thus arrested
by the ice, and forced to alter their
course, they now entered a great inlet,
of 14 or 15 leagues in breadth, which
they found extending to the southward.
They sailed along its eastern coast; its
middle part and western coa& being
blocked up with ice, as far as lat. 71,
north, when their farther progress
southward also was found to be impos
sible, by reason of the ice. In proceed
ing down this inlet, the magnetick at
traction increased so powerfully, that
the existence of the magnetickpole may
be conjectured to be somewhere in that
neighbourhood ; p obably in the lat. 70,
N. and long, of 100, W.
On their return io Barrow’s Straits,
it was found that the barrier of ice, ex
lending Prince Leopold’s
Isles io the north coast, had brukeu up,
so that the ships were now enabled to
pursue their course westward. Hav
ing reached long. 92, they found the
land on the north side of the Strait,
which had been continuous, from the
entrance of Sir James Lancaster’s
Sound now discontinuous, owing to a
great inlet. Land, however, was still
seen to the westward—so the expedi
tion continued its course in that direc
lion. In doing so, the ships passed a
number of great islands, all of them
apparently surrounded with ice; from
which ciicumstance partial detentions
were unavoidable ; and their course ran
in a son of zigzag style from lat. 73,
N- to lat. 75, N.
On the 4th of September, they were
in long. 110 ’ W.; and here they dis
covered an island which appeared to be
larger than any they had hitherto exam
, ined* and which, we understand, was
i named Melville Island, in honour of
the distinguished statesman now at the
j head of the Admiralty. This island,
'we are informed, extends from long,
j 106, W.to 114, W. On the B\h of
September* the ships reached 112, and
were enclosed for several days in the
ice. Winter was now fast approach
ing ; the ice Was rapidly increasing, and
violent north-westerly gales kept it in a
constant and dangerous state of agita
tion. . '
These circumstances, of course, ren
dered the navigation very difficult, and
began to endanger the safety of the
ships. Our gallant countrymen, how
ever, continued to contend with all
these difficulties till the 22d of Sep
tember, when it became evident, that
further navigation was at an end for the
season—and, therefore* prudence dic-x
tated their, retreat to a secure haven for
the polar winter. For this purpose,
they returned eastward, and found a
harbour io Melville Island. But the
ice had already formed from eight to
ten inches thick * and* therefore, the
crews were forced to cut a a passage for
three miles through the ice. The 26th
of September, fa short, had'arrived be-

: fore they were fixed in their winter
, quarters, in five fathoms water, and
within about 200 yards from the shore.
। The lat. of this harbour (if we recollect
। rightly, named Winter Harbour,) is
74 N. and long. UI, W. Hitherto,
they had never lost sight of a continu
ous barrier of ice to the southward, that
is, from west long. 90* to the extreme
of Melville Island-
Every thing was soon made snug for
the formidable winter of these regions.
The officers and crews formed various
plans for passing the dreary days, or
rather nights, of the polar regions.—
Plays were performed by the officers
for their own amusement and that o(
the crews—and we are told that a melo
drama was written, having for its ob
ject the probable success of the expe
dition, and their ultimate return to their
friends through Behrings’s Straits, af
ter having planted the British flag in
countries which had eluded the bold
and fearless darings of a Davis and a
Baffin.

The sun disappeared entirely on the
11th of November. The Themometer
was below zero of Fahrenheits’s scale
when the expedition entered Winter
Harbour. In the month of November
the spirit of wine thermometer was 55
below zero, and in February, the cold
est month of these regions, the spirit
of wine pointed to the tremendous cold
of 54 and 55 below zero. During
these intense colds, our adventurous
countrymen felt but little inconvenience .
so long as they remained under the
housing of their Ships. A slight cov
ering for the ears, and a shawl around
the neck, were considered as sufficient
protection against the most intense de
gree of cold; but when the atmosphere
was agitated by gales of wind, then the
cold became truly dreadful and insup
portable, and every one was forced to
seek shelter below. Nevertheless,
scarcely any accident occurred from
exposure to cold ; while the constant
and regular exercise, which formed a
necessary part of,the duty of the crews,
kept every one lively, and active, and
free from disease. One death only
took place during the expedition, and
that was in the caseof an individual, who
had c ontracted the disease of which he
died, before he left England.
When the sun had its greatest south
ern declination, a twilight was percepti
ble at noon in the southern horizon,
affording sufficient light to read a book
with difficulty. The day was like the
fine clear evening of winter in our cli
mate. The stars shone with great
brilliancy ; and when the moon appear
ed in the firmament, she shone with a
beauty and splendour unknown in the
more southern and temperate regions
of the globe. The northern lights ap
pear frequently, generally of a yelb w
colour, sometimes green, but rarely
red, and most commonly towards the
sduth-west. It was remarked, that this
brilliancy was seldom so great as'inour
country. No noise was ever heard to
proceed from them, and the magnetick
needle did not appear to be affected by
their presence. But we long to know
if they were visible the whole day, and
what were their various forms and mo
tions, and transparency. The sun re
appeared on the 3d of February, after
ap absence of 83 days, and those only
who have suffered the privation of “ its
glorious light” can feel and tell the
rapture with which the crews hailed the
first glimpse from the mast-head
They had calculated the exact period
of its return, and were anxiously, look
ing for it from the main-top.
In April some partial symptoms of
thaw appeared. By the end of May,
pools and streams of water made their
appearance, and shortly after, regular
thaw commenced. Nearly about this
time, Capt. Parry, with a party of his
officers and men, crossed Melville Isl
and, and reachea the sea on the oppo
site side, in lat. 75 N. where they dis
covered another Island. They were
fourteen days absent ; and, we have
heard, made many curious observa
tions on the forms of the hills, and
mountains of this Island, collecting
withal, very extensively, specimens of
its vegetable, animal, and minerable
productions. The remains%f an enor
mous whale, were found Jar inland* and
a few huts, intimating the presence of
mart, were discovered by some of the
plrty. Vegetation had now become
active; and sorrel was found in such
quantities as to remove all those symp
toms of scurvy which had begun to
make their appearance among the
crew. The ice in Winter Harbour was
also beginning to dissolve rapidly, and
by the end ot July, it had entirely dis
appeared. Yet the ships were still
quite blocked up by the exteriour ice.
It was not till the 30th, that the outside
ice began to crack. On the 31st July
it moved off very gently, and released
the crews from their winter piison
where they had been shot up 310 day.-.
On the 6h of August, they reached
the western extremity ofMelvilic Ibl
land, we believe, in long. 114
W. where the ice was found to be very
thick and impermeable. From this
island, new land was observed to the
south-west* Mtinufted to be twenty
J
A

leagues distant; to they may be said to
have seen land as far west, as long.
118. Many attempts were made to
reach this interesting terra incognita,
but in vain. And the commander and
his admirable crew* were* with feel
ings of the deepest regret, fenced to
return, owing to the vast barriers of ice.
Having failed in this attempt to reach
the south-western land, and the winter
again ‘pproaching, the vessels now
sailed directly eastward, through the
Polar Sea and Barrow’s Straits* into
Sir James Lancaster’s Sound, thence
into Baffin’s Bay, and by the usual track
homewards.
In their progress among the islands,
the officers shota few rein-deer, ptarmi
gan, partridge, and hares; and the howls
of the wolf were heafd frequently in
Melville Island. Several musk oxen
were killed—and, we are informed, the
crews considered it, after being prop
erly macerated, to get rid of th& musky
flavour, as preferable eating to that of
the rein-deer. One of the sailors, who ‘
had ventured beyond his companions
in search of rein-deer, returned io the
ship with his fingers frost-bitten, from
carrying his musket too long. When
the fingers were plunged into cold
water, ice was formed on its surface,
and this continued to be the case for
half an hour afterwards* as often as
the fingers were plunged into it. The
sailor lost five of his fingers.
From Lancaster’s Sound to Melville
Island; the compass, we understand,
was found to be totally useless, a cir
cumstance which left to the command
ers no other guides than the heavenly
bodies, and the trend of the land ; thus
at once presenting the striking specta- «
cle of modern navigators tracking the |
ocean without the compass, as was done
by the mariners of old. We cannot,
indeed, conceive a more striking scene
than that of our discovery ships, forc
ing their solitary course through un
known regions, surrounded with rug
ged, dreary, and desolate wastes, in
the midst of the most appalling dangers,
and deprived of the use of the compass.

“ It is important to notice an interest
ing fact, which has fallen under the ob
servation of the managers; and one that
may serve to correct a very erroneous,
though a very common opinion. It has
long been imagined that the labouring
classes could not sustain themselves un
der the weight of their daily employ
ments, and especially and
large manufacturing establishments,
where they are much exposed to heat,
and breathe a confined atmosphere, with
out the regular use of ardent spirits.
The results of an important experiment
made during the last season, by Mr. J.
P. Allaire, aq/1 by him communicated to
the board, establish the fallacy of this
opinion.
'“Mr. Allaire is the proprietor of a
large foundery at Corlaer’s Hook. Dur
ing the last season he employed up
wards of sixty workmen, more |ban
thirty of whom were men of families.—
In the course of the summer, he was in
formed that many of them were in debt;
and on investigating their concerns*
with surprise he ascertained the fact,
that every one who was in the habit of
using ardent spirits, was involved to an
extent beyond his ability to pay ; and,
with a satisfaction equal to his former
surprise, he learned the additional fact,
that those who made no use of spirits,
were in easy circumstances, and their
children were provided for at school.—
Nor did a difference of wages from
seventy-five cents to ten shillings per
day, make any perceptible change in
the situation of the former class of work
men.
“ With this picture before him, Mr.
Alteure was at once induced to prohibit
the use of ardent spirits altogether, in
his shops, during working hours. But
one person left his employ inconsequence
of this restriction ; and this man had
borrowed - of Mr. Allaire, while in his
service, upwards of S3OO to pay groce
ry bills.. In conclusion of this letter,
Mr. Allaire observes I have great rea
son to be pleased with the happy effects
of this regulation. I find my interest
better served; and that those who,
from excessive drinking, had become of
but little worth to me, and in many in
stances, of less to their families, have
now become able and steady; earn more
money; and their families, as well as
themselves, have expressed, in a lan
guage not to be misunderstood, the ma
ny comforts and the domestick happi
ness which they enjoy in consequence.”

TO THE FEDERAL ELECTORS OF MASSACHUSETTS:
As to those among us who think that the certainty of having good rulers can
not now be doubted, because of the great majority in this State, this very confi
dence is the greatest cause of alarm.. If this sense of security pervade the class
who are called Washington Federalists,, few of them will feel the necessity of
attending to the business of elections. Apathy and carelessness will not be over
looked, nor permitted to pass without profit, by their opponents. The conse
quence will be, that men will get into office who consider governing an ex
clusive privilege, a matter of trade, an affair of emolument and benefit, for
those of a particular dess, to the exclusion of all others. If it be answered that
there is no occasion for anxiety ; that the democrats are satisfied with the federal
administration of the State, and will not oppose; that the distinctions of party are
so entirely broken up that there is no ground for preference among candidates; —
we conceivethis to be an errour which cannot be too soon dispelled. The federal par
ty deceive themselves in •that their disposition to do away all other dis
tinctions than those which are founded in ability, honesty and fitness for office are
cordially met and reciprocated by the other party. The federalists are slow to
believe, that after they have expressed their respect and their confidence as to
the National Government, and after having given to Mr. MONROE an unanimous
vote for a new presidential term, that the democratick party can think of oppos
ing such men as Governour BROOKS and Lieutenant-Governour PHILLIPS.
But the true difference between these two parties is, that the one gives un,
and the other gains. The giving up is all on one side, the gain all on the other.
In a federal town, or county, there is abundant profession of the “era of good
feelings,-' and prepositions are often renewed to divide the power, and to annihilate
party spirit
But in towns or counties which are democratick,. no such professions and prop
ositions occur. r r
We remember hardly any instance of appointments made, or of confidence
expressed, by the National or State Governments, while held by politicians of the
Republican cast, (as they call themselves) except towards those who have given
due pedges ot the proper political faith.
We can remember not a few instances of turning out, for no other reason than
the absence of such faith.
we “ ay see the theor y of Republican Government
carried into fell effect, viz. that all citizens will unite in choosing the best men a
mongthemasrulers-we never shall see it; the nature of human passions and
feelings forbid it There will always be two classes of men differing from each
other most essentially, m opinion- as to objects of Government, and the pur
poses for which its powers should be used. The individuals who compose one of
these classes seem to have been made, as we find them, to compel the other to
proper care and.exertion to preserve their rights and liberties.
It is with States as with individuals—every thing worth having must be
earned ; and being acquired, must be continually guarded ti prevent spoil, waste
ana decay. r >
democratick partizans must be satisfied
with the State Government, because the democrats cannot pretend, that they can
make better laws than have been made, nor administer or execute laws better
tk a n they now see to be done. Unfortunately we do not understand this party as
well as they understand us. r J
Ao administfation with them- can be right which is not of their own making. In
short, they are not in power, and when this is so, nothing can be right °
• u" federal ' sts are wrapped in security, and think no exertion necessary
then is the favourable time for democracy to put itself in motion 3
It is now well understood, that the democratick party, throughout the State,
are calculating,, not only with hope, but with confidence, that thl peculiar state
of parties, and the condition of the Commonwealth, from peculiar causes, give
them chances of success, which are well worth great exertion. Organized means
are in use, and their consequences will be disastrously felt, if no efforts are made
io preserve the Administration as it is- e
We have read the democratick Address to Electors lately peblished It is
made up of remarks on three subjects dtseuwed in Convention; viz. the Senate
Harvard Lmversrty and the provision (in the Bill of Right.) for the support of
pubhek worship. These matters were considered by the Delegates of the whole
peop e a«J the result of their efforts is gone forth to be judged of We sui
posed that any thing done, or omitted to be done, by the Convention was nX
proper subjecyf remark in party elections.. The resort to such topicks b? de
mocratick partisans is the best proof of their poverty of means to effect these Z
% This address seems to be intended to arraign the motives and conduct of
the Delegates ; and to turn to party purposes, the doings of an assembly in which
no party spirit did or could appear. It concludes with the surprizing fotima
tion that William Eustis, and Levi Lincoln, are better entitled to the support of
the Electors of Massachusetts, than JOHN BROOK 9 and WILLIAM PHILLIPS • m
We will not institute a comparison between the candidates of the respective
parties. No Citizen of Massachusetts can be uninformed of the character a ? nd con
duct of those men whom the federalists propose to support on this occasion. Our
purpose is only to awaken the good old feelings, which have so long honoured and
preserved.the best interest of the State; and to remind our fellow-citizens of the
duty which they owe to themselves and to each.other. 1 “
If all who feel a just sense of the value of citizenship in Massachusetts whilfv
the government is administered by capable and upright men, will exercise their
rights, there can be no doubt of the result of the election.—Nor on fee other

Messrs. Manning Sc Trumbull—
Having been arraigned at the bar of the
publick upon indirect charge.', calculated and
intended, under the general excitement on the
subject of fees of office, to destroy publick
confidence in my honesty, and to give it a
bearing upon the election of Register of Deeds,
you will permit me, briefly as possible, on the
same stand, to make my defence.—This is due
to myself and family—it is due to my friends,
who have hitherto put confidence in me—and
it is due to the community, whose benevo
lence has been shamefully and foolishly requit
ed, if I have knowingly and iutentionably vi
olated their trust.
As I have seen no specifick charge, I can
not reply as to any particular case ; but I
will admit the probability, although I know not
the fact, that I have in some cases received
more for the recording an instrument, than the
law would strictly allow—for 1 know that I
have often taken Jess. Cannot this be ac- •
counted for without the intention of fraud ?—
Every man the least conversant with the office
must know that in the hurry of business, this
may happen without intention of doing wrong.
To be always accurate, it is obvious that there
must be great delay to those who bring in
struments for record, or that an extra Clerk
must be employed to determine precisely the
fee. All that can reasonably be required, is,
that the Principal, or his Clerk, for whose do
ings he is responsible, should exercise a sound
and honest judgment. How I obtained and
have exercised this judgment, it may be prop
er for me to explain.
Knowing my ignorance of the complicated
business of my new employment, the late Reg
ister, my venerable and highly valued friend,
whose unfinished business detained him in the
office some time after I succeeded him, gene
rously offered his instruction and assistance.—
Whenever he was present, I handed him the
instrument offered me for record, and received
his instruction in charging the fee. When he
was not present, I invariably handed it to Mr.
Ward, who, for some years, had been a Clerk
in the office, both correct and conscientious in
his duty. When alone, I compared it with
others, which had been received, and noted
the fee according to my best understanding
and judgment. While with Col. Clap, Mr.
Ward wrote by the deed, and received his pay
according to its length, which was indicated
by the amount of the fee received. This
might be an inducement to a dishonest Clerk
*o rate them higher than would be just. But
in my employment, however dishonest, he
could have no such temptation. I have paid
him a liberal allowance by the day, that he
might attend to the various concerns of the
office. His seat is the most accessible to those
who have business to transact. The instru
ments are generally and most naturally hand
ed to him, and he enters them. It will be
found most invariably that the fee is entered
on the instrument. This, however, is not al
ways the exact price for recording, as a charge
for a search in the case, or the extra trouble of
recording it out of season, or being called up
in the night, is sometimes included. In the
fee which I receive, is included, moreover, the
duty of 17 cents, which I pay to the County
Treasurer. Were I disposed to be dishonest,
one would think that I might have sense e
nough to withhold this evidence on the deed,
which would be so ready a means of convict
ing me.
in making charges for incidental business, I
am not conscious of ever exceeding the fees
established by the previous rules and customs
of the office, although, as it is intimated, pov
erty was extending its temptation. So far as
my predecessor was correct, (and in his thirty
years of service, I never heard that it was
doubted,) I have endeavoured to imitate his
example—and I had the proud satisfaction to
believe, that my endeavours had been success
ful, until it was otherwise insinuated, in some
what of an uncourteous manner, by your “ cor
respondent,” and “ subscriber.”
The above detail, I trust, will be sufficient
to satisfy every candid and honourable man,
that 1 have not, knowingly and intentionally,
deviated from my duty. With my accuser, I
cannot hope to be thus fortunate. From the
manner of his attacks it is impossible to as
cribe it to any other than personal views. A
providential misfortune is made the subject of
derision. From this course, I fear no injury.
How far it is a disqualification, those who
have had business at the office can judge. In
view of his object, he may yet regret that, in
addition to my deafness, his invectives have
not struck me dumb. His anxiety lest a “ poor
man” may not be able to respond for his mal
conduct will be relieved by applying at the
Clerk’s Office, where he will learn, what he
knew before, that he has competent bondomen.
It would be extraordinary if insinuations of a
nature to cause popular excitement, industri
ou'ly propagated, should not have produced a
sudden impression—but as the jury, by whom
I am to be tried, have not all declared ap opin
ion, I have confidence, that on further delib
eration, after a patient hearing of the defence,
and knowing the merits of the case, I shall re
ceive a verdict of acquittal, or have the benefit
of a review. —l submit the cause.
O. FISKE. '

we bid them u come in,” when a gen

The Committee, appointed, for the purpose, have prepared the following
ADDRESS :
To the Federal Electors of the County of Worcester.
FELLOW-CITIZENS—The period has nearly arrived, when it will ag:/tx
become your duty to designate those persons who shall manage the high and re
sponsible concerns of government. —It is the peculiar excellence of our republi
can system to proceed upon the maxim, that the people arc the fountain of pow
er, and government created for their exclusive benefit. The term of office is
made so short, that publick agents are frequently remiqded of the source of their
authority, and led to feel a due responsibility in the performance of their trust.—-
The people are thus enabled to canvass their measures with effect, and to pass,
such sentence upon them as their merits may deserve. But- though this is the
theory of our government, and numerous constitutional checks are dfevised to en
force and regulate it, it must depend for its main efficacy and support upon the
virtue aud intelligence of the community. The extent of power delegated may
be accurately defined, and limited by a written charter ; but the operation and ex
ercise of this power can only be controlled by publick sentiment. It becomes,
therefore, a matter of the highest importance, both that pains should be taken to
give this sentiment a right direction, and that such a full expression of it should
be obtained as will enable it to act with its proper energy.
In times of peace and tranquillity, when no particular pressure weighs upon
the community/there is danger that individual concerns will so entirely engross
the minds of the people as to leave them little disposition to attend-to the affairs
of state. They do not reflect that all the prosperity and comfort they are en
joying js the result of a wise system of government properly administered ; and
that to continue this state of things, it is necessary they should exercise a vigilant
and superintending care over their rulers. It unfortunately happens, too, that it is
the wise, the virtuous, the prudent and honest portion of the citizens, who are
most apt to be overcome by this apathy ami indifference. The contentions and
turmoil of the polls are objects of disgust to them ; and so long as they do not
realize any serious evil proceeding from the publick councils, they are' content to
retire within the bosoms of their families and occupations, and leave it to others
to contest the prize of publick favour. How much of patriotism there is in this
mode of proceeding, and how far it deserves the continuance of the blessings they
enjoy, may be safely left to their own intelligence and consciences to determine.
It will always be the case, in any community, and much more in a republick,
where the power resides in the people, that there will be a class of men who
will look with envy and jealousy upon the superiour influence of those who hold
a more advanced place in society than themselves. It is painful to them tc see
others in the enjoyment of advantages they themselves do not possess. Instead
of endeavouring to cultivate those qualities, and exercise those talents which
would raise them to the same point of elevation, all their energies are exerted
to reduce others to their own "level. The natural gradations and distinctionsilk
society, which grow out of the difference of capacity and condition, and are pro
motive, in the highest degree, of individual and the general welfare, are by them
viewed as arbitrary and oppressive, and become the objects of their sullen dis
content. Should these persons happen to constitute the minority in the State, in-,
stead of reforming themselves, they cry out for a reform of the government.
They do not examine the character of rulers, and the operation of their measures,
to see whether there is any thing reprehensible in either. It is enough for them,
that what they denominate the privileged class are in power, and they are out.
With these persons are associated some men'of talents, who are ready to avail
themselves of the passions and jealousies of their political comrades,, to subserve
their own ambitious- projects, and whose thirst for distinction will not allow them
to act in concert with a portion of the community where they must be content to
shine as lesser lights in the firmament.
The above considerations will alone furnish us with a rational solution of the
opposition which is kept up against the existing government of the State. The
democratick party do not, and cannot, pretend that the measures of the federal
party now in poiler have not been marked by moderation, wisdom, and an exclu
sive regard Jo the publick good. No proceedings of a political character, grow
ing out of the existing state of things, have taken place in our Legislature for a
number of years ; and nothing has been done in regard to them by which it could
be determined what party was predominant there.
Now for the other-side of the picture !—Observe the different principles and
motives which govern the federal party. No sooner did the national government
abandon that policy which we considered injurious to the true interests of the
country —no sooner did they return to those systems and doctrines which, in our
opinion, bore the stamp of wisdom and uprightness, than we withdrew all opposi
tion to them, and gave them our decided and hearty support. It was of no conse
quence to us who held the reins of government, whether a federalist or a demo
crat, so long as bis measures were wisely framed and honestly executed. - Our
opposition, as it never originated in selfish motives, was not continued under their
influence. In the recent election of President of the United States, Mr. Monroe
had the votes of every elector of the federal party throughout the Union.
Another example of the liberality of our conduct may be found in tlie recent
election of delegates to the Convention. In many towns in the State, where the
federalists have a decided ascendancy, they liberally accorded to their opponents
a share of this trust, while, in the democratick towns, we know not of a single in
stance of a similar liberal proceeding. It had been the subject of complaint with
that party for some time, that federalists here retained all the offices in their
hands, and, notwithstanding their professions of reconciliation, made no ovortures
in practice to evince it. Without animadverting upon the character of a parlywho would ground an opposition upon such professedly Selfish policy, the
instances furnish a sufficient test of the sincerity of our professions. But what
has been their fate? What we might and did expect—that, as these complaints
were invented merely as pretexts for no satisfaction was given by a
removal of them. The same persevering hostility is kept up against the present
State administration, and instead of being contented with of power,
nothing short of the wholeof it will satisfy them.
Among other engines which have been pressed into the electioneering cam*
paign this spring, by the democratick party, the doings of the late Convention
have made a distinguished figure. An attempt has been made to identify the re
sult of these doings with the federal party, and to make them, as a party, account
able for them. Upon the expediency of the proposed amendments to the Consti
tution, it is not our purpose at this time to comment; it is sufficient for us to ex
pose the injustice and mischief of the use which is made of them. It is well known
that in the choice of delegates to this body, with the exception of the democratick
towns, a single eye was had to the qualifications of the persons chosen, without re
gard to their political character. It was considered to be a question deeply affect
ing the interests and welfare of the whole State and not of a party, and of posteri
ty as well as the present generation. The influence of this sentiment pervaded
the Convention no less than the people at large ; as if by common consent, all
party distinctions were banished from their walls. The general aim seemed to be,
to weigh in the balance of unbiassed reason and mature experience all the princi
ples of the Constitution, and let their fate depend upon the result All the amend
ments which were adopted had persons of each party ranged both in their favour
and against them; and the most prominent ones, those which are now held up to
publick odium and reproach, received the support of a large number of the most
distinguished gentlemen of the democratick party. What pretence is there, then,
for considering these as the doings of a party, and converting them into an engine
with which to batter down the present administration. The result of the approach
ing election can have no influence upon their acceptance or rejection. They are
to be submitted to the good sense of the people, on the second Monday of April;
and if they have the hideous features asciibed to them, they will certainly be re
jected. The political use which is attempted to be made of some of them will be
jiroductive of a serious evil. Instead of leaving them to be examined on their
own merits, by the unbiassed judgment of individuals, the associating them with
one of the political parties has a direct tendency to prejudice the minds of the oth
er party against them, and to throw the clouds of passion over their understanding.
Perhaps this effect is intended; and what could not be gained by manly argument,'
is to be sought by insidious appeals. Such a course, however, can reflect no cred
it upon the party pursuing it, and is a strong evidence of their unfitness for the
power they seek.
Federal Republicans —However much it may surprize you, it is nevertheless a
fact, that very powerful exertions are made by the democratick party to effect
,the election of their State candidates. Their newspapers are loaded with col
umns upon columns of electioneering matter, presented in every possible shape
to delude the ignorant, and enlist the passions of the restless and discontented.—
These are their publick proceedings. In aid of them, there can be no doubt that
they have put their party in a complete state of organization throughout the
Commonwealth, and have their state, county and town committees, in active cor
respondence and efficient co-operation. Besides these measures, they are in the
practice of transmitting numerous copies of one of their newspapers in Boston to
postmasters in the different towns, to be by them disseminated among the party
free of expense, and, probably, without the charge of postage. Notwithstanding
the development of their former iniquitous proceedings, in this respect, two years
since, we are apprehensive they still continue the same practice. A fine com
mentary upon the honesty of their views, and the purity of their principles !
“ When bad men combine, good men must unite.” If you do not wish
success to the plans of such a party, actuated by such feelings, and pursuing such
measures, you must do your duty in endeavouring to counteract them. You must
show the same zeal in a good cause that they do in a bad. Exert yourselves then
to awaken your friends to a sense of their danger ; and impress upon them the
solemn obligations they are under to exercise their electoral rights. Bring out
the whole strength of the party on the first Monday of April, and let no private
consideration detain any man from the polls. With these exertions, we shall tri
umph—short of them, we may be defeated !

The pathetick appeal made by the present
Register of Deeds for this County in last week's
Spy, and the assertion that the opposition to
his re-election proceeds from private pique and
resentment, are artfully intended to prevent
an inquiry into his qualifications for the office,
and the manper in which he has executed the
trust reposed in him the last four years. Fel
low-citizens, be not deceived, nor let your gen
erous sensibility for’ one whom you may con
sider a persecuted man lead you to give such a
vote as you may have reason hereafter to think
was inconsistent with your interest and your
duty. Let not a mistaken sympathy induce
you to place in this highly important office a
man whose natural and habitual infirmities will
constantly expose innocent individuals to se
vere losses, if not to utter ruin. The plea of
poverty you may be assured has no foundation
in reality: it is at best but a poetick fiction.
It may, however, be the case that the present
Register has no property 'which his creditors
can take to satisfy their demands; but it is well
known that he is in possession of an estate the
income of which, added to his other means of
support, enables him to Eve in a style of fash
ion and comfort far beyond that of the greater
part of those who are called upoi to give him
their suffrages,. Witness his nuaerously at
tended and splendid entertainments, and then
say whether appearances are not vholly irrec
oncileable with the plea of necessity.—But
were it true that he is poor, this in itself would
be a sufficient objection to his re-election,
since it would be-out of his pow® to compen
sate those who might be injured by his mis
takes or carelessness; for the competent bonds
of which he speaks, are so small as to afford
very little protection to those who necessarily
must depend upon his care and correctness.
It is asserted that no specifick charge has
been made against him; but has it not been
said that his hardness of hearing has rendered
transacting business at the office, not only un
pleasant, but has made mistakes unavoidable,
and thereby destroyed all confidence in the
Register’s certificates ? And has he not ad
mitted, that more than lawful fees may have
been taken by him in some instances ? Can
any thing more than this be necessary to show
his unfitness for the office, and that publick
interest and private security would be bene
fited by the contemplated change ?
No man has a right to an office ; nor does
the circumstance of his having obtained it by
a small majority after repeated trials, entitle
him to re-election. Yet whenever the incum
bent can make it manifest that he has con
ducted the business entrusted to him with abil
ity, integrity and correctness, he may fairly
claim a preference to other candidates.
A course so natural and proper Doct. Fiske
has not chosen to pursue ; but he has adopted
a mode of electioneering, rather novel in this
part of our country, by denouncing and
threatening those who have had the temerity
to oppose him, or advocate other' candidates.
The wisdom of this measure remains to be
proved; but it is believed that the time has not
yet arrived, when free and independent citi
zens are to be deterred from exercising their
constitutional privileges by the imputation of
unworthy motives, or the threats of future
consequences; or that the publick are to be
biassed in favour of a candidate who resorts
to such dishonourable methods to insure his
election. It cannot be doubted that this ill
judged measure of his, will operate in a man
ner the reverse of what he hoped for and in
tended, and that the effect will be to place him
in the condition of those
“ Whose gun, when aimed at duck or plover,
Bears wide and kicks its owner over.”
A knowledge of the character and qualifica
tions of those who offer themselves, or who
are proposed by their friends, is principally
and perhaps most accurately obtained through
the medium of the newspapers. This chan
nel of communication should, therefore, be
guarded with particular care, and every at
tempt to shut it, especially when made by a
candidate, should be deeply resented: should
such attempts succeed, your right to chuse
your own rulers and servants would be no
more than an empty name, and the most dar
ing would become the most successful can
didate. Now is the proper time to put an ef
fectual check to so pernicious a practice; and
may your votes at the ensuing election
prove your sense of the indignity which has
in this instance been offered to the independ
ent citizens of the County of

The following stanza*, for beauty and exqui
site finish, are infinitely superiour to the verses
generally offered on similar occasions. They
were written by a friend of the late Dr. J. R.
Drake, of this city.
To commemorate the virtues and the tal
ents of a departed friend, or to weigh, with
impartiality, his claims to publick attention is,
indeed, no easy task ; bat the subject of these
lines was worthy of all the commendation and
all the sorrow here so beautifully expressed.—
A devotion to the Muses marked his early life,
and many of his unpublished productions would
not discredit (we speak it confidently) the pen
of a Moore or a Campbell. He fell an early
victim to the Consumption—a disease which
seems peculiarly to select for the objects of its
attack, the amiable, the intelligent and the vir
tuous.

On the late Dr. Joseph R. Drake.*
GREEN be the sod above thee,
Friend of my better days !
None knew thee but to love thee,
Nor nam'd tbee but to praise.
Tears fell when thou wert dying,
From eyes unus’d to weep ;
And long, where thou art lying.
Will tears thy cold turf steep.
When hearts, whose home was heaven,
Like thine are laid in earth,
There should a wreath be woven.
To teH the world their worth:
And I—who woke each morrow
To clasp thy hand in mine,
Who shar’d thy joy and sorrow,
Whose weal and wo were thine—
It should be mine to braid it
Around thy faded brow ;
But I’ve in vain essay’d it,
And feel I cannot now.
While mem’ry bids me weep thee,
Nor thoughts nor words are free,
The grief is fix’d too deeply
That mourns a man like thee.

FLORIDA TREATY.
The Treaty was signed on the 22d
of July, 1819, and having since been
duly ratified by the contracting parties,
was communicated to Congress on the
22d of February, 1821, by tbe Presi
dent.
The first article merely provides that
there shall be a firm and inviolable peace
between the two powers.
The 2d article cedes to the United States
all the territory belonging to his Catholick
Majesty eastward of the Missisippi, known
by the name of East and West Florida, ex
cept private property, together with all the
Islands, &c. belonging to the same.
Article 3d is as follows :--
“The boundary line between the two
countries, west of the Missisippi, shall be
gin on the Gulf of Mexico, at the mouth
of the river Sabine, in the sea, continuing
north, along the western bank of that river,
to the 32d degree of latitude; thence, by a
line due north, to the degree of latitude
where it strikes the Rio Roxo, Natchitoch
es, or Red River; then following the
course of the Rio Roxo westward, to the
degree of longitude too west from London,
and 13 from ashington ; then, crossing
the said Red River, and running thence, by
a line due north, to the river Arkansas ;
thence following the course of the south
ern bank of the Arkansas, to its source, in
_ latitude 41 north; and thence by that par
allel of latitude to die S >uth Sea. The
whole being as laid down in Melish’s tpap
of the United States, published at Phila
delphia, improved to the Ist of January,
1818. But, if the source of the Arkansas
river shall be found to fall north or south
of latitude 42, then the line shall run from
the said source due south or north, as the
case may be, till’it meets the said parallel
of latitude 4a, and thence, along the said
parallel, to the South Sea. All the islands
in the ■'abine and the said Red and Arkan
sas rivers, throughout the course thus de
scribed, to belong to the United States ;
but the use of the waters and the naviga
tion of the Sabine to the sea, and of the
said rivers Roxo and Arkansas, through
out the extent of the said boundary, on
their respective banks, shall be common
to the respective inhabitants of both na
tions.
The two high contracting parties agree
to cede and renounce all their rights, claims
and pretensions, to the territories describ
ed by the said line: that is to say ; the
United States hereby cede to his Catholick
Majesty, and renounce forever, all their
rights, claims and pretensions to the ter
ritories lying west and south of the above
described line, and, in like manner, his
Catholick Majesty cedes to the said United
States all his rights, claims and preten
sions, to any territories east and north of
the said line, and for himself, his heirs
and successors, renounces all claim to the
said territories forever.
Article 4, provides that each contract
mg power, “shall appoint a commissioner
and a surveyor,” to meet within one year
front the ratification of the treaty, at Natch
itoches, on thp Red river, to run the line
and put up landmarks between the two
nations when agreed upon, are to be
come a part of the treaty.
Article 5, recures to the Spaniards the
free exercise of their religion, and also
liberty to remove their effects to the Span
ish dominions, without payment of duties.
Article 6, provides that the inhabitants
shall be incorporated with the Union of
the United States.as soon as consistent
with the principles of the Federal Consti
tution.
Article 7. By this article the officers and
tr?ops of his Catholick Majesty, in the ter.
ntorieg ceded by this treaty, are to be
withdrawn within six months from the ex
cbange of the ratifications' of the treaties.
The United States are to furnish the trans
pors and escort necessary to convey the
Spanish troops, &c. to the Havana.
Article 8. All grants of lands made be
fore the 24th of January, 1818, by his
Catholick Majesty, arc ratified and con-

[ firmed to the persons m possession. Alt
those in possession, who nave been pre
vented from fulfilling the conditions of
thetr grants, in consequence of the revo
lutions tn Spain ana other nations of
Europe, are bound to complete them with
in the terms limited in the same, from the
date of this treaty, or they will be forfeit
ed. All grants made since the above date,
are by this treaty made null and void.
Article 9. By this article the high
contracting parties “ reciprocally renounce
all claims for damages or injuries which
they themselves” and their respective cit
izens and subjects, may have suffered, un
til the signing of this treaty. Including,
on the part of the United States, all the
injuries mentioned in the Convention of
11th of August, 1802-.-all claim* on ac
count of prizes made by French privateers,
and condemned by French consuls within
the jurisdiction of Spain—all claims on
account of the suspension of the right of
deposit at New-Orleans in 1802, and all
claims arising from the unlawful seizures
at sea, and in tbe ports and territories of
Spain, including those that have already
been presented to the department of
State, or our Minister in Spain since 1802.
The renunciation of his Catholick Majes
ty extends to all injuries, mentioned in
the Convention of 1802..-to the sums ad
vanced for the return of Capt. Pike, from
the Provinces Interuas—to all injuries
caused by Miranda’s expedition. -to all
claims of Spanish subjects on account of
unlawful seizures at sea, &c. Ac The
parties respectively renounce all claims
for recent events in the Floridas, except
the American government are to make
good all injuries which may have been sus
tained by Spanish subjects by the late
operations of the American army in Flor
ida.
Article 10, annuls the ratificationspf the
Convention of 11 th August, 1802.
Article 11. The Spanish government are
to pay a sum not exceeding five millionspf
dollars, to satisfy the claims of the United
States given up by the 9th article of this
treaty. Three persons, citizens of the
United States, are to be appointed by the
President and Senate Commissioners to
meet at Washington, in order to ascertain
the amount of all claims that may be pre
sented within three years after they meet,
which may come within the descriptions,
above mentioned. The payment of those
claims that may be allowed by the Com
missioners, not to exceed five millions of
dollars is to be made by the United States.
Article 12, establishes the principle that
the flag shall cover the property; with re
spect to those powers who recognize this
principle ; ‘ but if either of the contract
ing parties shall be at war with a third par
ty, and the other neutral, the flag of the
neutral shall cover the property of ene
mies, whose government acknowledge this
principle, and not of others.’
Article 13, Both parties agree that sai
lors who shall desert from their vessels in
the ports of the other shall be arrested and
delivered up, at the instance of the Court,
provided he prove that they belong to the
vessels claiming them, by tne document in
one case, called the “ Article,” and in the
other the “ roll of the vessel.”
Article 14. The United States certify
that they have received no compensation
from France for her spoliations on the
coasts and in the ports of Spain ; and
that she will furnish a list of the prizes,
and of their value, in order that Spain may
avail herself of the same in such a manner
as she may deem just and prooer.
Article 15, provides that Spanish ves
sels, directly from the ports of Spain, and

signed them,” &c. 'They were signed by

CONSTITUTION—No. 11.
By »he eecond article of amendments,
it is proposed to change the political
year from the last Wednesday in May,
to the first Wednesday of January, so
that there may not ordinarily be more
than one session of the General Court.
in a year—and it is provided that all the
elections shall be conformed to it.
Tne elections are to take place the
second Monday in November, and Rep.
resentatives to be voted for on the same
dsy with Senators. There are two
very obvious reasons for the proposed
change. ”1 he first is a very great saving
of expense, by finishing the business
at one session. The second is, that
the business will be belter done. The
members will more constantly attend.
And ordinarily the private business will
be delayed till the publick is finished,
instead of crowding out-all publick con
cerns as is now very frequently the case.
This alteration, though opposed by a
few members, was adopted by a very '
large majority, 408 being in favour of 1
it, and only 55 against it. No impor
tant alteration received so general sup-1
port in tbe Convention. The third and ■
fourth articles of amendment may i
be improvements inthe Constitution, 1
and there is no objection to adopting 1
them.
The sixth article, which provides for '
alterations in regard to the Council and 1
Senate and House of Representatives,
is unquestionably the most important, j
The number of Senators is proposed
to be thirty-six, to be proportioned on
the several districts in the State, ac
cording to the tax paid, in the same
way with the Constitution as it now
stands.
The Counsellors are reduced from
nine to seven, and to be chosen by the
Senate and House of Representatives,
in joint ballot from among the people
at large, excluding both Senators and
Representatives. But the great altur
ation is in proportioning Represents-,
tives. In regard to them, there is a ’
great and radical change proposed.—'
first, instead of being governed by:
the number of rateable polls which was
the basis adopted, probably because o
riginaily a poll-tax was the principal'
tax, this system is to be governed by ;
the number of inhabitants, and every j
town containing 1200 inhabitants is to i
have one Representative, and to have
the increase of one (nr 2400 additional:
inhabitants—provided, that if there I
shall be more than 275 Represents-1
tives, the members shall be proportion
ally increased after every census, so 1
as to reduce the whole number to 275. 1
No newly incorporated town can send '
a Representative, unless it have 2400
inhabitants. The towns which have
less than 1200,’ are to be classed by
the Legislature into two classes, the
largest towns into one class, and the
smallest another—the largest towns are •
to send a Representative the first year,;
and the smaller the second, and so on j
every year except the year a valuation ।
is to be settled, when each town may
send one—and if any two towns to be
classed, wish to be united to choose a
Representative every year, they are to
be united. If any one of those towns,
now under 1200, shall in future have
more, they are to be entitled to send
one every other year,and any town falling
short of that number is to be classed
—the towns thereby entitled to send
every other year, are never to lose that
privilege, be their numbers ever so
small, or reduced ever so low. And
the members are to be paid out of the
publick treasury, both for travel and
attendance.
The first inquiry that occurs, is,
whether this Alteration is better than
the old system t And a second, if it
is, whether a much better one may not
be proposed i
The ostensible object is to lessen the
number of Representatives, to dimin
ish the expense, and to facilitate bus
iness by having only such a number
that business may be done correctly and
expeditiously.
By the proposed system it is to he
calculated upon, that from 250 to 260
members will attend, and that they will
attend through the whole session as
they are to be paid out of the pubtick
Treasury, and may fix their own pay..
Until after the year 1800, upon the
present system, the number of Rep
resentatives borne on the roll, was
much less Chan it will be upon the new

THIRTY-SECOND YEAR.

[Whole No. 2504.

plan, and probably they did not attend
more than one third of the time on an
average. Since the year 1800, the
number of Representatives elected, has
exceedingly varied. In the year
1818, there were< only 167; and this
year short of 200. Probably the num
ber the present year, during the whole
time that the Legislature was in
slon would be much less than 150—a»
a calculation of expense, in ordinary
times, tbe present system would bo
much better than the one proposed.—
And if there should be, on extraordi.
nary occasions, a full representation, tbe
expense would not be very burdensome,
and much benefit might result to the
community.
But it may be said, with a degree of
truth, on the present system, there will
be grpat inequality; some towns will
elect a great number, when others
send none. And it may also be said,
that tbe members will not attend reg
ularly and constantly. These must
be admitted to be evils of no small
magnitude.
But they may easily be remedied.—
Let the compensation be such that the
pay will be no object. Let no member
receive his pay, who is not in his place
at the proper time—and let the attend
ance through the session, unless in ex
traordinary emergencies, be made a
condition of receiving payment for
travel. In Some such way the practi
cal evils of the present system may be
lessened, without recourse to a new and
complicated plan. It is very obvious
that in the proposed arrangement, the
smaller towns having 1200 inhabitants,
and but a few more, will acquire an
inconceivable advantage over the larger
ones.
West-Springfield, for instance, con
taining four parishes, now entitled to
send at least four Representatives, in
the new system is to send but one.—
And Palmer, now sending but one, is
to. retain the right. The new rule
will operate upon the largest towns
still mure unequally R OBton , sendintr
at present 45, and entitled to send
more, will probably be entitled to send
not more than 16 or 18. Salem, now
entitled to send 13, will then have a
right to send only four or five.
If I am rightly informed, there is
but one town in the whole five western
counties, which will be entitled to
send .wo Representatives. The in
creasing ratio is much too large, if
1200 is the lowest number.
In regard to the towns which are to
send every other year, the innovation
is a very great one. Some of them
will have a better lot than they new
have, and some of them a worse.—
Take them together, their situation is
not to be as good as the small towns,
who can barely send one Representa
tive ; but it is much better than tha
large ones.
There is a very flagrant injustice in
providing, that when tbe valuation is
fixed, every corporate town, whether
now entitled to send a Representative
or not, may each send one, while the
larger towns are entitled to no mpra
Representatives that year than usual.—
Montgomery, Russell and Holland, alt
of them together, by the last census,
had less than 1500 inhabitants—West-
Springfield more than double that
number. They each send one, and
West-Springfield is to send only one,
and to help pay for those from the oth
er towns.
By these means, those towns which'
pay very much less than half the tax
io the will be able to control
what ought to be the majority on this
subject. But if the present system
requires alteration, it ought to be snada
upon equal and consistent principles.
There is no method so equitable, as
that of fixing tbe representation upon
the population—giving to a certain
fixed number of inhabitants the right
to send a Representative, and making
the expense a common charge* will do
justice to all.
A division of the State into suitable
and convenient districts for electing
Representatives, is a convenient and
feasible mode of effecting this object.
The districts ought not to be so small
as to give oae town an undue Influence
in the election. The districts ought
not to be so large that the people may
not be well acquainted with those to be
elected. Each district may contain
about 15/100 inhabitants. This coun
ty might he divided into two districts
by the river— and each district toelect the number of Representatives
which should be required ; the number
of Representatives might be fixed at
ISO or 900—no town to be divided for
forming districts—the districts to re
main unalterable, and the number of
Representatives each district should
send, to be fixed once in ten years, ac*
cording to the Census.
This plan is not now in question.—
The only inquiry now is, whether the
alteration proposed by the Convention
ought to be adopted. Those who think
the improvement, in regard to the Sen
ate and Council and Representatives,
taken together, to be so great an im
provement that the alteration should be
adopted, will vote for it. But all those
who think that either had better stand
as it is, will vote against the whole, as
it is all to be adopted or rejected to
gether.
It is probable that adopting this, will
prevent any future amendments—but
if this be rejected, other alterations
may be made without connecting the
three together. PHOCION.

House of Commons, Feb, s.—The
following strong and manly assevera
tion of Mr. Brougham will be read
with particular pleasure ;—
“It could beonly known*’ said he “to
her Majesty herself, whether the charg
es were just or otherwise. Her own
conscience told her that she was inno
cent of those acts which had been false
ly imputed to her, in charges which had
been, as they were now told, finally a
bandoned. I have stated thus much,”
continued the honourable and learned
gentleman, “as to the conduct of the
Queen. It is fit I should now discharge
what I call a debt of gratitude to her.
I know it has been invidiously and ma
levolently asserted, and most industri
ously circulated, for purposes which
must be obvious to every man, that my
expressed opinions of her Majesty’s
conduct are not the same in fact with
my own conscientious conviction.—
(Hear.) It is necessary, sir, for me,
with that seriousness and sincerity
which it may be permitted to a man
upon the most solemn occasions to ex
press, to assert, and Ido now assert in
the face of this House—that if, instead
of an advocate, I had been sitting as a
judge, at another tribunal, I should
have been found among the number of
those men who, laying their hands up
on their hearts, conscientiously pro
nounced her Majesty, “Not guilty.”
(Reiterated cheers.) Fer the truth of
this assertion I desire to tender every
pledge that may be most valued and
most sacred. I wish to make it in eve
ry form which may be deemed most
solemn and most binding ; and if I be
lieve it not, as I now advance it, I here
imprecate on myself every curse which
is most horrid and most penal.” (It
would be difficult to describe the earn
est emphasis with which this assevera
tion was delivered, the deep interest
with which it was listened to, or the
enthusiastick and general cheering with
which it was greeted.)

LONDON, FEB. 8.
The Duke of Roxburgh, whom the
London Times has announced as being
appointed Chamberlain of the Queen
of England, never heard of the nom
ination. He is 85 years of age, lives
retired on his estates in Scotland, and
never purposes again to visit London.

A letter from Laybach, of a recent
date, announces that since the arrival
of Duke de Gallo, minister from Naples,
the negotiations and the conferences
have taken a turn which encourages
the hope that the tranquillity of Europe
will not be disturbed.

rived yesterday. There is nothing new
from Laybach. The King of Prussia
had not left Berlin on ihe 3d Inst. The
Neapolitan Prince Regent is said to
have ordered a conscription to supply

the place of the troops whose service

xi, to review the troops there, amount

ergency occur to place the safety or the

It is the general opinion here, that
the members of the alliance are desir
ous of avoiding a war with the Neapol
itans. A report has nevertheless been
circulated that the Peninsula will be
occupied by a military force. It is e
ven asserted that the Austrian army
has made a general movement for the
purpose of passing the Po.
LAYBACH, FEB. 2.
The Austrian army passed tne Po on
the 28th and 29th of January, and is ad
vancing upon Naples by three differ
ent routes, forty thousand men will
first advance to the frontiers, who will
announce, in case of resistance, that
they will be followed by 80,000 more !
His Majesty the King of Naples has
addressed a proclamation to the inhabit
ants of the Two Sicilies, in which he
orders the immediate dissolution of the
Parliament. He also calls on them to
receive the Austrians as friends, and
promises, on his return, to give them a
Constitution,

NORFOLK, MARCH 22.
Horrible and mysterious Murder !
We have seldom read, either in the
annals of real life, or in the pages of
romance, of deeds of blood and horrour,
equal in atrocity and shocking circum
stances, to one which has just fallen
under our notice—the particulars of
which, as far as we have been able to
collect them, we here lay before our
readers.
About the first of this month, two
Frenchmen came to this place from
Baltimore, and renteda small dwelling
house in a retired situation, near Plume’s
P.ope Walk, but seklon made use of it,
and then only at night. Their mysteri
ous movements excred considerable
curiosity in the neighbourhood, and
even suspicions not altogether favoura
ble to them.
Yesterday morning these two men,
and a third, were observed to be in the
house, and between 9 and 10 o’clock, a
Mrs. Lester, residing in an adjacent ten
ement, was alarmed by a sudden cry,
which seemed to be the cry of “ mur
der Some time after, two of the
men left the house. Mrs. Lester, under
the conviction that there was some
thing amiss going on in the house, related
the circumstances to a constable, who
entered the house, and discovered a
spectacle truly horrible, and revolting
to every feeling of humanity. In a
chamber of the second story was ex
tended on the floor the naked trunk of
a human being, divested of its head and
limbs, and in the fire-place lay the
head, feet and hands, burnt almost to
cinders !! The arms were separated
from the body, at the shoulder joints,
and again divided at the elbows ; and
the legs cut apart at the joints of the
knees. Indeed, the whole infernal op
eration appeared to have been perform
ed with the dexterity of a skilful sur
geon. The limbs thus separated were
thrown together in a bucket. On the
floor lay an axe, besmeared with blood,
with which the diabolical authors of
this foul massacre had dispatched their
victim, and two butcher knives, which
had served the office of dissection.
A Corner’s Inquest was immediately
summoned, but no evidence appeared
which could in the slightest degree

criminate any known individual. Neith
er the name of the deceased, nor that
of his companion, could be ascertained
with certainty; and all the decount that
could be given of them amounted to
no more than what we have before stat
ed, except that they had been the night
before at a house of no good repute in
Church-street; and the verdict of the
jury was as a matter of course, “ Wilful
murder by some person or persons un
known.”
There was no furniture of any kind
in the house, save a few articles of bed
ding, and two trunks. What then could
have been the purpose of these people
in taking the house ?
In one of these trunks were a num
ber of articles oi valuable cloathing;
in the other a number of valuable
vyatches, watch-chains, nnd sundry ar
ticles of jewelry— on the floor, too,
was an elegant gold patent lever watch.
The object in committing the murder
could not have been plunder, or the
murderers would have secured these
valuables. What then could have been
the motive ? We can imagine no other
but revenge.
Another idea suggests itself, howev
er, which does away this supposition.—
Their intention, evidently, was to cut
the whole body in pieces, and burn it
at their leisure ; and their leaving the
house was probably only for a time,
when they would return, complete their
hellish work, and carry off the property
without exciting suspicion.
In one of the trunks was found a ma
sonick diploma, from the Grand Lodge
ot Maryland, filled up in the name of
Peter Lagoardette, and dated, city of
Baltimore, 21st Dec. 1820.—But wheth
er that was the name of the deceased,
or of his companion, or, indeed of eith
er ot them, is a matter of uncertainty.
It was stated by a Frenchman, who said
he was acquainted with the person,
whom he supposed the deceased to be,
that his name was Dade.
An examination into this mysterious
case was subsequently instituted by the
Mayor, but after examining a number
of persons, the inquiry resulted in noth
ing satisfactory. It was stated that the
deceased and his companion had fre
quently been seen in company with two
Spaniards, who had lately arrived in
town from Baltimore, and about whom
there were some suspicious indications.
Should we be too hasty in surmising
that the deceased and his companion,
together with the two Spaniards, with
whom they associated, were a band of
depredators upon the community by all
the various arts of robbery and swind
ling ? Their incognito movements—but
above all, the implements for lock-pick
ing, found among the effects of the de
ceased, leave but little room to doubt
that such was their occupation.
NORFOIJC, MARCH 23.
In our paper of Wednesday, we gave
an account of a murder, of a most un
usual and horrifick character, perpe
trated on the body of a man, whose
name was (perhaps not incorrectly) be
lieved to be Peter Lagoardette. An
active and energetick investigation by
our police of all the circumstances
connected with this deed of darkness,
that could be collected from earnest and
unremitted inquiry, aided by the exer
tions of some gentlemen, in the vicini- (
ty, has resulted in the apprehension
of two Spaniards, who call themselves
Manuel Philip Garcia and Joseph Gar- .
cia, suspected of being the murderers. !
They were yesterday examined before
a Magistrate’s Court, and committed
for further examination at a Court to be
held for the purpose on Friday, the
30th instant. |
We were present at the examination,
and heard the interrogatories put to a i
number of witnesses, brought forward '
to identify these men as the persons who
were joint occupants of the house with
the deceased, to within a few hours of
the time at which he was found murder
ed, and from this and a variety of oth
er circumstances, suspected of being
the authors of his death.
We forbear, however, to touch up
on the evidence which was adduced, or
to offer any opinion of its competency
to convict those in custody of this atro
cious murder. Suffice it to say, that the
Court considered the testimony suffi
cient to justify their commitment.
NEWARK, (omo,) MARCH 15.
Singular Casualty.
Some time in the night of the 7th
inst. William Young entered a still-house
belonging to John Green, Esq. about
three miles from this place, and laid
himself down on one of the stills, for
the purpose, supposed, of warming him
self. Here, it is conjectured, he fell
asleep; and, turning over, precipitated
himself into the boiler, which stands
close to the place on .which he was ly
ing. The boiler contained water, near
ly boiling hot, in which the person of
Young, with the exception of his head
'and feet, was immersed. How long he
remained in this state is uncertain. He
was rescued by Mr. Green, who was
aroused from sleep by the suflerer’s
moans; nor was it until after repeated
attempts that the former succeeded in
his object.. He, in the first place,
catching hold of Young’s legs; but

failing in this, he next grasped his hsfr t
by which he was dragged out* When
Y oung's clothes were skipped off, his
skin almost all pealed off; and the flesh
on his fingers was so scalded, that it
left the bones naked. The unhappy
man survived the catastrophe but a
short time. He died in great agony.
