Fish from Market to Meal-time. 

Helpful Hints. 

1. In season use local fish to save transportation costs; they are fresher and better than 
even choice varieties from a distance. 

2. Frozen fish is wholesome food if frozen when caught, and kept frozen until it reaches 
the consumer. 

3. Canned fish of a reliable brand should be in every pantry for occasional use as well as 
for emergencies. 

4. Salt fish needs careful cookery; a dish of creamed codfish is delicious or detestable ac- 
cording to preparation. 

5. Smoked fish deserves more attention; it can be used as a relish, in sandwiches, grilled 
on toast, steamed, creamed or baked in milk. 

6. Broiling is the simplest and most wholesome way of cooking fish; it is easily done by 
gas, with no overheated cook. 

7. The boning of fish is especially desirable where children are served. 

8. Fish baked in a ventilated gas oven does not afi'ect other foods, so that the whole meal 
may be oven-cooked. 

9. A green salad, sliced tomatoes or an acid sauce combine well with fish. The juice of 
quartered lemons is obtained more easily than that of slices. 

10. Grape fruit is a' pleasing exception to the rule against serving fruit after fish, and 
makes a good finish. 

I I. Remove skin and bones from left-over fish while it is still warm. 

12. Use sal soda and hot suds to wash fish utensils and to scald the sink. 

13. Use dry mustard to remove fish odor from the hands. 

Fish. 

The increased use of fish has the advantage of conserving meats, and giving wholesome 
variety. It is economical food and easy to cook. Home-cooked fish is far superior to that 
in restaurants, as prompt service is important. With a good gas range fish cookery is simpli- 
fied and fuel cost is small. Many do not care for fish because it is not properly cooked. Care 
is more necessary than skill, and a little experience produces fine* results. Fish should be 
served as meat, not preceding it. Oily fish like shad and salmon are more like meat than 
cod and lake fish because of the fat they contain. In nutriment the fat is the main difference, 
and in digestibility fish compares favorably with meat. 

For real economy there should be no set day to eat fish, as this causes waste on other 
days and adds to the price we pay. Perhaps "every day will be fish day by and by." The 
variety that is scarce and high should be passed by for the kind that is plentiful and low. 



Price is regulated by distance as well as variety. Know your fish market. Personal inspec- 
tion is most important in buying fish. Firmness is the first consideration. Soft, watery flesh 
is the first sign of spoiling; a disagreeable odor is the second. At the season when fish is plenti- 
ful it is frozen in large quantities, to be held until needed, and to equalize distribution. Cold 
storage, when rightly maintained, is of great benefit to the public; but much harm follows 
through ignorance. People demand fresh fish and refuse the frozen variety, which forces the 
dealer to thaw his fish beforehand. Storage products lose flavor rapidly after thawing, and 
spoil quicker than fresh foods. The wise ones buy frozen fish and thaw it themselves. It 
will thaw at room temperature or in cold water, and if cooked at once is excellent. 

Salt fish has high food value, is always available and can be used in many ways. Smoked 
fish has its seasons, and dries out rapidly after ten days. Avoid extended cookery or high 
temperature for either. Canned salmon is a splendid food, with many possibilities. Fresh- 
cooked foods are fine, but on busy days, better a canned meal than a cross cook. Be prepared 
for the Lenten season and emergencies. Of fresh fish one thick slice is better than two thin 
ones; large fish at 25 cents per pound is cheaper than small at 20 cents, due to the propor- 
tion of waste. Left-over fish can be creamed, scalloped or made into fish balls, it is delicious 
served cold with mayonnaise and chili sauce. 

Fish should be cleaned as soons as it enters the house. Keep one pan for washing fish, 
use plenty of cold water, but do not soak it (except to thaw). Drain well and wipe dry when 
cleaned. If not to be cooked at once, wrap in dry cloth, then in heavy paper and put in a 
cool place. Do not put on ice, but the refrigerator shelves may be used, as paper prevents 
spreading odors. Split boned fish is easy to broil under gas flame, and attractive too. Who 
can complain of meatless days when choice broiled fish is obtainable? For guest affairs there 
are few superior dishes, it is easy for cook and carver alike, and popular with all good livers. 
Dip small fish in milk and roll in seasoned meal; saute in pork fat to save deep frying. Over- 
cooked fish is "wooly"; undercooked fish is unwholesome; the flakes separate readily when 
fish is done. Steaming is more economical than boiling unless the liquid is used for a fish 
sauce. There are many recipes, but all are included in a few general methods. Fish cookery 
is well worth mastering. 

There are many palatable fish which are little used, or comparatively unknown. Do 
not be afraid to try different varieties. Write to the Bureau of Fisheries, Washington, D. C, 
for free government circulars on fish. They are interesting and valuable. 

Meat, and How to Make the Most of It. 

Helpful Hints. 

1. Cook meat for several meals when possible, but use only a portion at a time; reserving 
balance before serving prevents anticipation of reappearance. 

2. Avoid washing meat — wipe with a damp cloth but do not waste juices with water. 

3. Extend use of cheaper cuts with dried vegetables or cereal products and plenty of 
gravy. 

4. Utilize every particle of meat fat to save butter, lard and commercial shortening. 

5. Brown all or part of meat for stews, etc., to improve color and flavor. 

6. Thicken liquid beforehand for casserole meat and ragout, to increase richness and 
shorten cooking process. 

7. A variety of seasonings, as bay leaves, garlic, cloves, pepper-corns, dried parsley and 
celery leaves — also different herbs — are valuable aids in meat cookery. 

8. A 5-pound stewing hen is more economical than a 3-pound roasting fowl, and admits of 
more variations. 

9. Sausage, bacon and small chops can be broiled on a rack in a pie pan, instead of using 
the large broiler. 

10. Prejudice against boiled meat may be overcome by draining meat when tender, dredg- 
ing with flour and browning it well in meat drippings, the gravy to be served separately. 

11. Real soup (the full meal variety) with vegetables, grains, bits of meat and the rich 
flavor from long, slow cooking is easily made with the steady heat of gas. 

Meat Economy. 

No sacrifice is necessary in the reduction of meat purchased, if every bit be used to best 
advantage. Marketing is a personal matter. Marketing offers a choice; ordering results in 
the dealer's choice. Good meat is firm and fat; lean meat lacks flavor and requires additional 



fat. Look for the government stamp to insure wholesomeness. For roasting and broiling, 
meat must be tender. Tough cuts are made tender by the acid of lemon juice or vinegar, by 
grinding, by pounding, or, best of all, by extended cookery, as stews and casserole dishes. 
The finished product contains no more nutriment than at the start, but may lose much in 
cooking; proper regulation of heat is essential. There is more loss in weight of meat roasted 
in the closed oven of a cook stove than in the ventilated oven of a gas range. Continued 
even heat softens the toughest fiber. Certainty of result is an incentive; "luck" has no place 
in gas cookery. 

All meats require strong heat at first to save juices. A large roast is more economical than 
a small one in food value, flavor and fuel. Place meat on a rack in roasting pan. Crisp 
quickly on each side under the gas flame, then season, reduce heat and finish cooking on lower 
slide or transfer to baking oven. Use no water for choice beef or mutton, but baste with its 
own fat. Make a stock in the oven at the same time with bone, meat trimmings and vegeta- 
bles as foundation for gravy. A full oven meal should be planned to conserve fuel. 

A fine broiled steak is a luxury to-day, but for a special treat there is nothing better. 
Boned meat is easy to carve, but flavor is finer with the bone. Cut edges of steak at intervals 
to prevent curling. The tough end may be removed before broiling, to be chopped for meat 
roll. Heat gas oven well to insure quick crisping. Brown each side under gas flame, and 
avoid piercing flesh with fork. Reduce flame, season lightly and finish cooking on a lower 
slide. Leave lower oven door open while broiling, to avoid smoke and smell. Many cooks 
give up broiling after a few unfortunate trials with the door closed. Oven heat during broil- 
ing serves admirably for pop-overs, biscuit, panned tomatoes, baked bananas, reheated 
potatoes or a simple pudding. Left-over steak, if thick and rare, is as good sliced as cold roast 
beef. The bone and trimmings are simmered afterward with cold water and seasonings to 
make a good cup of stock. 

Some Advantages of Slow Cookery for All Tough Meats, and Some Vegetables. 

1. Conserves food value. 

2. Softens meat tissue and vegetable cellulose. 

3. Aids digestibility. 

4. Develops flavor. 

5. Reduces cooking odors. 

6. Decreases evaporation of liquid. 

7. Retains moisture in food. 

8. Foods retain shape. 

9. Prevents scorching. 

10. Eliminates watchfulness. 

1 1. Reduces utensil wear. 

12. Lessens dish washing by preventing discoloration. 

13. Cuts fuel costs in half. 

It is so simple that few have faith in it; so easy that it seems too good to be true. A 
slight sound of bubbling is sufficient evidence of cooking. 

For Meatless Days. 

A well-balanced meal consists of meat, fish or its equivalent, one starchy and one green 
vegetable, with perhaps a simple sweet. In place of meat we use eggs, cheese, milk and the 
legumes, — lentils, peas and beans. The soy bean is high in food value and low in cost; it 
needs more soaking and longer cooking than other varieties. Split peas, yellow and green, 
also cow peas, are palatable foods if carefully seasoned. Milk as used in cream soups is an 
economical food and excellent for children. Cheese dishes are admirable if not overcooked. 
Even the notorious Welsh rarebit is a good luncheon dish, well balanced with a simple green 
salad. All meat substitutes need slow, careful cookery. Avoid intricate recipes and elaborate 
combinations; simple dishes are best. 

With food conservation a national issue, cooking is at a premium. As much food is wasted 
by bad cooking as by throwing away what might be used. Full garbage cans are direct evi- 
dence of extravagance; good food badly prepared eventually proves more wasteful through 
poorly nourished bodies. 



Vegetables. 

Helpful Hints. 

1. When cooking enough of any vegetable to allow for another meal, reserve the portion 
desired before adding sauce or butter, serving "just enough" and no more. 

2. Rice to serve with boiled mutton or fowl may be cooked in the same liquid, if placed 
in a cheesecloth bag, and easily drained for separate service. 

3. Never add salt to cold water when crisping cucumbers or other vegetables, as it 
toughens them. 

4. Vegetables that are odorous can be cooked early and kept hot. Any creamed vegeta- 
ble is improved by standing over hot water awhile; early preparation is also of practical ad- 
vantage in hot weather, and for guest dinners. 

5. Lettuce leaves that are unsightly, but edible, may be rolled tight and shredded with 
a sharp knife for salad or garnishing. 

6. Use celery leaves (fresh or dried) for soup; the coarse outer stalks may be creamed; 
use the next portion for salad, and the choice center for fresh service. 

7. Dry parsley quickly to retain color, rub through strainer or wire pie pan, and keep in 
tightly corked bottle for flavor and garnishing. 

8. To bake new potatoes, boil until almost done, drain well and bake in hot oven twenty 
or thirty minutes. 

9. Parboil thick slices of Spanish or other mild onion, season and spread with meat drip- 
pings, and grill under gas flame. Serve on rounds of toasted graham bread. 

10. Send to the Department of Publications in Washington for the government bulletin 
on "Care of Foods in the Home." 



Vegetable Economy. 

The use of more vegetables in our diet reduces meat costs, improves health and helps con- 
servation by using perishable foods. The use of local supplies avoids transportation prob- 
lems. We need vegetables for bulk, for food value, for mineral salts and flavor. Green stuffs 
are good body regulators, and their generous use cuts down doctors' bills and the profits of 
tonic makers. Simple salads of vegetables are better than heavy combinations; use them 
cooked or raw, with oil or cream (sweet or sour). When in doubt between a salad or a cooked 
dessert choose the salad. 

Personal marketing is imperative to obtain good value. Overripe products are far more 
dangerous than immature ones; badly wilted vegetables are never a bargain. Dried vegeta- 
bles as meat substitutes cost about half the price of commercially canned goods; the cooking 
is simple and fuel cost small. Natural products, home-cooked, give the best returns for 
the investment. Prepared foods are never real substitutes for the meal cooked in our own 
kitchens. 

In buying, plan for second service and save time and fuel; most vegetables may be re- 
heated, and many serve well in salads. A cool, airy space is necessary for storing vegetables. 
Baskets or wire racks are better containers than boxes or tight compartments. Overcrowding 
soon causes decay. When refrigeration is necessary odorous foods can be wrapped in clean 
paper. Melons or bananas will not affect other foods if placed in paper bags. Peeled or cut 
vegetables wrapped in wet cloth can be placed in such bags to retain moisture and eliminate 
odors. 

Cleaning and cutting vegetables just before the evening meal is both inconvenient and 
unnecessary. Except potatoes (which can be cooked in many ways without paring while raw), 
vegetables can be prepared in advance. Fibrous vegetables, like turnips and kohl-rabi, can 
be sliced, green and wax beans cut or broken, and placed in cloth as suggested for refrigerator 
use. Celery, onions, sprouts and cut cabbage can be left in cold water. Parsnips, carrots 
and salsify are easily peeled when partly cooked, then finished as usual. Methods depend 
upon the kind of vegetable. 

Careful cookery retains food value and flavor. More vegetables are spoiled through bad 
cookery than any other foods. Most vegetables are more than half water, so why flood with 
water in cooking? Adding insult to injury, this common method washes out valuable salts 
and flavor; then pours them into an unappreciative sink. Rapid cooking saves no time but 
wastes it by the watchfulness required to prevent scorching. Vegetables boiled furiously in 
a volume of water lose all character. The boiling point, 212°, is all that can be utilized; half 



the gas generally used will accomplish this. Fuel economy is easily practiced by slow cookery. 
The simmering burner is often advised for slow surface cookery, but the medium burners give 
steadier heat, with no discoloration of utensil (as sometimes occurs with simmering burner). 
The heat is spread under entire surface, resulting in even cookery without increased gas con- 
sumption. 

Water must be boiling at the start (except for green corn and dried vegetables). Water 
from the boiler should never be used. A quart of fresh cold water can be brought to the boil- 
ing point in four minutes, so there is no excuse for keeping water in the teakettle to become 
flat. Broad flat-bottomed utensils are desirable. Salt green vegetables at once, others when 
partly done. Reduce flame as soon as contents are boiling. Certain vegetables are better 
cooked with so little water that when done it just serves to moisten the product. With tightly 
covered utensil and low flame contents cannot boil over or cook dry. With seasoning, a little 
fat of some kind, and slight thickening if desired, the result is a savory dish and food value is 
all there. Try this out thoroughly, for seeing is believing, and the next time you smell burning 
food rest content that it is in your neighbor's kitchen, not your own. Asparagus, green, wax 
and fresh lima beans, new carrots, celery, peas and summer squash are in this class. Spinach 
requires no moisture but the water which clings after washing; drain this and use in cream 
soup. 

Potatoes. — If bought by the peck, sort on arrival, reserving large ones to bake and small 
to boil in jackets. When possible cook enough for two meals at one time. Use water to cover 
and moderate heat. If peeled, save water for bread making. Rapid boiling cooks them to 
pieces; slow cooking makes them soggy. The easiest way of paring is to boil potatoes ten 
minutes, drain and skin like scalded tomatoes, then finish cooking in any way desired. This 
saves potato, time and one's hands. Test with sharp skewer or pointed knife; a fork may 
break them. Drain at once when done, and cover with soft cloth to absorb moisture. They 
can be kept hot half an hour, and are more mealy than when served at once. 

Perfect baked potatoes are essentially home-cooked, and no better food can be found. 
Thorough scrubbing insures skins that may be eaten. Save time in emergencies by placing 
potatoes in a deep pan and covering with boiling water for ten minutes, while heating the 
oven. Dry off before placing in oven, as wet potatoes take ten minutes longer to bake than 
dry. A crusty skin is produced by greasing the potato before baking. Test by pinching — 
never pierce — and serve as soon as done. If they must wait, roll each one gently in a cloth 
and soften without breaking skins. An oven temperature of 375° to 400° bakes potatoes well; 
too slow an oven ruins them, and one too hot wastes both fuel and food. 

Artichokes, brussels sprouts, cabbage, cauliflower, kohl-rabi, turnips, okra, onions, pars- 
nips and salsify require water to cover, afterward drained off for soups. Cabbage in the form 
of sauer kraut is most digestible and wholesome. Mushrooms and tomatoes are cooked with- 
out water. Rice and macaroni need considerable water and medium fire; grease inside of 
kettle to prevent sticking or boiling over. The water can be used in bread making, meat 
cookery or soup. Lentils, soy, kidney and navy beans require long soaking; use the same 
liquid for cooking. Never use soda in vegetable cookery. Cook hominy grits in double boiler, 
to serve as cereal or with meat. 

Butter in vegetable cookery may be substituted by any reliable butterine or oleo (a per- 
fectly wholesome, clean product), or by home-rendered drippings. Delicate vegetables call 
for the former; strong ones may be enriched with meat fats. Milk in vegetable cookery is 
an important factor, improving some and extending others. Vegetable soups and chowders 
made with milk form almost a whole meal. Cream soups of liquid from vegetables and full 
milk are excellent for children. A thickening of flour, cornstarch, arrowroot, rice flour or soft 
bread crumbs is often desirable; a hot, smooth, well-seasoned sauce works wonders in agree- 
able service. Beaten egg yolk added at the last moment enriches and gives delicacy. Cream 
seems extravagant, but when compared with butter at present prices is equivalent, and often 
more pleasing. 

When the oven is in use boil vegetables there. Begin cookery on top as usual and place 
utensils on oven bottom when bubbling. Enamel or aluminum is best for both covers and con- 
tainers, the latter without handles for saving space. The cost of a few such articles will be 
more than paid for in the saving of gas. When meat stock is available it may be substituted 
for water with savory results. 



Household Fats. 

" To make one wise dollar do the work of two foolish ones." 
Helpful Hints. 

1. Give preference to vegetable fats, when it is necessary to buy, to conserve meat 
products. 

2. For cooking and salad use, corn oil is excellent and cottonseed oil satisfactory; vegeta- 
ble fats in solid form answer perfectly for shortening. Deep frying is tabooed during fat short- 
age. 

3. Butter economy in cooking is best effected by use of oleo or butterine. Cooking butter 
is a poor substitute. Butterine is a clean, perfectly wholesome food; every pound is govern- 
ment-inspected. 

4. Home-rendered fats are most economical, and rnay be used in general cookery if care- 
fully prepared. 

5. Use strained fat from bacon or ham instead of butter in white sauce for milk toast, 
baked or creamed potatoes, in meat dressing and vegetable cookery. 

6. Pork fat is good in baked beans, hashed potatoes, fried apples or bananas, dried vegeta- 
bles and fish cookery. 

7. Beef fat may be used in cooked salad dressing, bread making, crust for meat pies, 
tomato sauce or savory-made dishes. 

8. Combined or single fats of bland flavor serve as shortening for hot breads, simple 
batters, in soups and vegetable combinations. 

9. Savory fats can be used in meat and vegetable cookery. 

10. Chicken fat makes good pastry. 

11. Corn bread, muffms, biscuit, etc., served hot are palatable with almost any rendered 
fat. 

Care and Use of Fats. 

Fat is an important food. It furnishes heat and energy in most concentrated form, and 
is almost completely digested by a normal person. Olive oil, butter, bacon, cream and vegeta- 
ble fats are valuable foods for children. The laborer at hard work can take care of the heavier 
fats from beef, mutton and fresh pork. The digestibility of fat depends upon the character 
and sweetness of it, the temperature to which it has been heated, and the quantity eaten. 
The energy value of various fats does not differ greatly, but flavor and appearance add to 
cost of products on the market. True economy consists in utilizing every atom of fat rather 
than cutting down the supply eaten. 

Fat of all kinds should be saved and used. Butchers trim meat and fowl to improve ap- 
pearance; if we do not claim what we have paid for the dealer sells it a second time for soap 
making, or renders it himself. Fat is also trimmed from meat at home. It may take several 
days to accumulate enough. to be worth preparing, but in a cool place clear fat will keep for 
some time. Mutton fat has strong flavor, so is not used as much in cooking as it might be 
if carefully prepared. 

Solid fats from raw or cooked meats must be rendered. Used fats and drippings are* 
clarified. For rendering, the outer skin and all lean parts are removed, then the fat is cut 
small, or run through food chopper with coarse adjustment. Strong fat is improved by soaking 
some hours in cold salt water, rinsing well before heating. To i pound of fat add one-third 
cup of water and cook very slowly. It burns easily after water evaporates, so watch carefully 
after bubbling ceases. Hot fat, when still, is fairly dry. Overheated fat has bad flavor and is 
indigestible. In a shallow, closely covered utensil, with flame turned to lowest point, there 
is no danger of fat cooking too rapidly, and when almost done the cover may be removed 
to complete evaporation. The steady, even heat of gas accomplishes this at about half a cent 
an hour. If the oven is in use it is desirable to render fat there and avoid cooking odors. Low 
temperature is best, but the utensil can be placed in a pan of water in oven if heat is too 
great. Fats may also be melted in a double boiler without being mixed with liquid, except 
in the case of mutton, when the use of milk is desirable; one-half cup to a pound of fat will 
remove some of the strong taste. A pinch of soda or a few pieces of charcoal may also be 
added to neutralize flavor. Good results are obtained by combining either beef or mutton 
fat and vegetable oil, in proportion of 3 to i ; the blend improves consistency and modifies 
flavor. Various seasonings make possible the use of strong fat of duck or goose. The addi- 



tit)n of a sour apple, slice of onion, bay leaf, salt and pepper is good. A combination of herbs 
also makes savory fat. 

The fat skimmed from soup or boiled fowl, corned beef, etc., and the drippings from 
roasts may be clarified by heating slowly with sliced raw potato until it ceases to bubble. Or, 
add boiling water to fat, let boil a few minutes and set aside. When cold the fat is removed 
in a solid cake and the impurities clinging to it scraped off. This process may be repeated 
several times to make it more clear. Fat must be free from moisture to keep well. The sur- 
plus fats from roasts and broiled meats have fine flavor, and should be strained while hot 
to use in future cookery, for basting meat deficient in fat, or reheating meat and making good 
gravy. Ham and bacon fat may be rendered with crushed egg shells to remove smoky flavor. 
All rendered and clarified fats must be strained through muslin while hot. As earthenware 
absorbs odors it is best to keep fats in enamelware or tin, closely covered and in a cool, dark 
place. Jelly glasses answer well for small amounts, coffee cans for larger quantities. 

Spices, molasses and chocolate serve admirably to conceal fats which, while pure and 
wholesome, have too pronounced a taste. Additional salt is necessary with all fats to give the 
butter taste. 

The cracklings, or crisp bits of sweet rendered fat, are appetizing morsels for sandwich 
filling, in scrambled eggs, an omelet or stuffed eggs, in corn bread, with hominy grits and 
sprinkled over milk toast. 

Good white soap can be made at home from accumulated fats. 

All fats cannot be used for the same purpose, but all are of practical use, as every thrifty 
housewife discovers. If one questions whether it be worth while to prepare fat of slight cost 
as a substitute for expensive products, compare the time spent with the result obtained to 
determine the real economy. 

Canning Fruit Syrups, i 

Fruits may be satisfactorily canned without sugar, and those put up especially for young 
children might better have sugar omitted. The adult taste requires sweetened fruit, and less 
»• sugar is required if the fruit is sweetened when canned. Sugar is added in syrup form when 
the product is canned, and permeates it well during the processing or sterilizing. 

It is more economical to can fruits with sugar than to add sugar when using. 

in directions given, various grades of syrup are mentioned. These are in the following 
proportions: — 

Thin. — One part sugar to 4 parts water. 

Medium. — One part sugar to 2 parts water. 

Thick. — One part sugar to 1 part water. 

In making the syrup liave the water boiling, then add the sugar very gradually. Stir 
constantly, keeping the liquid boiling until all of the sugar is dissolved. A clear syrup, which 
rarely needs skimming, results if this method is used. 

Thin syrups are used for all sweet fruits, such as cherries, peaches and apples. Use medium 
syrups with sour fruits, such as strawberries, gooseberries, apricots. 

Thick syrup is suitable for preserving, and especially sun-cooked preserves. Thin syrup 
is not sticky; medium syrup is sticky when cooled on spoon; thick syrup when poured has a 
thickened appearance. 

Care should be taken while using the syrups. The liquid should be added boiling hot to 
the filled jars, but between times, if allowfKi to continue boiling, it will change in quality, — 
a thin syrup in small quantity, rapidly becoming thick. The commission will be glad to 
answer any questions written on one side of the paper and sent in a self-addressed stamped 
envelope.

On the other hand, we would not inter-

We would also give to the products of

with sound expediency and moral and re-
ligious obligation, a fair measure of legis-
lative regard and protection.

In our state legislation, we desire to
repeal the oppressive laws which degrade
the black man without benefiting the
white: whose legitimate tendency is to
drive from among us the respectable, the
intelligent and the pious men of color,
and leave only the ignorant, and the vi-
cious, rendered ten fold more dangerous,
by the removal of the most powerful re-
straining influence which can be brought
to bear upon them.

We would encourage the self improve-
ment of the colored people in virtue and
knowledge, by suitable legislative provi-
sions.

We would secure to every man a spee-
dy and impartial trial by jury, in all ca-
ses where life or liberty shall be in ques-
tion.

We would secure to the whole popula-
tion of the state, the benefits of general
education ; a sound currency ; an adequate
market; and an economical expenditure
in all the departments of the state go-
vernment.

These are the principles, these the ob-
jects of the LIBERTY PARTY. No
honest man need be ashamed of them.—
They are indissolubly connected with the
prosperity and honor of our country and
our State.

If there were any rational prospect that
either of the other parties would bend its
exertions to accomplish these objects, we
should not unfurl the flag of a separate
organization. But there is none. Each
of them depends for its ascendancy on
the slave power. Each, consequently,
must shape its ends and measures in ac-
cordance with the demands of the slave
power.

We, therefore, give to the breeze the
banner of Constitutional Liberty. We
inscribe onits folds LIBERTY_EQUAL
RIGHTS—PROTECTION TO FREE
LABOR—GENERAL EDUCATION—
PUBLIC ECONOMY. We rally under
it with firm resolution, never to abandon
the contest, never to relax our exertions,
until our great object shall be happily ac-
complished. Last year the Liberty par-
ty counted her votes by thousands ; this
year she counted them by tens of thou-
sands. next year she hopes to count them
by hundreds of thousands. We feel as-
sured that the time is not far distant,
when the people will come to the rescue
of their own institutions and their own
interests from the grasp of slavery. In
vain will the laborer, the mechanic, the
manufacturer, the farmer, the merchant,
look for stability in public policy and se-
curity for the earnings of industry, until
the disturbing forces of slavery is remov-
ed from our political system. Let all
unite in effecting its removal, and we
venture to predict that a measure of per-
manent prosperity and public happiness,
such as the country has never yet witness-
ed, will be the result. A safe and perma-
nent market, at home and abroad will be se-
cured for the products of labor ; the most
prolific source of domestic discord will be
removed; a sound currency will be es-
tablished ; the benefits of general educa-
tion will be secured; and above all, the
blessings of that just God, who presides
over the destinies of nations, will be up-
on our beloved country and all her insti-
tutions.

and successful efforts may be made for the pro.
motion of the cause of abolition by the organiza--
tion of a new society, to be called the Eastern“

| counties who are favorable to the measure, to

| ject.
I” Itis our opinion that there are hundreds in

i ratively nothing for the cause. A nucleus will
, be formed, around which the free hearts of men
and women may rally at the summons of free-
dom, and a great work may yet be accomplished

the movements of our friends in other parts of)

THE LEGISLATURE—THE PRINTERS.

This body isnow under way—but, much as
we feared it would be, there appears to be a spi-
rit of party strife pervading too many of the
members. ‘There isa want of that calm, patient
examination ci’ the merits of the various ques-
tions coming before them, in the House especial-
ly. It appears to be determined by each party,
that whatever move is made by the other on any
question affecting the peculiar policy of either,
is to be opposed or supported according to por-
ty alliances. Weare not a little Surprized at
this ; for there are those in the Assembly this
Winter, whom we have been accustomed to es-
teem as independent men. Such men as could
appreciate the merits of a proposition from
what source soever emanating ; men, who would
legislate for the people—for the common good.
But we fear we have weighed them in the
wrong balance. They were elected because they
were parlizans; they are here as such and must

carry out the plans and purposes of their sup-
porters. They hold their offices, and the pros-
pect of office by this tenure alone.

to the times, and contained some of the best
thoughts on the great question of human liberty
that could have been uttered.
throughout evinced a high degree cf oriental re-

more especially a clear conception of the charac-
ter of his countrymen. Ireland will never lose
the high reputation she enjoys, cither for litera.
ture or Patriotism, while euch sons stand forth as
her representatives. Mr. Robinson, is a noble

Albany Female Academy.
HE next quarter will cuminence on
the 15th of February next.

Arrangements have been made to ac-
commodate a larger number of scholars
i from abroad.

This institution (founded in the year
| 1814, occupying an elegant edifice, erected
especially for its accommodation)comprises,
exclusive of the classes composed of those
pupils from the higher departments pursu-
ing the study of the French and Latin
languages, Natural History, Chemistry and
Botany, six departments, three of which
are subdivided, and the whole under the
charge of sixteen professors and teachers,
besides the seven who have charge of the
ornamental branches, and subject tomonth-
ly visitations by committees of the board
of trustees.

| As the Academy has been honored with
ia large share of the public patronage, it
may be proper in order to prevent misap-
prehension to state, that at no time has the
average number of pupils to a teacher ex-
ceeded twenty. Orifin making this esti-
mate we include the teachers of the orna-
mental branches, and as nearly all the pu-
pils in the higher departments are instruc-
ted in these branches, it is only just to do
so, then the average number of pupils to a
teacher has never exceeded fifteen. |

The course of instruction is designed to
be useful and practical, and to embrace all
the various branches of a complete female
education.

The institution is furnished sith mana,
charts, globes, models, a superior chemical
and philosophical apparatus, an orrery and
ouranotype, with numerous working mod-
elsand diagrams for the illustration of the
science of astronomy, constituting an appa-
ratus for this purpose not surpassed, it is
believed, by that of any other institution
in the country, and an extensive library,
containing about six thousand volumes;
in addition to which, in each of the three
lower departments, is a smaller library
carefully selected, with reference to the
capacities and attainments of the younger
pupils instructed in them.

Ample arrangements have been made,
under such regulations as the trustees feel
confident will prove sitisfactory to parents,
in the establishment, connected with the
family of the Principal, as well as in seve-
ral private families, for the accommodation
of pupils frum adistance And in view
of the increased and increasing number of
pupils from distance, it is proper to add,
that during the present year these arange-
ments have been considerably extended.
The expense incurred by a young lady for
board and tuition, including all the studies

Late Pastor of the M. E. Church, Hal-; taught in the Acedemy, will. not exceed

$225 per annum and in these establish-
ments the best facilities are afforded for
acquiring a nowledge of music, drawing,
or any of the ornamental branches of fe-
male education at a moderate additional
charge.

Mr. Molinard, late professor of theFrench
language at the U. S. Military Academy,
at West Point, hasthecharge of the French
department. The great celebrity and suc-
cess of their Professor as a teacher of the
French language, warrant the Trustees in
assuring their patrons that in no other in-
stitution can be found superior facilities
for proficiency in this important branch of
education.

Mr. Molinard has provided a commodi-
‘ous house in a pleasant part of the city, for
| receiving young ladies as boarders in his

family, in which the French language

alone will be spoken. The expense in-
curred by a young lady in this family for
board and tuition including all the studies
taught in the Academy, will not excced
#250 perannum.

The academical year commences on the
first of September and is divided into four
terms, commencing respectively on the Ist
j of September, 23d of November, 15th of
February, and the Sth of May; a vacation
of six weeks following the examination in
July, and a second of one week on the
iclose of the quarter ending the Ist of May.
| For terms of instruction, which have
been placed ona liberal footing, or for any
other information which may be required
in relation to the institution, reference may
be had to A. Critrenton, A. M., the prin-
cipal, or to either of the Trustees.

For general information concerning the
character of the institution, &c. the tras-
tees beg leave to refer to Chancellor Kent
of the city of New-York, Rev. Dr. Ludlow,
provost of the University of Pennsylvania,
Rev. Dr. Ferris, New York, who during
their residence in Albany, have successive-
ly presided over the institution: to Benja-
min F. Butler, Jate Attorney General of
the U. S., New York ; Hon. Jacob South-
erland, Geneva, New York, and J. T. Nor-
ton, Esq., Parmington, Conn., late trustees.

A moet animating and glorious scene was wit- |

nessed at the meeting of our Freeman's Vigilant
Total Abstinence Society, held at the Medical Col-
lege this evening, which I will briefly describe.

. The name of Thomas F. Marshall, a member of

Congress from Kentucky, nephew of the late
Chief Justice Marshall, is doubtless familiar to
you. His intellect is of a very high order, and
hia mind of that peculiar and original cast which
gives pungency, power anid eloquence to all his
efurts in the House of Representatives; and he
possesses also a warm, generous and philanthro-
pic heart. But while he has been admired for the
splendor of his genius, and loved for the quali-
ties of his heart, and while we have felt proud
of him as an American orator, all have wept over
him. Yes, all—political friends and political op-
ponents—have wept over him as a lost an: ruined
man. But this day, ‘Thomas F. Marshall, while
in the Hall of Representatives, came to the con-
elusion that he was lost forever, without a speedy
and entire refurmation, and deliberately formed
the resolution to join a temperance society. This
evening he was accompanied by his friend Mr.
Briggs and myself to the temperance meeting at
the college, where he placed his name on the
parchment roll, and took the total abstinence
pledge; after which, he rose and made a most
touching and eloquent address, detailing some in-
teresting incidents in the history of his life.
Among other things, he said he was not ashamed
of the act which he had consummated; that he
was not only willing that this step should be
known to the society, but to Congress—to the
nation—to the work!. After he sat down, Mr.
Briggs rose—and from an overtlowing heart made
an address full of power and pathos. Several
other speeches followed, and an impression was
made upon the audience which will not soon be
effaced. Several other members of Congress fol-

lowed Mr. Marshall's example, and placed their | 200 Pictorial Mlustrations of the Scriptures, ,

mames under his upon the roll.

IT need not tell you, that this event, while it is
destined! to heal a mother’s wounds, will cause a
whole state—nay, a whole nation, to rejoice over
the return of a lost favorite son.

Let us now have the example of the President
and his Cabinet; let them banish from their tables
and social parties, the use of wine and other in.
toxieating drinks; and let the members of Con-
gress sustain us by the influence of their exam-
ple, and the great object will soon be accomplish-
ed, and we shall become a happy, virtuous and
wealthy people.

Very truly yours,
THOMAS SEWALL.

TENNESSEE,

Mr. Johnson introduced a resolution in-
to the Legislature of Tennessee, Dec. 6,
for the appointment of a Joint Committee
of members from East Tennessee, to re-
port on the subject of ceding that district
to the general government, to form the
State of Frankland; and instructing the
Governor to correspond with the Gover-
nors of Georgia, North Carolina and Vir-
ginia, in regard to a cession of portions of
their territory for the same purpose. East
Tennessee contains 14,000 square miles,
being 31 per cent. of the territory of the
State, (nearly one third ;) 234,259 inhab-
itants, being 25.8 per cent, or more than
one quarter of the whole ; 18,754 slaves,
or only 10 per centof the slaves in the
State, a less number than were in New
York 40 years ago, and only 8 per cent.
of the whole population. It is supposed
the adjoining mountain districts of Georgia,
North Carolina, and Virginia are much in
the same condition, so far as slavery is
concerned. In the year 1800, New Jer-
sey had 10,35] slaves, in a population of
211,149; she now has but 674 slaves, in
a population of 373,306. We shall watch
the progress of this movement in the
‘Switzerland of America.”—The spirit
of liberty was stsong there, twenty years
ago, but has been sadly overborne by the
temptations arising from the high price of
cotton in the Southwest. Butas cotton
is now down, and down for ever, that
source of temptation will never exist again
in East Tennessee, and we may hope that
truth and justice will now again dare to
speak out, and will be heard. Some may
think it would be better polity for the
Emancipator to keep still during the in-
cipient stages of this movement, lest our
“interference” should insure its defeat.
But we must be pardoned for thinking we
understand our own business Our ob-
ject is to destroy slavery in ths land, and

GOVERNOR’S MESSAGE.

We give this copious document entire, and
leave our readers to judge of its merits or de.
merits for themselves. Onsome points we think
the views of His Excellency are correct, and
ought to be sustained. Iis position in regard to
the Virginia question is still firmly and manful-
ly maintained. On the school question, we think
the governor’s views indisputably correct. We
cannot approve the commendatory manner in
which Mr, Seward speaks of the internal improve-
ments of the state, so long as it is necessary to
increase our enormous debt to accomplish them.
No improvement can be adequate in utility to
the evil of crushing a state under a heavy em-
barrassment, without the power of that self-sup-
port which every improvement should possess.
The benefit of a given portion of community
should not be a justification for involving the state.
That is the doctrine of slavery. Rob the color-
ed man to bless and happify the white. Despoil
the principles of liberty to save despots, or tax
a state to accommodate a community.

We owe an apology to our valued friend, “T.

last, in his interesting communication on the sub.
ject of “ Capital Punishment.” The first line on
the 3d column, at the top, belongs at the top of
the 2d column, and the word “extent” should be
“extend.” The first line on the 2d paragraph of
2d column, the word Punishment should read
punishments. The note onthe 3d column, should
be, “ Observations on the visiting, &c. of Female
Prisons.” These are the most important, though
not all the mistakes that occurred in this excel-
lent article. We find a great many other typo
graphical errors in other portions of the paper,
especially in our remarks upon the “ Enquirer,”
by F.C. Delavan. The word human should be
humane, at the close of the first paragraph on the

will not severely blame our brother Printers, on
condition that we all do begin the New Year on

His buried lambs to find,
lig his silly poultry out,

IRISH AGITATION

Our Irish friends are likely to make the '
Peel administration feel exquisitely in a’
very tender point, to wit, the pocket. :
Through the prevalence of the temperance
reform they have already diverted $2,500,-
000 from that destination! An item that
will not fail to be felt in making up the
Parlimentary budget! They are now
consolidatinig a solemn league to abstain
from the purchase and use of British man-
ufactures, while their rights are withheld
from them by the mother country! O’-
Connell has actually pledged 60,000 of his
co-laborers to this course! Thus British
industry will receive a severe wound,
while Irish ingenuity and application will
be fostered and made available. What will
not men do in defence of their own blessed
rights? What if such enthusiasm should
gleam along the ranks of those who advo-
cate equai freedom in this country?) What
if they should attempt to issolate the south-
ern oppressor, and proscribe the broducts
extorted from the laborer by the gory lash?
Would not the world—would not posterity
applaud the deed¢ Would not conscience
respond heartily to the high resolve ?

It is a rich treat to speak to an assem-
blage of Irishmen on the subject of right
and liberty. There is sucha full gush
from the depths of the heart, that all with-:
in you is stirred and rises up to meet it!

y Irish friends will bear with ine,.
when I tell them that however long and
dreary the night of their father land, how- |
ever copious and bitter the tears shed by |
their own mother’s children—a darkness |
as deep, now pervades half of our own Re-
public—wrongs as grevious tu be borne,
are daily inflicted, and sufferings as acute
are constantly endured within its borders.
Let me tell them, that, when we have de-
nounced the government of England for
its policy toward Ireland, as tyrannical and
infamous in the extreme, it is only fair
to turn rouud upon our own, and pro-
nounce the curse of heaven upon it for
the uncounted deeds of atrocious cruelty
practised upon 2,500,000 of innocent per-
sons, under its official toleration and sanc-
tion. How long can Irish hearts remain
unmoved by the spectacle of peerless
villanies practised under the sacred name
of republicism? How long shall humanity
and justice plead with the countrymen of
O’Connell in vain?—Am. Citizen.

and show of high life—jarties of pleasure Hall.
and scenes of mirth, had bewitching and
unwonted influence upon this young man.
And to aid the excitement, the side-buard
of choicest liquors was thrown Open, and at
all times used freely. Soon the etleet was
seen. Having showed himself aman in
college, he must needs do an ignob/e part
in the convivial scenes, with those older
in such practices, and more accustomed to
drink than he.

This soon proved too much {or frail na-
ture—he was attacked with delirium tre-
mens, in one of its most horrible forms,
and went raving through those same halls ;
frighted by ali the vhosts and spectres of
his disordered imagination.

The scene was now changed. A fond
mother’s lamentation, and a father’s tears
tilled the place of joy and mirth. As the
last and only hope to restore their ruined
son, they resolve to take him to an Insane
Asylum. But before they had completed
the necessary preparations, he left. their
dwelling, and went forth-a wretehed mad
man, wandering whithergoever the spirit
led him.

After days of dilligent: search, he was
found many miles from home, in a desu-
late place, one of the most pitiable spec-
tacles ever beheld—(without his ordinary
clothing, and what yet remained, was be-
smeared and tattered) still raving in his
phrenzy, and haunted with all the horrid
imagery of the nether world.

This same young inan, once the just
pride of the honored circle in which he
moved, who promised to be an ornament
to society, an honor to his country, and the
glory and crown of the grey hairs of his
aged parents, is now in one of our castern
insane asylums, still a living monument
of the ruinons effects of Aleohol, while the
parents are in a state scarcely less unhap-
py, though still surrounded with all their
wealth and splendor.

Here are some of the plain facts of one
more of the thousands slain by this de-
stroyer of man and of happiness, the truth
of which can be attested at any time. Ke-
gard for the feelings of friends, now drink-
ing the dregs of the cup of bitterness, on-
ly has induced me to withhold names.
dates, &c.

But when will men learn to be wise ?
© when shall this desulating scourge be
stayed, and the sons of the great and the
pride of the nation, in common with all
other classes of soviety, no longer contin-
ue to fall before this curse of the earth ¢

The Right of Sutlrage—Duty of Colored Men.

Until the adoption of the present Constitution
in 1821, the Constitution of this State hnew no
distinction on account of color,
time the right of sutfrage, limited it is trae, was
enjoyed on the same terms by the colored man
Liberal principles had been
constantly advancing until free suffrage was de-
manded.

Previous to that

A Convention was called to revise the
Constitution, having this as a prominent object
in view.

This Convention was called by the Democratic
party. They had a large majority in the Con-
vention, and formed a Constitution to suit them.
selves. The colored people, who were voters,
with very few exceptions, had always voted with
the Bederal party. In extending the right of
suffrage it became an object with the Democratic
party to exclude the colored men, lest by thes .
Unuing to vote with the Federal party the id
turn the scale, and throw the power in e
hands of the Federal party. It would not do,
however, to exclude them entirely, hence the
odious distinction and property qualification.

Since then the colored people who have been
entitled to vote, have all, with very few excep-
lions, continued to vote on one side, and free
suffrage is still denied them by those whom they
have constantly opposed. Selfish political men
must be more influenced by principle than I sup-
pose them to be, or they will NEvER yield to
15,000 colored men the privilege of voting against
their party. We should have supposed that the
Whig party, satisfied as they must have been,
that these men would have voted with them,
having had the power to do so, would have taken
measures to extend tethem the right of suffrage.
But, no; the Whig party were so much preju-
diced against the colored man that they refused
hin the privilege of even voting the Whig ticket.
Thus. while the Democratic party have been
governed by their interest, the Whig party have
been governed by their prejudice.

What course, then, shall the colored people
take in order to obtain this right? Most clearly
stand aloof from both the Whig and Democratic
parties. The Whigs have had the power, but
would not grant the right. The Democrats will
not, so long as you vote for the Whig tichet-
And in this case, as in all others, fo do right is the
highest expediency. The Liberty Party chal.
lenges your support. Hs object is to carry out
the great principle that all men are created equal,
and entitled to equal rights and laws. It regards
the freb colored man at the north degraded hy
the operation of partial and unequal laws, as
well as the poor bondman, robbed of all his

Tire Mysrernious Music.—One of the wonders
of the southwest is the mysterious music at West
Pascagoula, A correspondent of the Baltimore
Republican, who examined it altentively, thus
takes the mantle of romance from it.

«© During several of my voyages on the Spanish
main, inthe neighborhood of ¢ Baragua,’ and ‘San
Juan de Nicheragua,’ from the nature of the coast
we were compelled to anchor at a considerable
distance from the shore; and every evening, from
dusk to late at night, our ears were delighted with
Lolian music that could be heard beneath the
counter of our schooner. At first, [ thought it
was the sea breeze sweeping through the strings
of my violin (the bridge of which [ had inadver-
tently left standing) ; bat, after examination, found
if was not so. I then placed my ear on the rail
of the vessel, when I was continually charmed
with the must heavenly strains that ever fell up-
on my ear. They did not sound as close to us,
but were sweet and mellow and ewrial; like the
soft breathings of a thousand lutes, touched by the
soft fingers of the deep sea nymphs, atan immense
distance. ‘Io the lone mariner, far from home
and kindred, at the still hour of twilight, the
notes were soothing, but melancholy.

‘© Although I have considerable ‘ music in my
soul,’ one night J became tired, and determined
to fish. My luck in half an hour was aatonishing
—I had half filled my bucket with the finest white
cat fish I ever saw; and it being late and the cook
asleep, and the moon shining, J filled my bucket
with water, and touk fish and all into my cabin for
the night.

“Thad not yet fallen asleep, when the same sweet

notes fell upon my ear; and getting up what was
my surprise to find my ‘cat-fish’ discoursing
sweet sounds to the side of my bucket.
«f examined them closely, and discovered that
there was attached to each lower lip an excre-
scence, divided by soft wiry fibres, and by the
pressure of the upper lip thereon, and by the ex-

SONNETS BY HARTLEY COLERIDOE.

‘WHO IS THE POET?”

Who is the Poet { Who ¢—the man whose lines
Live in the souls of men like household words /
Whose thought, spontaneous as the song of birds,
With eldest truth coeval, sal combines

With each day's product, and like morning shines,
Exempt from age? ‘Tis he. and only he,

Who knows that Pruth is free, and only free—
That Virtue acting in the strict contines

Of positive kiw, lustracts the infant spirit

In its best strength, and proves ats mere demerif
Rooted in earth, yet tending to the skv.—

With patient hope surveys the narcow bond,
Cnlls every Hower that loves the lowly ground,

And, fraught with sweetness, Wings her way on high,

THE USE OF A POET.
A thousand thoughts were stirring in my mind,
‘That strove in vain to fashion utterance meet,
And each the other cross’d—swilt as a fleet
Of April clouds, perpiexed by custs of wind,
That veer, and veer, around, before, behind
Now History pomted to the customed beat,
Now Fancy’s clue unraveliing, led their feet
Through mazes manitold, and qraindly twined,
So were they striving —so had ever strayed;
Had not the wiser poets of the past
The vivid chart of human life display'd,
And taught the laws that regulate the blast,
Wedding wild impulse to caim forms of beauty,
And making peace ‘iwixt liberty and duty

Whither is gone the wisdom and the power
That ancient sages scattered with the notes
Of thought-suggesting lyres ? The music floats
In the vivid air; e’en at this breathing hour,
In every cell and every blooming bower

The sweetness of old lays is hovering still:
Sut the strong soul. the seif-constrainine will,
The rugged root that bare the winsome Hower
Is weak and wither'd. Were we like the fays
That sweetly nestle in the fox-glove bells,

Or lurk and inurmur in the rose-lipp'd shells
Which Neptune to the earth for quit-rent pays,
Phen might our pretty modern Philomeils
Sustain our spirits with their roundelays.

HOMER.

Far from ali measured space. yet clear and plain
As sun al noon, ‘a mighty orb of song "’

Ittumes extremest Heaven. Beyond the throng
Of lesser stars, that rise. and wax. and wane,
Che transicut rulers of the fickle main,

One stedfast light gleams through the dark, and long,
And narrowing aisle of memory. How strung,
How fortified with all the numerous train

Of human truths, Great Poet of thy kind,

Wert thou, whose verse, capacious as the sea,
And various as the voices of the wind,

Swell'd with the giadness of the battle’s glee
And yet could glorify infirmity,

When Priam wept, or shaume-struck Helen pined

SHAKSPEARE.

The soul of man is larger than the sky,

Deeper than ocean, or the abysmal dark

Of the unfathomed centre. Like that ark,
Which in its sacred hold uplifted high,

O’er the drown’'d hills, the homan family,

And stoch reserved of every living kind,

So, in the compass of the single mind,

The seeds and pregnant forms in essence lie.
That make all worlds. Great Poet, twas thy art
To know thyself, and in thyself to be

Whate'er love, hace, arnbition, destiny,

Or the firm, fatal purpose of the heart,

Can make of man. Yet thou wert stil the same.
Serene of thought, unhurt by thy own flame

TO WORDSWORTH.

There have been poets that in verse display
Fbe.clemental eorms of human passion? i

And all the wilful humors of the ay

Have furnish'd matter for a polish’d tay ;

And many are the smooth elaborate tribe,

Who, emulous of thee, the shape describe,

And tain would every shifting hue pourtray

OF restless Nature. But thou. mighty Seer!

Tis thine to celebrate the thoughts that make
The life of souls, the truths for whose sweet sake
We to ourselves and to our God are dear.

Of Natnre’s inner shrine thou art the priest,

The Philadelphia Stave Case,
Three slaves were arrested by hired kidnappers
at Newport, Pa. some months since. One of them
burst from his captors, one of whom fired a Pistol
at him, when the slave plunged into the canal and
was drowned. The indignation of the citizens
was roused, and they would not allow the kid-
nappers to depart with the other two slaves till
the result of the coroner’s inquest was known.—
The excitement became very great, and the hun.
ters saw fitto decamp without their prey, for fear
of consequences. The claimants of the slaves |
brought an action of trespass against a large
number of citizens of Newport, for violently res-
cuing their slave property from the hands of their
agents?
Judge Baldwin allowed no man to sit on the ju-
ry who had any scruples of conscience as to the
right of property in slaves under the laws and
Constitution of the United States! With sucha
packed jury, what could be expected but a ver.
dict in favor of the claimants, for the value of
the slaves? It was given. I hope the case will
be carried up to the Supreme Court. This, and

ANNUAL MEETING

ALBANY VIGILANCE COMMITTEE.

The public meeting of citizens was held in Hamilton-street Church on
Fyjday evening, 12th Dec., and was organized by the appointment of Rey.
Ma. Pixacy, Moderator, and Ane. Brown, Secretary.

Prayer was offered by Rev. Mr. Townsend, pastor of the Church in
which we convened.

Mesers. E. P. Freeman, Thompson, Benjamin Paul and Thomas Paul,
were appointed a Committee to drafta Constitution and nominate a Com-
mittee for the ensuing year.

Rev. C. T. Torrey read the Annual Report, which was listened to with
thrilling interest by the audience. It appeared from the report, that not
less than 350 fugitives had been aided toa place of safety by the Com.
mittee, at an expense of more than $1000. The Slave Catchers from
Baltimore, Washington and other places, had in connection with certain
Albany Constables, Police Officers and Judges, watched and harrassed the
Committee as well as the fugitives ; had even indited certain members of
the Committee for their just exposures of their infamous plans, had
threatened them with violence, &c. &c, unless they ceased to snatch from
their blood hound chase their human prey. The Committee however,
have amid @ storm of rage, gone steadily forward, and nearly succeeded
in tarning the current of public sentiment upon their opposers. (Letevery
person read the report, and they will be prepared to appreciate the labors
of the Committee.)

The report was accepted and adopted, and appropriate remarks made
by E. Goodwin, Esq.

The Committee appointed to draft a Constitution, through their chair.
mas, E, P. Freeman, reported the following’ which was unanimoosly

adopted.

CONSTITUTION
or THR

ALBANY VIGILANCE COMMITTEE,

ARTICLE 1.

The objeets of this association shall be, to aid fugitive slaves to escap®
from their wicked masters, and to defend the rights of free people of color
from the assaults of slaveboldera and their agents and abettors.

, ARTICLE 11,

Any person who contributes to its funds shall be allowed to vote at its
peblic meetings, in the transaction of its business, for one year from the
time be contributes.

ARTICLE 111. .

The Annual Meeting to elect the Committee and hear the Annual Re’
port, shail be held onor near the 1st Monday in December. Public Meet-
ings may be called at any time by the Officers of the Society.

ARTICLE IY.

At the Annual Meeting an Executive Committee of 10 shall be chosen,
B of whom shall constitute a quorum to transact business, who shall elect
theic own Chairman, Secretary and Treasurer. The Executive Commit-
tee shail condact all the business of the association, keep written records
of all their doings and report to a public meeting of the contributors, an-
nually, and oftener, if they judge best.

ARTICLE Y.

This Constitution may be amended at the Annual Meeting, by the vote
of the majority of the members of the Society.

ed under the direction of the Committee.

w& the extent of the law, all, whether professed officers of justice, or pri.
vate citizens, who trample upon the rights of our colored brethren.

in fact, to be Faux from being pollated by the tread of the hunter for fu-

Every Stave on EartH was A RIGHT TO BE Free! Gop
stamped upon every human being his image. And it is only in
a state of freedom that man can properly exercise those pow-
ers that constitute the Divine image in man, for his own wel-
fare, the welfare of his kind, and the honor of his Maker.—
Whoever holds man in slavery tramples on the Divine Imace,
and audaciously assails the rights of God. God gave to every
man a right to be as free as He himself; controlled only by the
great principles of eternal rectitude and those rules of public jus-
tice, by which the good of all is promoted, while the happiness
of individuals is not sacrified, except in consequence of their own
crimes. No man has any right to restrain his fellow man, inno-
cent of crime, of the freedom Gop gave him.

The only right objeet of human laws and constitutions of Go-
vernment, is to secure to men the peaceable enjoyment of those
rights which God gave, or to use the words of the great Bible of
Liberty,

“ The unalienable rights of life, liberty, and the pursuit of hap-

iness” with which “all men are endowed by their Creator.”

If any Constitution or law presumes to take away, or impair
those rights, it is utterly null and void, in the sight of Heaven.
And no man can be under any moral or rightful obligation to obey
it. He may be, in some cases, bound to submit to it, just as we
must submit to sickness, and death, or other evils we cannot es-
cape from, by any proper use of our powers. But when we can
avoid submission to unjust jaws, we are as much bound to do s9
as we are to save our healths and lives, or to avoid theft and
murder. If the people of the United States have, by their Con-
stitution and laws, sanctioned the impious claim of the mansteal-
er, to hold his fellow man as a slave, every human being is bid-
den, by his duty to God, and his duty to his fellow man to disre-
gard that Constitution and those laws, and to submit to their
wicked requirments no farther than the violence of others com-
pels him to do so. Todo otherwise is to make wicked human
enactments of higher obligation than the ‘ unalienable rights” o
men and the laws of the Creator.

If Jaws and Constitutions exist, that take away rights, it is the
duty of every human being to use all his influence to change, or to
subvert them. If those to whoin such wicked laws concede the

right of suffrage can, by a peaceful use of their political power,
change them, and restore the rights of the people, it is their high-
est political duty to doit. If they will not, the disfranchised
have an indisputable right to assert their claims in any way they
may be able.

No man is at liberty to set down at ease under a wicked Go-
vernment, that takes away the rights of its subjects. And when
the Government ceases to answer the great ends for which it was
formed, it is the right, it is the duty of the people to subvert it,
‘‘ peaceably if they can, forcibly if they must,” and to establisif
instead of it, a just Government, which will secure the rights of
men to all who live under it. No man can innocently avoid using
all the power God has given him, to change every law, and every
Constitution, whether State or National, by which any man is
made a slave, or by which any of hisnatural rights is taken away,
or the fre exercise of them impaired. ‘To delay to act is a crime.
No plea of convenience or interests, however important, can ex-
cuse or palliate the omission or delay of our duty. For the ques-
tion is not one of interest or convenience, but of RicuT; of per-
manent, social, and moral obligation to God and man. I have
no right to postpone another man’s right to consult my interests
or convenience, any more than I have to steal money to build me
a house, because it is aconvenient way to gct money, or to swear
falsely that the Patroon left me $500,000 by his will, because it
would promote my interests very greatly to have so much mo-
ney, and the power to enjoy myself and to do good that so much
wealth would give me.

Such are the doctrines of the Declaration of Independence.—
Such are the doctrines our fathers bled to maintain. Such are
the principles of our own, and every just Government. And
they are evelasting truths. They strike an answering chord in
ever human bosom, not dead to the nobler sympathies of our na-
ture, or blinded by perverted dogmas, engendered in the school
of tyranny or fanaticism. The American avho disputes them is
false to his country, unfaithful to human liberty.

Two inferences follow from them. First. if the slave can es-
cape from the tyranny of his master, it is his right and his duty
to do so. No man can have the right to use his labor without
wages, to control his employinent, to buy or sell him, or his wife
or children, to deprive him of the means of education, or of free
access to the Bible and to all knowledge, secular and religious ;
or to do any one of those acts which constitute a man a slave-
holder. The slave is bound to submit to such tyranny no longer
than he can help it. “If thou mayst be free use it rather.”—
“Get your liberty if you can; but while you are compelled to
submit, be cheerful and submissive, duing service as unto God,
not man, not to please your tyrant master, but to please God;
who will reward you for all your sufferings.”” This is the doc-
trine of the New Testament, the doctrine of Republicanism, the
voice of truth. Slavery creat:s no right. The title of the slave
to his own earnings, is not changed or weakened. When he es-
capes from the power of his taskmaster, it is no theft to take
with him all his earnings if he can get it, whether he takes it se-
cretly, or openly, or by guile, as the children of Israel did, who

The concluding portion of our report relates to the

NUMBER AND CHARACTER OF THE FUGITIVES.

As nearly as we can now ascertain, from our very imperfect
records, we have aided about 350 fugitives since the Opening of
navigation last spring.

Of these about 150 have been men, 150 women, and 50 child-
ren and youth. Many of them have been with us too short a
time to allow us to learn their history. But we know that ma-
ny of them have been members and some of them officers of
Christian churches, fleeing sometimes from their own professed
Christian brethren, who sold and enslaved them. Christian fath-
ers and mothers, with their little children, whom they sought
to rescue from a life of slavery ; wives who fled from their task-
master’s lash, while the husband .could not; husbands who were
forced to leave a tender companion behind ; parents who fled
from the slave-trader who had already victimized their offspring ;
children whose parents had been sold from them; individuals all
of whose relatives had been sold to the trader; men and women
of every color, from the deepest black to the clearest white; all
these have been succored and sent to a place of safety.

In the deep ignorance and superstition and vices of some we
have seen the debasing influence of slavery. In the manly ener-
gy and partial education of others, we have seen indications of a
noble character, which could rise above the most depressing con-
dition of life, and assert its native dignity and worth. We can
give but a few of the many illustrations afforded us, in the histo-
ry of those fugitives, of the nature and effects of slavery. It should
be borne in mind that most of them have come from Maryland,
Virginia and the District of Columbia, where slavery is said to
Wear its mildest form. Nearly or quite 100 have come from
Washington and Georgetown. The facts which follow are se-
lected, not because they are peculiarly horrible, but because they
illustrate some principles of the slave system.

A friend in the west writes,——

Our friends are sanguine that Ontario
will double her vote. They are hard at
work, and will not slack a nerve. The
whigs are in great trouble. Who to
nominate for Congress bothers them much,
From the general tone of remark I hear,
fam satisfied that the whigs will lose the
State. Luther Bradish cannot “ gam-
mon” the abolitionists. His adhesion to
Clay hus defeated his election, O, Whig-
gery! itis your fate to jump up two feet,
and fall back three feet. The whigs in
this State are ruined by their Wall-street
clique in New York city. Had they been
willing to have nominated Mr. Bradish,
and left it unsettled as to his adhesion to
Mr. Clay, he would have injured the
Liberty Party a good deal. But this could
not be allowed by the New Yorkers. Mr.
Bradish must pledge himself, and he will
be run under by a good round imajority,
or else there is no truth in astrology.

The Syracuse convention is well spoken
of by all who attended it whom I have
seen. It has infused new courage into
our friends, and they are promising to do
well. Let us see to it, that our efforts
now be turned chiefly toward marshalling
our entire strength rather than making
converts, and we shall, as a party, at this
election hear the last sneer from those
men, who, up to the hour of their ruin,
have despised and hated, while they have
tried to seduce us.

ed in our midst. The King and chiefs have just
held their annual council, and, at that meet-
ing, the King came forward and signed the
total abstinence pledge from all that intoxi-
cates, of both native and foreign manufacture,
ameasyre which he would never listen to, for
a moment, heretofore, and so did all the
chiefs. The King has so much improved in
his conduct and dignity, that the common
people notice it, and call him the ‘New
King.’ After signing the pledge, (which isa
great deal more prohibitory than any thing |
ever saw in Knglish,) they began to fix some
penalty fora violation of the pledge—some
proposed a fine, and some to have the name
of the person found guilty, published in a na-
tive paper. Aftera few minutes, the King
rose and said, ‘for him to violate the pledge
and pay aime, would be only like cutting off
his little finger; but to break the pledge, and

The western rail road depot at Greenbush is
proceeding onward with great despateh, and
hopes are entertained that it will be ready, both
for goods and passengers, before the close of nay-
igation,

The merehandise depot is 420 by 90 feet in the
clear. On the canal-side it is 420 feet long and
its roof has a_ projection of 32 feet, covering a
platform of 20 feet outside of the building and
covering also the canal-boats so far as to be able
to Joad and unload in bad weather.

Van Rensselaer Istand, on which this depot is
made, is raised about 20 feet above its natural
level. It is elevated so as to be higher than the
highest freshet ever known in the Hudson river,
This will place all the operations of the road
above the reach of damage by high water,

The canal above spoken of, ts across the Tstand
and is parallel to the south wall of the merchan..
dise depot. It will admit of several boats loading
and unloading at the same time. The platform
outside of the merchandise depot, will be used to
great advantage, for the inspection of the flour.—
The loading and unloading of the eanal boats will
be done by steam, with great despatch,

The passenger house is 200 by 3% feet. [t is
On the Island. ‘Travetlers will pass thence, thro’
a covered passage-way, directly into the ferry
boat ** Boston,” owned by the company. The
distance between the wharf at which this ferry
boat will be, at the iskand, aud the Pier at Albany

near the centre of the Erie cana! basin) is 30
feet. ‘This distance has been thus shortened by
building out the isiand to the channel of the Hud-
son river.

Van Rensselaer island is joined to the iain
Jand by a rail road bridge of about 20U feet. On
the main tand, a very large engine house is al-
ready built, and there will be a machine shop and
Other large accommodations.

When we take into view the extensive buai-
ness which, by working night and day, the inde-
fatigable Mr. Witt has been enabled to transact,
atthe present temporary depot of the Western
railroad at Greenbush; and when we compare
these temporary and very limited aeccommoda-
tions, with the ainple space and arrangements of
the permanent depot, we cannot resist the con-

clusion that the Western railroad will be able to

encompass the great increase of business, which
it is destined to receive next year.

The Engines will not enter eitber the freight
house or the passenger house; thus avoiding the
risk of tire and the inconvenience of the smoke.

A projection to the roof of the merchandize
depot, on itsnorth side, in exact symmetry with
the projection on its south side, is confidently
spoken of. This projection, 32 feet wide, will
furnish shelter, from the damage by sun and by
the rain, to the cars, on the track outside of the
freight house, on the north side of the depot.—
Great loss arises, on most railroads, by the want
of attention in placing passenger and freight cars
under cover. ‘The darting rays of the burning
summer sun, while the cars are at rest, and then
the alternate wet by rain and then drying up of
the cars contribute very much to their destruc.
tion. No rail road in America has sutticient shed
room either to dry its firewood orto keep its cars
sheltered from the injuries of the Weather. Much
shed room will be wanted at the Greenbash de-

Rensselaerville, Nov. 14, 1842.

Mr. Epvitor: Dear Sir—The election
is past, and from the different counties com-
ing in, appear to indicate a large majority
for the so called democratic candidates at
any rate, enough is heard frum to show,
that Clay is defeated in this staie. This 1s
well. Wel trust shall no lonzer be taunt-
ed with the inquiry, what have the aboli-
tionists done? No doubt it is mainly to
be ascribed to their exertions, that the
influence of this state has not gone for that
distinguished duellist, gambler and slave-
holder. Should the Clay party now drop
him, the whole furm of our action would
be changed. Our whole force would be di-
rected against the so called Democratic
party, with John C. Calhoun or Martin
Van Buren at their head. But I set down
a moment to write this letter for another
purpose, though I will observe further that
however many the lessons of instruction
mankind might learn from the result of an
election, they seldom learn but onc—and it
is proverbial of the whig party that they
never take lessons froin experience. ‘That
one lesson that the parties might learn is
this. That no slaveholder can be elected
President by the electoral vote of this
State, from this time henceforth. Should
the Democratic party bring forth Calhoun,
its a gone case with them in this State.—
Should they bring forward Van Buren, we
have an old grudge against him. We re-
member his threatend veto—should the
election be tried over again to-day, we
should get 100 to 150 Liberty votes in this
town. So great has been the change in
public sentiment here, since last Tuesday —
so soon as people voted, the scales of pre-
judice seemed to fall from their eyes, and
a great number have pledged themselves
publicly, that they will never vote with
either of the old political parties again.—
It was an insult to the moral sense of this
community, when so much has been said
about slavery, to nominate such a man as
Henry Clay, even to say nothing of his
elaveholding--and yet, one of the good
deacons of our church, and one of the el-
ders even, voted forhim. I was grieved a
little about the deacon’s vote. He wanted
to vote a whig vote as he called it “ once
more, and so to balance one of the op-
posite party, who had made up his mind to
vote our ticket, voted with his party; so you
see by the vote of this good man we lost
two, and it made four difference with us
Whereas if they had both voted our ticket,
the result with the other parties would have
been precisely the same as now, with the
exception of one the lessforeach. But I in-
tended to call your attention to another fact,
viz: The strong hold with which Ameri-
can slavery appears to take on the church.
She clings to the church with a death grasp,
and it’s nostraw she clings toeither. It is
the church that sustains and upholds that
whole system of iniquity in our land —and |
am fully persuaded that should the church
in the north discipline her members for the
sin of pro-slavery voting, the days of sla-
very would be numbered. 1 would call

our attention to a letter of Gerrit Smith,

ublished in the Anti-slavery Reporter, for
Nov. inst.,an extract fiom which here fol-
lows, which I wish you would publish in
your paper, so that the people this way
may know what we think of pro-slavery
voting and pro-slavery ministers and church
member. The extract is as foilows:

‘6 Ministers of the Gospel frequently ex-
cuse themselves from reading notices of
antislavery meetings, on the ground that
such meetings are political, and that they
might as well read notices of the meetings
of the democratic and whig parties. And
why should they not read notices of the
latter meetings ? If the aims of these par-
ties are honest and benevolent. then noth-
ing is more proper than that notices of their
meetings be read from the pulpit; and if
they have other and opposite aims, then
why do they and their church members be-
long to these parties? The idea that mi-
nisters and church members can properly
belong to a political party, the notices of
whose meetings would polute the pulpit,
is disgusting and ludicrous. I say not in
this place, whether it is right or wrong to
read in the pulpit notices of the meetings
of the whig and democratic parties. But
this I say, that if it is wrong, then the mi-
nisters and church members should be dis-
ciplined for the sin of belonging to them.”

Yours for the slave,
G. W. DURANT.

Dear Sir,

I thank you for sending me the three

to hear Weller’s accounts from the land of

many, however, will vote for Bradish who
would never vote for Mr. Clay.

I have been inquired of repeatedly, of
late, about a law passed by the Floridi-
ans, authorizing the sale of free negroes,
&c. passed last spring. I have never seen
or heard of such a law until lately, but am
prepared to expect almost any iniquity
from that quarter. The inquiry is, has
Congress sanctioned og approved of it? 1]
