Remarks.—I will endevor to give, next week,

the features of the atrocious Florida law refer-
red to, if they can be procured. By the law or-
ganizing the Territorial government of Florida,
all laws passed by its legislature must be laid
before Congress, for their approval, on the day
of their meeting in December. The territorial
laws are considered as approved by Congress
uoless il is otherwise decided. Congress may
repeal any territorial law, at any time, by a
special act ; but no act of Congress is needed to
give validity to such laws. I fear that some
friends have made unauthorised statements, to
show that Congress approved of the recent laws
of Florida by a positive act. This must have
arisen from their not understanding the usual
course of business in such cases, or freim misin-
formation. The attemptof Hon Millard Fill.
more to manufacture Whig stock out of such a
mistake, (if Mr. Brown made it,) and thus to
cover up the guilt of a silent approval of laws
contrary to human rights, is an illustration of
the shifts to which men of the highest character
are obliged to resort to uphold a bad cause.
An unsuccessful cffurt was made to use Mr.
Slade’s naine and influence, just before the elec.
tion, ina similar way, coupled with a bitter as.
sault on the liberty party. But I will revert to

And now, having presented these pro-
positions in detail, what shalt we say of
them as a mass? Where can a philan-
thrapic mind find language strong enough
to express its deep abhorence of the atro-
cities which this convention would perpe-
trate! Whocan read them without feel-
ing every principle of his nature gutra-
ged, and his bosom awelling with indig-
nation at every sentence they contain;

| that he belongs to the same race, nay to

héartless remorseless oppressors.

Most men seek to hide their atrocities
by some spurious excuse, or palliate their
guilt and shame, by some fancied neces-
sity. He is a bold villain, as well as a
shameless one, whg avows his depravity
but offers no reasons for his course. The
robber has his plea, the thief his excuse.
Every violator of the Jaw, the tyrant that
that tramples under his feet the principles
of justice, has ready some pretext for his
justification. But here we have a body
of men from all parts of a state, a free
state, a state too, that has given birth to
proud and lofty names, names intimately

tu perpetuate the doom of the slave, but

and this world, to a level with the brutes
that perish. What shall we say of such
men ? are they sons of those who died at
Bunker-hill, at Saratoga, at York-town,
at Bladensburgh and Baltimore; or are
they the spawn of despotism, begotten in
the foul bed of tyranny and nursed b
the foster mother of oppression and spoil.
They are Americans, free citizens of our
own land, men that talk loudest of demo-
cracy, of human rights, and the blessings

sons of those who, sixty years ago, endur-
ed privation and want, hunger and cold
and nakedness. Who perilled their for-
tunes, who fought and bled and died in
defence of human rights! These are
they who now propose to plunder freemen

est tothem. If, in our infaney, we exhi-

certain unalienable rights among which

ness.” Now their degenerate sons give
the lie to those glorious principles by pro-
posing to reduce freemen to the condition

dently desired. And so it turned out, the
report was a hoax.

ruary inclusive. A protracted debate on electoral

on the 15th in a majority of 41 for ministers; the

convincing speech made by M. Guizot. A ma-
jority in favor of the proposed reform was confi-
dently expected, and the result is considered an
overwhelming defeat for the opposition.

Lyons was so insignificant when Caesar
conquered Gaul, that he passed by it
without seeing or giving it a name. He
mercly made a halt with his legions on
that hill now called Fourviere, and in-
trenched his temporary camp with lines
so deep that nineteen centuries have fail-
ed entirely to obliterate them.

Some time after the death of this con-
queror, who subjugated three hundred
nations and slaughtered three millions of
men, one of his proscribed clients, seeking
for a spot to found a colony and escorted
by a band of soldiers who remained faith-
ful to him, discovered a number of Vien-
nese—driven from their country by the
Allobroges who hd descended from the
mountains—pitching their tents on that
tongue of land fortified by immense ditches
which Gop had formed, and through
which dashed the waters of the Rhone and
the Saone. The proscribed formed an al-
liance with the vanquished; and under
the name of Lucit Dunum* (i.e. the town
of Lucius—Lucius Manutius Plaucus hav-
ing been the proscribed client and the
founder of the totwn,) were laid the foun-
dations of that city which was destined
shortly to become the citadel of Gaul, and
the centre of communication of those four
great roads, traced by Agrippa, which still
furrow modern France from the Alps,
the Rhine, and trom the Mediterranean to
the Ocean. 7

Sixty cities of, Gaul recognized Lucii
Dunn fortheir quten ; and, at joint ex-
pense, raised in it a temple to Augustus,
whom they acknowledged as their god.

Under Caligula, this temple was chan-
ged into a hall for the sittings of an Acad-
emy—one regulation of which depicts the
character of the imperial fool who founded
it. This was a rule that whenever an aca-
demic competitot produced a bad work,
he should efface it entirely with his
tongue ; or, if he preferred thealternative,
be precipitated into the Rhine.

Lucii Dunum was not yet a century old,
and already rivalled in splendor the Gre-
cian Massilia andthe Roman Narbo,when
a fire, suppused to have originated from
lightning, reduced it to ashes, and that so
rapidly, says Seneca, the concise historian
of this conflagration, that between the
crowded city and an annihilated city, but
one night intervened.

Under the mighty patronage of Trajan,
Lucii Dunum rose again from her ashes,
and on the hill above was erected a mag-
nificent edifice for a market. This was
scarcely opened when the Britons hastened
thither with their bucklers ornamented in
various colors, and the Iberians with their
weapons of steel, which they alone knew
how to temper. Corinth and Athens, too,
sent by the route of Marseilles their pic-
(ures painted on wood, their engraved
stones and their bronze statues. Africa
contributed her lions, tigers, and panthers,
thirsting for the blood of the Amphithea-
tres; and Persia, her horses, so supple
that they emulated the reputation of the
Numidian coursers, whose dams, says
Herodotus, were impregnated by the
winds.

This edifice, which crumbled away in
the 840th year of our era, is called by the
writers of the ninth century forum relus,
and fort viel by those of the fifteenth.
The moderns have made of these two
words Fourrzéres, a name which the hill
whereon it stood now bears.

Three monuments still remain in Lyons
which may be likened to stakes planted
by different ages, and at nearly equal dis-
tances, as types of the progress and decay
of art: the church of Ainai, the Cathedral
of St. John, and the Hotel de Ville. Tie
first contemporaneous with Charlemagne ;
the second, with St. Louis; and the third,
with Louis XIV.

The last of these, the Hotel de Ville, is
the edifice that the Lyonnese point ont to
strangers with the greatest complacency.
Built after the designs of Simon Maupin,
it presents all the characteristics—all the
heavy, cold and stiff grandeur—of the
architecture of the time of Louis XIV,
which, however, was better than that of
Louis XV., which was better than that of
the Thermidor, which was better than
that of Napoleon, which was better than
that of Louis Phillippe.

so that that the bridge is thrown not di-

that covers the river.

To the Hon. the General Assembly of Kentucky: °

‘* When I last had the honor of an appointment

tucky, I intimated, in my letter of acceptance, the

been two extra sessions of congress, I have alrea-
dy attended, since that appointment, as many ses-
sions of congress, as ordinarily happen during a

“I have for several years desired to retire into
private life, but have been hitherto prevented
from executing my wish by constderations of
public duty. 1 should have resigned my seat in
the Senate, at the commencement of the present
session, but for several reasons, one of which was

title of an Executive appointment.

public service, and bestow some attention on my
private affairs, which have suffered much by the
vccupation 0: the largest part of my life in the

claim mine.

signation of the office which I hold of senator, in

1842; and I request that the General Assembly
will appoint my successor to take his seat on that
day. 1 have xed that day to allow me an op-
portunity of assisting in the completion of sop
measures which have been originated by me.

ral Assembly my most profuund and grateful ae.
knowledgments for the numerous’and distinguish -
ed proofs, by which I have been honored, of its
warm attachments and generous confidence dut-
ing a long series of years.

A correspondent of the N. ¥. Herald,
thus speaks of the convention :

The national repeal convention is still
in session, and its deliberations attract
quite a gay and crowded auditory. The
following resolution,offered by Mr. Wright,
of Boston, elicited quite a warm debate :

Resolved, That as misgovernment has
produced in Ireland human suffering, in
degree and duration, unparalleled in the
history of civilized man; the friends of Ire-
land in America, will not be diverted from
giving at their repeal meetings,their whole
hearts and minds to the proper objects of
such meeiings, by the introduction of any
tepics of discord, connected with the do-
mestic institutions of the republic.

After reading this resolution, Mr.
Wright remarked that an effort had been
made in Boston, by the more violent abo-
litionists, to connect the subject of Irish
repeal with American abolition—but it had
fortunately failed through the good sense
of the repealers there. (Applause.) He
said the saine attempt had been made in
other sections of the country, and he con-
sidered it exceedingly proper, under such
circumstances, that this national conven-
tion should send forth to the Union, a de-
cided expression of its opinion against the
connection of the two subjects. (Great
applause.)

He then noticed the boasted philanthro-
py of English abolitionists, which reaches
across the ocean for its objects, while it
leaves thousands to perish at its feet; and
indulged in some severe strictures upon
the rash course of the English philanthro-
pists. His reinarks were warmly received
by the convention, and urged the adoption
of the resolution with considerable ear-
nestness.

Mr. Hogan, of Washington, hoped no
action would be taken on this resolution,
which he regarded as not distinctly enough
sepudiating al} connexion with abolition
and abolitionists. —[ Morning Atlas.

We regard the Resolution introduced
by Mr. Wright and advocated by him in
the Philadelphia Repeal Convention as
directly opposed to the fundamental princi-
ples of Irish Repeal, as set forth by Mr.
Mooney the noted Irish repealer lately
from Ireland, who is travelling and lectu-
ring extensively in this country for the
purpose of creating sympathy and obtain-
ing funds in favor of his grand object, and
as set by his coadjutor, Capt. Fitzgibbons
of New-York, both of whom we have had
the pleasure of hearing. It is opposed
also to hose principles set forth in an able
adevess adopted by the Albany Irish Re-
peal association; and above and beyond
all opposed to the high, and noble and
known principles of Daniel O’Connell the
head and front of Irish Repeal, all and each
of whom we consider are highly censured
in the above resolution and remarks of
Mr. Wright. We shall be exceeding sorry
and disappointed if the great body of Irish-
men fall in with this effort to appease the
wrath, and do the bidding of slavehold-

ers,

NATURE’S THANKSGIVING HYMN.
BY pOcT. WM. J. YOUNG.

Father of light! we rear no shrine
Of fabled worth, in pride to thee,

Where folly worships for divine,
Frail passions of mortality,

But bow with adoration meet.
To Nature's universal Lord,
Where c’er His aspect we may greet,
Behold His hand, or hear His word.

Lo, He is here! Lo, He is there!
Morn—Noon—and Eve—and Starry Night,
Alike His presence all declare
A God of Love—a God of Light.

Nor less His glory beameth out,
To gladden and inspire the soul,

Where floats yon mote beneath the sun,
Than where unnumber’d worlds may roll!

 

When winter on the lap of May,
Yields forth its last expiring breath
We greet his presence in the ray
That brightens e’en the pall of death.

In summer's green or golden tide,
That waves o’er valley, hill and plain,
We mark His blessings far and wide—
Adore in rapture burning strain.

And when glad autumn’s wealth we hoard
The gift of Love omnipotence,

We see His hand—we hear his word,
And know from whence the boon is sent.

Then let the bigot rear his fanes,
And gloomy adorations pay

At shrines where doubt or error reigns,
To cloud his homage e’er and aye ;

We know our God ’s a God of Love,
Whose goodness fills unbounded space,

Whom, wheresoe’er our feet may rove,
We still may worship “ face to face.”

Where e’er we look—where e’er we we turn,
Adoring homage still is seen

Tn faith anil hope, that breathe and burn,
In childhood’s bright and fearless mien.

And in the bard’s inspiring lay,
And in affection’s soothing care,
We see the impulse, day by day
Of homage—God is every where!

Then consecrate, oh, God! to Thee,—
The bounding heart and beaming eye,—
Extend thy Mercies far and free,
*Till all shall know thee ‘neath the sky.

Till all shall know thee, and adore
A God indeed—not gorgon-dire,
Of passions baleful, dark or hoar,
That terror, doubt, and dread inspire.
TH every land and avarv clime
here glows the sun's reviving ray,

Supplies a higher trust for time,
A nobler, for eternity.

These are our thanks, Almighty sire,
No slavish fear awakes the strain;
Man ever feels that Thou art nigher,
The less he deems Thy presence pain.
Albany, Dee. 9th, 1841.

marvellous in our eyes! it is going on; and

Our present vantage ground has been ob-

ained by the circulation of the simple pledge,
and while it is true, that many of our ardent
friends have been anxious to enlist legislative
interference, by the enactment of prohibitory
laws, and by other extraneous means to carry
forward this reformation; all experience has
taught us, that we need no other influence
than than which is thus exerted. If, in this
respect, any are still incredulous, we point
them to the wonderful success of lather Ma-
thew in Ireland, and the reformers in our own
country, through the instrumentality of this
agency. Behold a nation disenthralled by the
inculcation of our practice and principles in
the spirit of kindness and persuasion.

Our plan is simple. We believe no man is
safe who habitually uses intoxicating beve-
rages in the“mildest form and greatest mode-
ration; and the sad experience of many a
noble, talented, strong-minded man, fully sus-
tains this truth; and being thus impressed, we
voluntarily sign the pledge for our own secu-
rity against the drinking fashions and habits
of society ; and we call upon our fellow-men
to unite with us, in view of the varied relations
which they sustain, and by a regard, not only
to‘their pecuniary, but to their eternal inte-
rests ; and we call upon them now at a Crisis,
when this momentous moral reform, which has
for its object the happiness of millions, and
an incalculable advantage to the public pros-
perity and character, is sweeping over our
land with resistless energy.

We have urged our fellow-citizens to the
adoption of our principles as a mere matter of
interest; and we have done this in the belief,
that if all the wealth which has been swallow-
ed by the ocean, consumed by the devouring
element, or that has been lost in consequence
of an inflated and disordered currency, or of
the multiplied bankruptcies, frauds and vil-
lanies of man, could, as a matter of computa
tion, be ascertained, it would fall far below
the amount which has been sacrificed upon
the altar of the demon of intemperance. -

bear testimony to the onward march of the re-
formation in our own land, and throughout the
world, there are defects in the foreground of
the picture we have delineated, which should
not escape notice.

Mr. Fuller: My heart is too full of
emotion to permit me to speak, when 1]
look at the centre of this Hall. I am an
old countryman myself: and the hope of
meeting you here to-night has brought me
several hundred miles. (cheers.) My
brother Garrison has the first rightto stand
before you to-night, but I will give place
to no man after him. Thirty-five years
have I been an abolitionist, at home and
abroad ; and (throwing off his coat, amid
rapturous cheers,) I mean to stand up for
the cause to the last. Irishmen! I stood’
in our Irish house of Peers, when Castle«
reach took the bribe for the betrayal of
Ireland (groans and cries “ yes, and went
home and cut his throat !")—-and I know
what feelings and sufferings bring an Irish-
man to America. What did you come
from the other side for? Oppression drove
you here, and you came for universal lib-
ty! (tremendous cheering.) I must bea
radical reformer here, as I was in the old
country. My Irish friends know what
that means (shouts and cheers, and cries,
‘‘yest yes!) Hard-handed laborers, see
to it that not one of you bows down to this
deadly influence of slavery. I speak as

ing.) Let me tell you, my friends, that

A CALL,

For the Organization of an Eastern New-York
Liberty Association,

The undersigned, believing that more efficient
and successful offorts may be made for the pro-
motion of the cause of abolition by the organiza.
tion of a new society, to be called the Eastern
New-York Anti-Slavery Society, embracing the
Eastern and River counties of this State, do
invite our Anti-slavery friends in all these coun.
ties who are favorable to the measure,to meet
us in the city of Albany,on the 22d and 23d April
next, at 10 o’clock A. M., for the purpose of ef.-
fecting said object,

Itis our opinion that there are hundreds in
this region who may be induced to co-operate
with us in this way, who are now doing compa-
ratively nothing for the cause. A nucleus will
be formed around which the free hearts of men
and women may rally at the summons of free-
dom, and a great work may yet be accomplished
for the redemption of the imprisoned captive.

It is not our intention or wish to conflict with
the movements of our friends in other parts of
the State, but to co-operate with them in a more
efficient capacity, in all important movements.

We invite all who are willing to join us in
this movement to attend the meeting, and to

‘send in their names, that they may be appended

to this call, and that all consistent exertions may
be made to secure a full representation from the
counties in Eastern New-York.

IMPORTANT FROM INDIA—DEFEAT OF THE AFF.
GHANS

The Ulster Times of Thursday says--When
our reporter was yesterday in Lisburn, attending
the mecting there, a gentleman of that town read
to him the following extract of a letter which
had just been received:
{Extract ofa letter from Cawnpore, dated 16th Fel]

We have just received™letters from the Com-
mander-in-Chief's camp, giving Candahar news
up to the 12th ult. An acuon had taken place
between our troops andthe Affghans, in which
we were victors, killing 153, and wounding 200
of the enemy. Our Joss was only three officers
wounded slightly, two privates killed, and 20
wounded. Letters from Gen. Sale have been re-
ceived up to the 30th ultimo, on which date the
troops were in high spirits, having captured 175
bullocks—a great windfall for them! But the
most important piece of news (our letter contin-
ues) is, that Shah Soojah, who has cost us mil-
lions of money, has all along been playing a false
game. He has addressed a letter to Sheer Singh,
and other native Princes, imploring them to aid
him in getting rid of his enemies— meaning the
British—but too cautious to name us. It now ap-
pears that he could have procured provisions for
our starving troops at Cabool, fighting his battles,
‘The day of retribution is not far off—a soldier's
death would be too good for him; and [I hope,
ere long, the gallows will claim him as its own.

A letter had been received from Lady Mac-
naghten, stating that the prisoners are well trea-
ted. She has had only the few clothes she hat
on, and expected to be soon released.

THE DISASTERS OF THE
AFFGHANISTAN.

(The London correspondent of the New-York Eve.
Post, furnishes the following history of events and ;
movements, anterior to as well as during, the late de-
atruction of the British army in Affghanistan. ]

By letters from Bombay of the Ist February, |
intelligence has been received of the greatest dis- |
aster which has ever yet befallen the British in |
the East, At least five thousand English and An-
glo-Indian troops have been destroyed in their re- |
treat from Cabool!

Success in the Kast had become so much a mat- |
ter of course, that the first accounts of this tre-
mendous disaster were at first discredited. Sub- |
sequent accounts however, leave no doubt of the |
accuracy of the leading features of the intelli- |
gence. Between 5,000 and 6,000 troops have been |
destroyed—the British commander, General El- |
phinstone,
English officers have fallen—the British Envoy,
Sir William M’Naghten, has been treacherously |
assassinated—the murder of Sir Alexander Burnes,
is confirmed—and Lady M’Naghten and sixteen
other ladies are in the power of the Affghans.

Such is an outline of the disasters. In order,
however, to give your readers a view of the
whole circumstances of the case, it will be neces-
sary to revert to the past. The position of the
British in India, and the extent of their domin-
ions, is but imperfectly known in England, and!
cannot be supposed to be very familiar to the |
generality of American readers.

The spread of Russian influence inthe East,
has ever been a source of jealousy to England.— |
Accordingly, a couple of years ago when Russia
marched on Khirech, and was known to be in-
triguing against us in Persia, the Anglo-Indian
government took the alarm. It was resolved that
a grand blow should be struck. Russian influ-
ence was. dominant in Persia; Affghanistan lies
between Persia and British dominions, so that
when it was found that the Russians were intrigu-
ing against them at Herat, and were gradually
extending their influence eastward, England de-
termined to extend hers westward. In doing this, |
she committed a great and unpardonable blunder |
—she quarrelled with the Affghans, and made |
them enemies instead of friends, She took up, as |
her protege and

 

puppet, an indolent, imbecile old |
profligate named Shah Soojah-ol-Molk, who had |
been very properly kicked out of Cabool by his
subjects, and in order to place him on the throne |

 

self to me in conversation substantially as he has in!
his letter to you of March 18, 1842. i
“ Yours very sincerely,
“JOHN SAVAGE. |

“ Epwarp C. Denavan, Esq.”
In like manner during the provocations of 1842, I
have endeavored not to forget or disregard the com-
mand—“ If it be possible, as much as lieth in you,
live peaceably with all men.” Ou the first definite
intimation of the approaching attack, conveyed by
the note of the committee, I hastened to its chair-
man, and although conscious of having suffered
some wrong, but not having done any, made offers
fur peace, which he pronounced ‘honorable and
Christianly.” They were not accepted. hat the
public may judge whether they ought not have been, |
Lam induced to repubhsh them in this connection : |
“* Albany, March 9, 1842. |
“To ARCHIBALD McIntyre, &c.
‘ GenTLEMEN—In reply to your communication, I
have only to say that I was not, previous to its receipt, '
aware that such a report was in circulation thro’ the
city; nor am I now aware of having myself used |
to any person the expressions concerning him, im ,
puted to me in said letter. If U had snid or done any |

 

thing to injure Dr, Sprayue, I should, as a member
of a Christian church, have been better pleased to |
have had an opportunity of giving him satisfaction
in the way the gospel points out, than in the way
thus offered. Still, sensible of my own liability to

A meeting of the citizens, without distinction
of party, assembled at the City Hall, last Saturday
evening, and was addressed by Calvin Pepper, Jr.
esq., our late townsman, but now of New York,
and by Elder Abel Brown, in an appropriate and
spirited manner, The meeting, though not very
large, was well attended. After tne discussion of
a series of resolutions to a late hour, the meeting
adjourned, laying them on the table to be taken
up and again considered at a meeting appointed
for the next Thursday evening.

Thursday evening, April 16.
The meeting was numerously attended, and ad-

|
| dressed by Abel Brown, H. H. Garnet and others,

when the following resolutions were unanimously
adopted:

i In regard to the decision of the Supreme Court of

the United States.

Resolved, That we regard personal rights as the
most sacred and inviolable, and that in all communi-
ties where these are not iespected and protected by
laws the most vigorous, allclaim of being a free re-
publican nation is but a name, and a libel upon truth
and great principles.

Whereas, Ry the late decision of the Supreme Court
of the United States, in the case of Spriggs vs. Penn-
sylvania, the slave holders of theSouthern states are
allowed to seize any person whom they may choose
to designate as their slave, and drag him or her be-
fore a magistrate, there to have the invaluable right
to personal liberty settled, upon the oath or oaths of
individuals, without due process of law, i.e. by jury
trial, thus compromising, invading and annihilating
the Heaven originated gift of personal rights—There-
ore,

Resolved, That while we regard the said decision as
the paramount law of the land while it exists—and
while that decision may be in accordance with the in-
tent of the constitution—yet we feel it to be a solemn
and important duty resting upon every citizen of this
nation to take immediate measures so to amend the
constitution as to arrest so flagrant an outrage up-
on human rights.

Resolved, That it is the sense of this meeting that
the legislature of this state should pass a law imme-
diately, imposing severe penalties and punishments
upon any person (except officers of the United States
Government, to whom it properly belongs according
to the said decision,) who shall be found aiding, abet-
ting, or in any way assisting a slave holder or his a-
gent, in arresting or recovering any person claimed as
au fugitive slave.

Relative to the case of Mr. Giddings and the Creole
affair.

Wuereas having heard with alarm and indignation
that the Hon. Joshua R. Giddings, of Ohio, was virtu-
ally thrust from the Halls of Congress by a deliberate
vote of the House of Representatives, for having of-
fered certain resolutions for the consideration of that
body, in the words following, to wit:

* Resolved, That prior to the adoption of the feder-
al Constitution each of the several states Composing
this Union exercised full and exclusive juris iction
over the subject of slavery within its own territory,
aud possessed full power to continue or abolish it at

| pleasure.

‘© Resolved, That by adopting the constitution no
part of the aforesaid powers were delegated to the
federal government, but were reserved by and still
pertain to each of the several states.

‘Resolved, That by the eighth section of the first
article of the constitution, each of the several states
surrendered to the federal government all jurisdiction
over the subjects of commerce and navigation upon
the high seas.

“ Resolved, That slavery, beingan abridgment of the
natural rights of man, can exist only by force of po-
sitive municipal law, and is necessarily confined to
the territorial jurisdiction of the power ercating it.

‘ Resolved, That when a ship belonging to the citi-
zens of any state of this Union, leaves the waters and
territory of such state, and enters upon the high seas,
the persons on board cease to be subject to the slave
laws of such state, and thenceforth are governed in
their relations to each other by, and are amenable to,
the laws of the United States,

ing.

Fi fter which, John Hutchins submitted
the following resolutions, which, bemy
seconded by George Parsons, were passed
by acclamation ; but four voices dissent-
ing.

Resolved, That the right of a Represnta-
tive in Congress to express freely his
views, upon the questions of public policy,
is secured by the constitution, and is in-
dispensibly necessary to enable him to
carry out the will of his copstituents, and
its werestracted exercise should be sacred-
ly guarded by all free deliberative bodies
in a republican government.

Resolred, That to pass a vote of censure
upon a member for thus freely expressing
his views when he violates no rule of order,
is transcending the powers of congress,
subversive of the constitution, an infringe-
ment of the rights of the people, an inter-
ference with the freedom of opinion and
directly at war with the spirit of our insti-
tutions.

Resolved, That we approve of the course

of the Hon. Josnua R. Gipninas, from this
district in resigning his seat in congress,
on account of the vote of censure for intro-
ducing his series of resolutions relative to
the brig ‘* Creole.”
Resolved, That Mr. Ginnines be re-
quested without any formal nomination,
to permit his name to be brought hefore
this congressional district for re-election ;
so that his constituents may have an op-
portunity of passing upon his conduct in
resigning, and upon the matters which led
to his resignation.

After the adoption of the foregoing reso-
lutions, on motion of John Hutchings, it
was

Resolved, That the proceedings of this
meeting be signed by the chairman and
secretary, and forwarded to the Hon. John
White, Speaker of the United States
House of Representatives, and that he be
requested to lay them before that body.

in the papers of the town, the meeting ac-
joarned.

wife. The assault was made with an axe, and
the wounds, two or three in number, were upon
the head, and either one of them such as to prove
fatal almost instantly. The murderer was arres-

justify the act. We take from the report of the
Eve. Journal the material facts elicted on the ex-
amination. Burke is described as addicted to
drink and of dissipated habits; and the victim an
amiable and industrious woman.

Nassau, N. P., April 18, 1842.
A special session of the Admiralty Court: con-
vened this day to hear the charge of piracy against
the 17 negroes imprisoned from the “Creole.”
The Attorney General made his motion for «delay

of trial on the ground that it was impossible to

obtain the necessary evidence here, and offered
for the perusal of the court a number of affidavits

of the captain, mate, and crew and passengers of

the Creole, showing that sufficient evidence could

‘be procured from the United States, if time was

allowed. After an examination of the testimony
offered, the court replied, that were the captain,
crew and passengers, as set forth in the aflidavits,
here present to testify in this case, they should
consider them as not entitled to belief or credit,
and should charge the jury to that effect; and that
no evidence could be procured to convict the
peisoners at the bar, for they were perfectly jus-
tified in the course pursued on board the Creole,
and were now about to be set free.

The Chief Justice then addressed the negroes
something in this style:—It hath pleased God to
set you free from the bonds of slavery; may you
hereafter live the lives of good and faithful sub-
jects of her Majosty’s government. They were
then set at liberiy by proclamation.

Avsany, April 15, 1842.

Gatlemeu,—My engagements have not
permitted an earlier acknowledgment of
of your communication of the fifth of

known to me the favorable sentiments of

in Rochester, concerning th» grounds
maintained by the Executive department
in the controversy which has occured be-
tween this State and Virginia and South
Carolina.

The verdict between New-York and
her sister States is to be rendered by a
future generation, when the present com-
binattons, interests, excitements and pre:
judices shall have ceased. Hoping, with
much confidence, that tine will show that
the principles which have been defended,
will ultimately be found as compatible
with the right construction of the Cousti-
tution, and as conducive to the harmony
of the States, as they are humane and in
accordance with the principles of natural
justice I can not but be grateful for every
evidence of their approval by my fellow-
citizens.

Accept assurances of the respect and
estecm, with which I remain,

Your fellow citizen.

CABUL AND AFFGHANISTAN.

[From the Oswego Palladium. }

As the region of country west of the Indus
will immediately become the scene of a great
struggle, and perhaps is destined to be the field
of a mighty contest between the two greatest
powers of Europe and Asia, we have thought
some notice of its inhabitants, topography and
resources might interest our readers.

This region, sometimes called Independant
Persia, or the Kingdom of Cabul, or Affghanis-
tan, is composed of several provinces indepen-
dent of each other. It extends from the Paro-
pamisan mountains on the north to the Indian
ocean on the south, about 800 miles, and about
700 miles eastward from the great Desert to the
Indus. The northern part of this territory con-
tains the kingdom of Cabul, with the provinces
of Seistan and Affghanistan; the southern part
the large districts of Beloochistan and Mekran.—
The features of the country are strikingly con-
trasted— prodigious mountains on the nor:h, and
the plains of salt and sand on the south. The
Affghan land is a region of vast mountains, high
table Jands and rapid rivers. The mountains are
spurs of the Himelayah, and some of the peaks
exceed 20,000 feat in altitude. It is inthis region
of the world that the mountains are the most stu-
pendous. The highest peaks of the Cordilleras
of South America, are inferior to those of the
Himelayah, It is therefore one of the most im-
practicable countries on earth, yet it is capable
of sustaining a great population, has been the
seat of empire, of high oriential civilization,
and of an enlightened agriculture. Upon one of
the sources of the Indus are yet to be seen the
ruins of Ghizni, in the 11th century the seat of
the great empire of Mahmood the first of the
Sultans, The name of Mahmood the Ghaznevide
is still venerable in the east. His subjects enjoy-
ed the blessings of prosperity and peace. His
reign is illustrated by romantic anecdotes of the
rigor and impartiality of Mahometan justice, and
was adorned by the songs of Fedusi, among the
most celebrated of eastern poets. It is through
this impenetrable country of prodigious moun-
tains and deep defiles, that the British arms seem
to be struggling to meet the Russian on the banks
of the Caspian. ‘he latter are contending with
a similar country anda similar people amid the
mountains of the Caucasus. Either of thease two
great monarchies has heart enough for the whole
earth. The occupation of the passage from
Southern to Northera Asia, through the terrible
defile called by the ancients, the Gates of the
Caspian, may be an object of eager solicitude to
both governments. With the British govern-
ment, especially, the occupation of the pass may
be connected with the establishment of a port
upon the Caspian.

A very large portion of the Affghan country is
of course wild and desolate, and sometimes inac- |
cessible. There are, however, extensive districts
of table land which are said to surpass in fertili-
ty the most productive soils of Europe. The
summer climate resembles that of the table lands
of Mexico, and must be among the most detight-
ful in the world. ‘The winters are severe—the
higher peaks of the mountains are clad in perpet-
ual snow—and on the higher table lands the snow
lies deep for four or five months in the year, ac-
companied by a Norwegian temperature. The
productions of such a region are of course deter.
mined by the degree of elevation. At Peshawar
(which has a central situation in respect to lati-
tude,) the tropical fruits mingle with those of
Europe. Wheat, barley gnd rice, the pome-
grante, the «tate and the orange, all belong to the
varied vegetation of Cabulistan, The vine, the
peach and the apricot, grow wild, being indigen-
ous to the soil. ‘The mountains are covered With
vast forests of pine, mingled with the cypress and
the oak. On the plains are seen the mulberry,
the (amarind, the plane, the poplar and the wil-
low.

The historian, Gibbon, in discoursing upon the
Ghaznevide Empire, in the latter part of the last
century, declares that Gazna, (Chisni) which is
not far from the city of Caboo!l, had been visited
by no modern traveller. Since his time the Bri-
tish arms have advanced from Ceylon to the Him-
elah, from the Irrawaddy to the Indus. The
great pass of the latter river, at Attoch, which has
witnessed the presence of the greatest conquerors
of the earth,—Sesostris and Alexander, Mahom-
med, Zingis and Tamerlane, Nadir and Aureng-
zebe—now tranquilly reposes ander the dominion
of «© The ald Lion of the Punjaub,” Runjet Singh,
the robber chief of Lahore, the devoted ally and
vassal of ‘The Honorable India Company.”—
Books of travels, Letters from the East, Reports
of Engineers, Literary and Scientitie Discourses,
are rapidly publishing to the world the hitherto
unexplored secrets of Cabulistan. The writings
of Elphinstone, Pottinger and of the ill-fated Sir
Alexander Burns, are full of information respec-
ting the nalural and political features of the coun-
try. The population is thus estimated by the

IMPORTANT FROM MEXICO—-ENGLISH
LOAN TO SANTA ANNA—INVASION OF
TEXAS CERTAIN.

From the N. Y. Herald, extra, ¢
Sunday, 2 P. M. 5

By the British mail steamer, Medway, which
arrived here from Havana on Friday last, and
sailed for Halifax on Saturday, to connect with
the Britannia, on her way to Liverpool, we have
received highly important intelligence from Mex-
ico by private correspondence from that capital,
of the most authentic character.

Santa Anna has, at Jength, positively procured
a loan ia London, to the amount of £3,000,000
sterling—or $15,000,000—for a period of four-
teen years without the payment of annua) inter-
est, until the period of reimbursement, when the
holders of the stock will receive $1410 for $100,
out and out. The agents for this loan in London
are James Morrison & Co. of London. The British
government becomes the guarantee for its repay -
ment to the English stockholders, and in consid-
eration thereof, all English manufactures are to
be admitted into Vera Cruz and the other ports
of Mexico, at a nominal «duty, for the same peri-
od at which the loan is taken.

We have also learned some particulars of the
history of this loan, which we now give, and
shall add more hereafter.

At the close of last year, or the beginning of
the present, an agent from Santa Anna proceeded
to London, for the purpose of effecting aloan, on
any terms or conditions. After a good deal of
negotiation in London, an agent of the great
banking house of Morrison& Co., of London, pro-
ceeded to Mexico, by one of the west steamers.
On reaching Mexico, after some negotiation, the
terms of the loan were arranged, according to
the statement we have given. On this being ef-
fected, Santa Anna, being almost like to burst,
wrote and published the recent letters to General
Houston, President of Texas, and to General
Hamilton, the ‘exian envoy in Europe. It was
the union of the English abolition and Mexican
influence in London, that prevented the success
of the Texian loan attempted by General Hamil-
ton—and the same union that was successful in
the Mexican, aided by the Mexican mines and
trade. In the mean time, about six or eight
weeks ago, the agents of the Morrisons, accom.
panied by an aid de camp of Santa, whose name
we believe is M. Escandon, left Vera Cruz, and
reached Havana in time to take the steamer Mei-
way, which touched here on Friday last. The
names of both are in the list of passengers.—
They were alse accompanied by M. A. Caldera
de la Barea, the Spanish minister at Mexico, on
his return toSpain. By these persons, the intelli-
gence was brought to this city, and several com-
mercial letters were also received here, stating
positively the faets as we have related them.

We further learn that it is the intention of the
Mexican government, as soon as they shall have
received steamships, muskets, and other munitions
of war from England, and brought to them under
the English flag, the proceeds of their lo-n, that
a terrible invasion of Texas will be made both by
sea and land, and thata number of Britivh navy
and army officers will be engaged to lead
their troops to battle. The loan will take no
money from England, but simply ships, steamers,
and munitions of war. In Mexico they have men,
provisions, every thing except good officers and
munitions of war. Santa Anna is furious for the
invasion of Texas—and if he should succeed in
driving the Texians into the United States, he in-
tends to invade Louisisana and Arkansas—be-
sides threatening the whole valley of the Missis-
sippi with his vengeance.

BEAUTIES OF WEBSTER.—No. 1.

What an absurdity is the institution of
slavery! Men cannot write or talk in de-
fence of it without involving themselves
in all sorts of blunders, absurdities, and
contradictions, both of tezms and of moral
principles. Even the great “ intellect of
New-England,” appears imbecile and yj-
diculous on this subject. Daniel Web-
ster on Bunker Hill, or Daniel Webster
on the floor of Congress, and Daniel
Webster in the Chair of State! Nigh:
and noonday =: not in greater contrast.
The Lion and the Jackall are not more un-
like than these two Daniel Websters.

In Mr. Webster's statement of the Cre-
ole case we find the following language :

“The Brig Creole, of Richmond, Vir-
ginia, with a cargo of merchandise, prin-
cipally tobacco and slaves, ahout 135° in
number.”

Now, here the slaves of the Creole, are
classed with tobacco, under the term
merchandise. If it be said that the sen-
tence can be read so as to separate the
slaves from the tobacco; we reply that
such would not be the common under-
standing of its meaning ; it is not suffi-
ciently perspicuous to be so understood
by one ina hundred, or one in a thon-
sand of its readers. If Mr. Webster did
not mean to include slaves in the general
term ‘ merchandize,” this sentence js
certainly a slovenly performance.

In other parts of this blundering des-
patch, we find Mr. Webster classing
slaves with merchandise in terms too un-
equivocal to be misunderstood. And yet,
Mr. W. talks about these same slaves—
1. e. this same merchandise as pirates and
mutineers. This merchandise—the slare
merchandise—not the tobacco merchandise
was guilty of mutiny and piracy during
the voyage to New-Orleans—hence, this
trouble with England. To speak of the
slaves as “ merchandise,” is quite cousis-
tent with /aw, on slavery ; for slaves un-
der American law are ‘to be deemed, ta-
ken, held as goods and chattels in the
hands of their owners, &e., for ever.’°—
But to talk about “ goods and chattels—
things which have no inoral agency or mo-
ral responsibility, becoming all of a sud-
den” mutineers and pirates, is what “ ex-
cites our special wonder.’ To talk of
merchandise committing® the “ highest
crime known to our laws’ is the very “sub-
lime of the ridiculous.” How fortunate
for the flesh merchants of the Creole, how
fortunate for the country, that frobacco did
not take a notion to mutiny and murder!

REPORT

Of the committee on privileges and elec-
tions, on the petition for an amendment
of the Constitution, extending the elec-
tive franchise to the colored popidation.

In AssEmBty, March 29, 1842.

Mr. Cramer, from the committee on pri-
vileges and elections, to which was teferr-
ed various petitions asking that an @aend-
ment of the Constitution may be proposed,
whereby the colored population shall be
placed on an equality with the white, in
the exercise of the elective franchise.

REPORTS }

Under the former Constitution of this
State, a residence of six months, the own-
ership of a freehold of the value of fifty
dollars, or the renting of a tenemeut of the

yearly value of five dollars and the paye.

ment of taxes assessed thereon, were ree
quisite to constitute a qualified voter for
member of Assembly. A freehold of the

value of two hundred and fifty dollars was!

requisite to constitute a voter for Senator
or Governor. No distinction was made in
regard to color,

At the time of the adoption of that Con-
stitution the number of free negroes was
so small, that their admission to the exer-
cise of the elective franchise can hardly
be supposed, at that time, to have been a
subject of consideration, The subsequent
abolition of slavery opened the baflot box
to a large population of this kind, though
comparatively few ever attained even the
simple qualifications required bythe old
Constitution, .

In the formation of the new Constitu-

tion, and by the amendments, all proper- :

ty qualifications for white electors are
abolished ; but by an express provision a
citizenship of two years, the ownership
and possession of a freehold of the value
of two hundred and fifty dollars and the:
payment of taxes assessed thereon, are ree!
quired, in addition to the requisites for the |
white population, to constitute a negro a_
qualified voter,

The petitioners seek to have these ree
strictions removed, and thereby to raise
an unfortunate and a degraded pedple ta
an equality with the founders of the Re-
public and their descendants, They al-
lege that the negroes are deprived of
rights which the principles of the declara-
tion of independence and of democratic
government should guarantee,

In the Convention of 1821, the whole
subject was fully and ably discussed.
The existing restrictions were adopted by

a decisive majority of that Convention, |!

and sanctioned by the people.

The memorials which have come be-
fore the committee do not, in their judg-
ment, overcome, by facts or by arguments,
the well considered reasons of the framers
of our present Constitution.

But it is insisted that these restrictions |

conflict with the principles of the declara-
tion of independence, declaring that ‘all
men are created free and equal.”
axiom is acknowledged. It formsthe ba-
sis on which rest all our cherished insti-
tutions. But that principle is not infring-
ed by any constitutional restriction on the
right of suffrage. The equality declar-
ed in that sacred instrument is the equali-
ty of nature, the gift of the Creator. None
of the inalienable rights of man, neither of
“life,” liberty,” or ‘* the pursuit of hap-
piness,” nor of property are withheld by
the conditions on which the elective fran-
chise is bestowed on the African. The
right of suffrage, is not a natural right;
it is a political privilege ; some restric.
tions are indispensible.
constitution, the people, with a view to
their security and happiness, confer the
elective franchise upon such conditions as
to them may seem reasonable and saluta-
ry. They may, and often do err; the re-
strictions may be unequal; they may be
inexpedient, but no rights of nature are

‘and happiness.

Nor can they justly complain that they
'are deprived of privileges before enjoyed.
‘As we before remarked, when the first
constitution was formed their existence,
| in the political system, was practically un-
‘known. The abolition of slavery was not

1

| anticipated, and hence no provision, in
‘contemplation thereof, was made. By
‘that cause, and by voluntary emancipa-
‘tion, vast hordes of negro voters were
brought within the qualifications intended
only, by the Constitution of 1777, for the
/ White populatiod. The framers of the
new Constitution but provided against this
unforeseen evil by the adoption of the
present freehold qualification.

: A comparison with the practice of other
| States is not unfavorable to our liberality.
In few, even of the non-slaveholding
| States, are the political privileges conferr-
ed upon the African, broader or more easi-
, ly attainable than here; while in Connecti-
cut, Ohio, Indiana, Illinois and Michigan,
‘negroes are wholly and expressly exclu-
‘ded from all right of suffrage. In some
of the States conditions are imposed upon
the white yoters, as onerous, and in some
cases more so, than are prescribed by our
Constitution for the negroes.

It thus appears that in every State of
‘the Union, there exists either total exclu-
_sion or restrictions ; and where there hap-
“pens to be neither, few of the African race
are to be found. Can we, therefore be
justly told that the restrictions in our Con-
stitution are illiberal and oppressive, and
hostile to the principles of democratic
government ?

; The claim of the African for an unre-
stricted admission to the clective fran-
-chise, becomes wholly a question of expe-
diency : that as a mass, they are not quali-
fied to exercise this high privilege, will
not be denicd, It may then, and most
wisely too, be asked, could the public wel-
fare be promoted by granting the prayer
of the petitioners? If not, is there any ob-
‘gation resting on us to make the experi-
| ment of free negro suffrage, in the hope
‘of elevating the character of that popula-
‘tion Y Ifthere be nut sufficient intelligence,
_and industry, and self-respect in that class,
to induce even a small portion of them to
attain the property qualification required,
_yourcommittee can not believe there would
, be more intelligence, more industry, more
self-respect, and more improvement, by
wholly removing a restriction imposed as
“a motive to ambition, as well as a check
to licentiousness.

That the Africans, as a people, are in
‘comparison a degraded population, will
not probably be denied. In the social re-
lations of life, they are not on ternis of
equality with ourselves. ‘They do not as-
/sociate with us in society; they are not
seated with us around the same table, nor

‘do they sit with us in the jury box, or even
in our temples of worship, where, more
‘than in all other places, “such distinctions
(if causeless) would be annthilated. While
this instinctive repugnance exists in the
white race to admit the black to terms of
intimacy and equality, in any of the so-
cial or public relations of life, is it not un-
reasonable to suppose that a political equali-
ty would be endured by the people? It
may be alleged that this feeling and
practice originated in prejudice, and that
both should be overcome. Were this con-
ceded to be so, can either be removed by
legislation, or by constitutions? We ap-
prehend not. The foundation of that re-
; pugnance lies deeper. It is organic, uni-
versal, and permanent.

These remarks are made in no spirit of
-unkindness. The fact is not only known,
but itis felt. Colour, though the most
striking, is said by an eminent professor
-of science, not to be the mcst considera-
ible of the differences existing between the

The Colonists of Liberia —The Rev. '

John Clark, a Baptist Missionary, who has
lately visited Liberia, states in a letter
dated April 5th, that the desire manifest-
ed by the colonists to return to America
is so great that, if the vessels were sup-
plied, such a number would leave in them,
that those willing to remain would find
themselves too few to protect themselves
from the natives, and would therefore
leave on this account. No obstacle but
the want of means prevents the return of
the colonists to America; but this is a
sufficient one, and confines them to the
land of their exile—N. Y. Mechanic.

REPORT & BILL FOR THE REVISION OF

THE TARIFF.

Mr. Forward, Secretary of the Treasury, has
submitted a Report and Bill to the house for the
revision of the Tariff. ‘The N. ¥Y. Tribune con-
tains a synopsis of the report, from which we
gather the following particulars;

The report estimates the annual expenses of the
government during each of the next three years
for national defence and all ordinary purposes at
$24,424,358 45, to which is to be added apart $1,-
000,000 for Indian annuities, debts of the cities in
the dist ict of Columbia, 3 and 5 per cent. funds
due certain states, &c., and a further sum of about
$6,500,000 to defray the interest and extinguish
the principal of our public debt. This requires
an aggregate of $98,242,953 78 in the three years.
or nearly $33,000,000 per annum; to meet which
even with the restoration of the land proceeds to
the treasury, (estimated at $5,000,000 for the
three years,) will require a decided increase ot
our tariff of duties. ‘The dutiable importations for
the ensuing year are estimated at $93,817,985, es-
timated to yield, under the Secretary’s proposed
tariff, an aggregate of $32,603,335; from which
must be deducted for drawback, bounties, expen-
ses of collection, &c., $5,160,000; leaving a net
reveage of $27,443,337 27. By this means the
whole existing debt is to be paid off in three
years, after which the duties are to cease on Tea,
Cotfee, &e. Such is an outline of the Secretary's
plan of Finance.

Mr. Forward thinks that a uniform system of
Home valuation will be found impracticable, and
recommends some departures from it. He sug-
gests that the government should retain the priv-
ilege of taking imported goods by paying the
costs and charges, and ten per cent. advance.—
The principle of cash duties he firmly adheres to,
adducing ample and cogent reasons therefor. He
does not regard with favor the project of a gene-
ral ware-housing system. ‘The expediency ofal-
lowing drawback on American manufactures from
foreign materials is suggested to the considera-
tion of congress, with an assurance that it is not
impracticable.

‘The hymn goes up, the song is heard,
And men by thousands,—free

Tell joyous things through this broad land,
OF life—of liberty ;

And they are gathering, stern and strong,
To meet the bitterest foe

That man e’er met, or e’er can meet,
This side the world of woe.

They come from hill-side and from plain,
_ There’s joy on every brow,
Wand high resolve in every eye
To meet and conquer now,
They're coming from the northern lakes—
And breezes from the sea
Bring tidings that they’re rousing there,
Determined to be free.

They come from mountain and from glen,
From cot and pillard hall;

They're rousing, rousing, these stern men,
They're rousing one and all!

No more the ribald shout is heard :
No more the senseless sopg—

But hymns of joy o‘er hill and dell
Go bounding now along.

And hills and dells are echoing
With praise from many hearts—
From the green west, the sunny south,
The “land o’ cakes” and tarts,
The voice of joy and hope is heard:
Ten thousand hearts are glad—
Ten thousand homes are happy now—
Ten thousand less are sad.

The broken heart is now bound up,
The bruised limbs are healed,

The hungry fed, the naked clothed,—
The worst of sorrews yield—

And men have turned Samaritans,
And he who met with theives,

Was robbed, and left for dead, revives—
And “ Inns” forever leaves.

And shall this stop? shall this work cease?
Not while an aching heart

By this fell monster torn, is found—
Not while a tear may start .

From eyes that now have wept too oft—
Not while is found one drop

Of liquid fire, far worse than that
From Etna’s burning top.

Respscrep Farenpn—I received the accompa-
nying deeply interesting letter this morning. I
trust it will go far in convincing our English and
more distant temperance friends that there is
little danger of re-action in our great national
movement, and that Sir Robert Peel’s statements
have caused them unnecessary alarm. One
thing only we want to make success permanent,
and that is, the example of the middle classes—
which, I am sorry to say, is shamefully withheld.
The poor man nobly gives up his only gratifica-
tion, ruinous though it was to him—the rich man
clings to that one among his many, as though
every thing depended on it. Alas! alas! that
there should be found those, too, who drink more
to ‘‘ antagonise” our principles. While I cannot
go the fulllength with our estimable friend in
exculpating Sir R. Peel for endeavoring to raise
more revenue from so polluting a source as whis-
key—for Wetraying such utter ignorance respect-
ing our great cause as to suppose that “ whiskey
could be drank with due regard to moderation,”
for knowing so little about a movement which
has saved thousands of lives, and made the home
of the suffering and destitute happy—or so much
about another, which has swept thousands off
the face of the earth, and spread desolation and
untold of miseries amongst the people of a dis-
tant land—yet surely we cannot but admire, in
the great apostle of temperance, that universal
charity which hopes the best, thinks the best,
says the best, of every man, and tries to win all
by the power of love. Cordially can 1 respond
to the beautiful sentiment, “thal the sweet and
beneficent spirit of the Gospel, that thinketh no
evil, was diffused from pole to pole, uniting all
mankind as one family, making a world happy.”
Then would war aod rapine cease, and we might
hope that the blessed religion of the Saviour,
which is now trampled under foot by many of the
heathens, because of the wicked conduct of its
professors, would spread far and wide, speak-
ing peace to the destitute widow and children,
made so by the Christian soldiers in India and
Chiaa.

I have only to add that I hope the remark re-
specting temperance cordials (falsely so called)
will sink deep into the heart of every teetotaller,
and that I understand from a highly respectable
fource, that the English distillers have been large-
ly importing Irish spirits, which will go far for
answering for the npparent increased consump-
tion. Respectfully,

Ricnarn ALLEN.

Interesting Incident.

What we are about to relate came within our
official notice ; and we honestly confess that it
has made a very deep impression upon our minds
in favor of the Temperance Cause.

One morning in the early part of last week, a
Police Magistrate in one of the largest and most
populous wards in this cily, was visited at his
private dwelling by a police constable and ano-
ther person, who said they had called for the
purpose of procuring the release of a man who
had been committed as a vagrant and disorderly
person a few nights previous. The person ac-
companying the officer, remarked to the Magis.
trate, thatthe poor fellow in confinement had
seen his error and acknowledged it, and was now
fully resolved to leave off drinking intoxicating
liquors, Which had brought him into the present
difficulty, and which in time past, had caused
him so much sorrow. On the Magistrate's in-
timating to the person thus pleading for the pri
soner, that security would be required for his
good behaviour, and that some costs had alrea-
dy accrued, the kind hearted fellow declared
that, although he was a poor man himself, he
was able, and would willingly become the securi-
ty and pay all the costs; for he had full confi-
dence in the prisoner’s assurances of amendment,
inasmuch as he had promised to take the pledge of
of total abstinence,and was anxious to join the so.
ciety of those who had abjured the use of all intox-
icating drinks. “ Do you think,” said the Magis.
trate, ‘‘the prisoner will abide by his pledge af-
ter he has taken it?” ‘‘ I dosir,” said the man,
emphatically; and Iam determined to release
him, and stand by him till he becomes a totally
changed man. “1 feel cont dent that he will not
deceive me; “and if he does, why then, I shall
have the ‘satisfaction of knowing and feeling
that I have done my best, to reclaim from beast-
ly intoxication one who is good workman, and a
good fellow, whenever he is sober aud in his
right senses.” Struck with silent admiration at
the speaker's disinterested friendship, Christian
philanthropy, and noble sentiments, the Mazis-
trate paused for a few moments, and then said
he would accompany the generous man to the

. Temperance among Seamen.

In the month of February, at the suggestion
of Captain Gibbs, a Seamen's Total Abstinence
Seciety was formed, and the effect has been truly
surprising. In several instances, seamen, whu
have been for a long series of years accustomed
to participate in the intoxicating bowl, have been
reformed, and have become warm and zealous
advocates of the Temperance reform. Almost
entire crews have taken the pledge, and have re-
mained faithful during the protracted delay of
many weeks in this port; and such has been the
almost miraculous change in many vessels, that
their Captains have cheerfully volunteered their
testimony to your Chaplain, in regard to the in-
fluence the Temperance movement has had upon
their men; and it was remarked to me by a sailor
who had had considerable experience on the
subject, thit it was the quietest St. Patrick’s
Day he had ever witnessed among Irish seaincy
ina foreign port. And itis worthy of remark,
that there were an unusual number of Irish ves-
sels in port on that day. It has not unfrequently
occurred, that seamen have risen in our meet-
ings, and testified to the change which had been
produced in their own persons, and have with a
touching eloquence referred to the present hap-
py and prosperous condition of their families,
compared to what it was previous to their having .
joined the Total Abstinence Society.

Our Seaman’s Society numbers now two hun-
dred and seventy members, and almost exclusive-
ly seamen.

There is one melancholy fact connected with
this subject, 1 beg Jeave briefly to allude to. It
is the case of that unhappy sailor now under
sentence of death.

During the revival of last winter, he was in-
duced to accompany his shipmates of the ship
Thetis to the Bethel, and according to his own
confession, he was almost the only one of that
crew who was not brought under the influence
of the truth; but that he had been induced to
leave the vessel. He remarked to me the first
time I visited him in yonder jail—Oh, sir, if 1
had only taken your advice, as did my shipmates,
I would not have been here. Oh! sir, it was the
fatal glass I yot in one of those dens that has
brought me to this.

He tells me he has a widowed mother and
sisters to mourn his melancholy end. ——Sailor's
Magazine.

 

Death’s Prime Minister.

Death, the king of terrors, was determined to
choose a prime minister, and his pale courtiers,
the ghastly train of diseases, were all summoned
to attend, when each preferred his claim to the
nonor of this illustrious office. Fever urged the
numbers he destroyed ; cold Palsy set forth his
pretensions by shaking all his limbs; Gout hob-
bled up, and alleged his great power in racking
in every joint; and Asthma’s inability to speak
was a strong, though silcnt argument, in favor of
his claim. Stone and Cholic, pleaded their vio- .
lence ; Plague, his rapid progress in destruction ;
and Consumption, though slow, insisted that he
was sure.

In the midst of this contention, the court was
disturbed with the noise of music, dancing, feast.
ing, and revelry; when immediately entered a
lady, with a bold lascivious air, and flushed, jo-
vial countenance. She was attended, on one
hand by a troop of cooks and bacchanals; and
On the other, by a train of wanton youths and
damsels, who danced half naked to the softest
musical instruments; her name was INTEMPE-
RANCE. She waved her hand, and thus address-
ed the crowd of diseases: ‘‘Give way, ye sickly
band of pretenders, nor dare to vie with my su-
perior merits in the service of this monarch ; am
[ not your parent—the author of your being?
Do ye not derive your power of shortening hu-
man life almost wholly from me? Who then so
fit as myself for this important office?” The
grisly mouarch grinned a smile of approbation,
placed her at his right hand, and she immediate-
ly became his principal favorite and Prime Mini-
ster.~—-.4dditson.

E. W. Gooowin, Esq. :—I have just re- |

turned from attending a meeting of the
Schoharie Co. Anti-Slavery Society. The
meeting was held at the Court House, was
tolerably well attended, and passed off
with profit to the cause. Rev. Benj. Shaw
has been laboring in that Co. for the past
month, and has awakened a happy interest
in behalf of the poor slave. He labors in-
cessantly and will doubtless reap a rich
reward. He read a report of his labors to
the society, which was just such a docu-
ment as you would expect from a_ plain
honest man. It was full of truth, so kind-
ly t that none could be angry, even
Lol it cut them in pieces.

I found some noble men in that county,
where lives one of those loco foco, hypo-
critical would-be democrat’s, who voted to
censure Hon. J. Q. Adams and Hon. J.
R. Giddings, for attempting to do their du-
ty. I hope there will be sufficient regard
for common humanity and decency in that
Co. at the next congressional election to
leave that honorable despiser of the poor
at home. If he has any sense of shame,
he never will show himself at the north
again. Such a man would do better, I

think to turn negro driver and drive him-:

self to Texas, where he may find a country
more congenial to him, than I trust Scho-
harie will be at the next election.

Yours, A. BROWN.

 

Special Meeting of Schoharie Co. A. S.
Society.
The meeting was called to order by the
President and opened by prayer.
A Business Committee consisting of A.
Brown, B. Shaw, Judge Holliday and Rev.
E. G. Johnson was appointed. The fol-

lowing resolutions were freely discussed |

and unanimously adopted.

1. Resolved, That the Schoharie Co. A.
S. Society become auxiliary to the East-
ern N. Y. A. S. Society.

2. Resolved, That slavery under all cir-
cumstances is not only sinful, but a gross
immorality and ought to be immediately
abandoned.

3. Resolred, That we believe it to be
the duty of al! persons to labor in all suita-
ble ways to effect the immediate abolition
of slavery.

4. Resolved, That efforts to secure the
election of rulers who will use their of-
ficial influence to overthrow slavery are
among the most efficient means to advance
the anti-slavery cause, and a proof of our
sincerity when we pray God to abolish
slavery.

5. Resolved, That those ministers who
oppose immediate emancipation or neglect
to rebuke the sin of slavery as they do oth-
er sins, dishonor their high calling and
greatly impair the confidence of the friends
of the slave in them as religious teachers

6. Rosolved, That we highly appreciate
the services of Hon. J. Q. Adams and Hon.
J. R. Giddings, in rebuking slavery and
in laboring to defeat the wiched plans of
slaveholders, to involve the nation in war
and bloodshed for the support of this sys-
tem of complicated wickedness.

7. Resolred, That we look with pity
and shame upon those Representatives in

Congress, (especially the representative |

from this district,) who have basely sold
the honor of the north, by voting to censure
Hon. J. Q. Adams and J. R. Giddings for
their fearless advocacy of principles and
measures, calculated to benefit and bless
the entire nation.

A. Brown, Cor. Sec'y of the E. N. Y.
Anti-Slavery Society, in the evening ad-
dressed the meeting by request of the So-
ciety.

the direction of the southwest to the northeast.

port, experienced the shock before they saw the
houses agitated, which seemed to indicate that the
shock came from the west.

distinctly felt, the first not so long as the second,

person strove to get out of the houses, and the
streets were filied With the affrighted population.

Prince would have been the theatre ot a disaster
similar to that of 1770, of which disastrous year
the remembrance was rushing into all minds.

house or a wall that has not suffered a little.—

front of the Senate House, where the arms of the
Republic are sculptured, is detached and broken.

day, there were other shocks. Mass was inter-
rupted, and the persons present ran hither and
thither, while many women fainted.

Although money is generally very abundant, a
great and sudden pressure was felt in the market
on the Hith and [Sth May. Tt was ascribed to va-
rious causes. ‘The more prevalent opinion tn
well informed quarters, and that which seems
most reconcileable with the circumstances of the
ease, is, that the scarcity of money, which so sud-
denly sprung up on the Stock Exchange, was 0C-
casioned. by the operations of the great insurance
companies, Who were losers by the great fire at
Hamburg. ‘Vhese corporations have always a
considerable amount of their assets invested at
call or on short loans, to meet emergencies, and
it is supposed that they have felt it expedient to
call up a portion of their money so lent to remit

With their roguish eyes, as if to see
What nature is about.

For their wooing time has come;

As they build their summer home.
Tis a pleasant thing to look upon

The giadness of the earth,

STANLY AND WISE,

The congressional bullies, who have so long
outraged common decency and parliamentary
decorum, on the floor of the H. of R., have trans-
ferred their brawls to a more appropriate field —
the race-course and the public highway. ‘The
latest collision between this “noble pair,” took
place over a mud-puddle. = The circumstances
are thus narrated by the Washington correspon-
dent of the N. Y. American :

Washington, May 8.

More cause of quarrel in the case of Stanty and
Wise. Yesterday both went to the race-course,
and at the close of the races it happened, very
unfortunately, that both of them mounted their
horses to return at the same moment, and near the
same place. Starting off together, before they
could separate to find more congenial company,
a large puddle in the middle of the road compel-
led them to approximate, just after a carriage had
passed between them, at which Stanly’s horse, a
very clumsy, awkward draught horse, suddenly
shied, before his rider could check him, and ran
against Wise’s horse, su that the legs of both the
riders were brought in collision, and thrown out
of the stirrup on that side.
Stanly’s horse shot ahead, but was checked by
his rider, who was just turning to apologize to
Wise for the unintentional collision, when he re-
ceived a blow on the right side of his head just
above the temple, from Wise, who struck him
from behind, with a heavy lead ball mounted on
the end of a rattan,—a very fashionable weapon
bere. For a few moments, Stanly was so stunned
as to be almost blinded, and he with difficulty re-
covered his senses, and then but imperfectly.—
He had no weapon whatever, not even a riding
whip or stick, though it is evident that Wise came
prepared to take advantage of any convenient op-
portunity fur an assault.
Stanly, partially recovering his senses, said,
“You have done a cowardly act, in striking me
a blow from behind my back while I was unarm-
ed. ‘The collision of our horses was unintention-
al on my part, and I was about to say so to you
when you assaulted me.” Wise answered, “I
called you a coward the other day in the House,
and now I have struck you. If you can put up
with that, do so.” ‘The rush of a crowd of peo-
ple upon thei prevented any bluws from passing,
which would have been difficult even without any
interference, as both of them were on horseback.
Wise evidently has been determined to force a
challenge from Stanly, all this week; and he has
probably succeeded. It is now generally believ-
ed that murder will come ot it, in the usual forms
of “chivally.”
The facts in the case, T have from the testimo-
ny of a gentleman who was approaching at the
moment to converse with Wise. The statement
may be depended on.

Prof. Eaton, whose death is here announced, was
born at New Concord, Ct., May 17th, 1776, where
he continued to reside until 1790 when he came
to Duanesburgh, Schenectady county,as an appren-
tice to Mr. Russell Bebce a blacksmith. In Sep-
tember 1791 he returned home to New Concord,
and commenced his studiea with Richard C. Eve-
rett, of N. Britain. Daniel Cady, eag., of Johns-
town, Professor Eaton’s senior by three years, was
a pupil of Mr. Everett's at the same time. He
studied and taught school by turns from this period
up to 1796, when he entered Williams’ College,
and where he graduated in 1799, After gradua-
ting he commenced the study of law, with Alex-
ander Hamilton, in New-York, and was admitted
to practice, in due course. Svon after his admis-
sion as an attorney he married a sister of Mr. Ca-
dy. He subsequently abandoned his profession
and until the year 1815 or 1816, was engaged as
agent for the Livingston estates in Columbia,
Greene and Schoharie counties, and as a Jand sur-
veyor generally. About this time, himself in
conjunction with his father, purchased a tract of
land in Greene county. The title of their pur-
chase proved cefective; an ejectment was com-
mencei against him, and to sustain himself in the
title, he resorted to means which ended unfortu-
tunately for his personal reputation. In 1818 he
went to reside at Troy, where he has continued
to reside since.

‘The first work he published, was in 1800 and
was entitled, ‘« Art without Science, or Mennsra-

this work was prepared when he was only 17, but
he could find no one to publish it, and had not the
means to do it himself. About 1817 he publish-
eda work on Mechanical and Experimental Phil-
osophy, under the title of ‘« Webster's Philoso-
phy.” The succeeding year he published the first
American work on Geology, entitled ‘ An Index
to the Geology of the Northern States of America.”
He had lectured on this subject at Williams Col-
lege the previous year. .In 1818, on the invita-

the Legistature. In !820 he was employed by

RESOLPTIONS OF THE CHURCH IN
CORNNISH.

Ata meeting of the Baptist Curch in
Cornish, holden Dec. 18, 1841, the fol-
lowing preamble and resolutions were
adopted, and at a subsequent meeting it
was voted that they be signed by the clerk,
and sent to the editor of the New-Hamp-
shire Baptist Register for publication.

Whereas slavery as it exists in the south-
ern States has been long defended and
practised by christian by christian church-
es which have been fellowshiped as such
by this church; and whereas it is the duty
of all Christians to publicly renounce all

‘connection with moral evil, and to do all

in their power to remove it from the
world—

Therefore, 1. Resolved, That to hold a
fellow-being as a slave, under all possible
circuinstances, is a palpable and enormous
violation of the law and gospel of God,
and subversive of every interest, temporal
and eternal, for which Jesus Christ died,
and God governs the world.

2. Resolved, That, entertaining these
sentiments, it is our solemn duty to with-
draw all donominational and christian
fellowship from all churches and individu-
als holding slaves, or defending the prac-
tice; and we hereby exclude them from
our pulpit, our communion and member-
ship.

3. Resolved, That to receive a member
by letter from a slaveholding church, with-
out confession and renunciation of the sin,
as to recommend a member to such a
church, would involve fellowship with
slavery, and, in our view, be totally in-
consistent with gospel principles and puri-
ty.

4, Resolved, That while the northern
and southern churches have hitherto fel-
lowshiped slavery, for professed Christians
to be silent and inactive on the subject
while our brethern for whom Jesus Christ
died are deprived of at RIGHTS, and re-
duced to all the liabilities and evils in-
volved in slavery, is highly crimnal, and
contrary to obvious and explicit duty en-
joined in Scripture,and palpably indicative
of gross lack of christian benevolence and
character.

5. Resolved, That it is our duty as a
church, ond as private members, to use
the same means for the removal of slave-
ry as for the removal of other enormous
moral evils, and to do all consistent in our
power to elevate the colored population in
our country to the highest religions and
civil privileges to which any Christian is
eligible.

ARAUNAH BURNAP, Clerk.

from Jamaica, and purchased a farm in

state of slavery on the one hand, and the
results of emancipation in the British co-
i lonies on the other, I feel it to be a duty
; 1 owe to God and to the slave, to publish
‘to the world my knowledge of the effects
iof slavery, and to bear testimony to the
happy results of emancipation in the West
Indies. AsI haveresided thirty-one years
| in Jamaica and the island of Old Provi-
‘dence, during which time I was a slave-
holder, it may be supposed that I can
give a pretty accurate statement of the
horrors of slavery. IT was considered by
my neighbors in Jamaica as too indulgent
to my slaves. ‘They said I spoiled them—-
made them lazy—and that thus they were
a bad example to other slaves around me.—-
Yet my treatment of them was harsh and
arbitrary in the extreme. | would often
flog men and women without mercy, and
without sutlicient cause. I thank God
that he has awakened in me a_ sense ot
my guilt in treating my fellow men worse
than the beasts of burthen. I have seen
enough of slavery to convince me that it is
a system that every Christian should shud-
der at, and look upon as revolting to hu-
manity, aud contrary to the blessed pre-
cepts of our Lord Jesus Christ, viz., “what-
soever ye would that men should do to
you, do ye even so to them.”

What man or woman in this world
would prefer a state of bondage to that of
freedom? Surely not an individual of
this free and enlightened republic, where
all pride themselves on their rights and
privileges, and in their enjoyment of in-
stitutions under that great charter which
declares that all men are created free and
equal. | would ask if it is consistent
with reason and justice, that because a
man’s skin is black, he should be preclu-
ded from the rights to which he is enti-
led by the Declaration of Independence ¢

] can assert, without the fear of contra-
diction, that emancipation in the Island of
Jamaica has been a blessing to all classes
of its inhabitants, and has had the eftect
of intluencing the emancipated to be in-
| dustrious, orderly, and useful members of
| society. So faras my knowledge goes.
this is the case in all the British Colonies,

Great Britain and Texas.

The long pending treaties between
(ireat Britain and Texas, were ratitied on
the 28th ult. They consist of a treaty of
amity, navigation and commerce—a treaty
undertaking mediation by Great Britain,
between the republics of Mexico and Tex-
as—and a treaty granting reciprocal right
of search for the suppression of the Afri-
ean slave trade.

In the treaty of meditation, Texas en-
gages to give Great Britain one million
pounds sterling, if by her mediation, an
unlimited truce shall be established with
Mexico within thirty days after the latter
power is informed of the treaty, and also
a permanent peace established within six
